abstract: This work discusses various optimization techniques which were proposed in models for controlling arm movements. In particular, the minimum-muscle-tension-change model is investigated. A dynamic simulator of the monkey's arm, including seventeen single and double joint muscles, is utilized to generate horizontal hand movements. The hand trajectories produced by this algorithm are discussed.
originalAbstract: This work discusses various optimization techniques which were proposed in models for controlling arm movements. In particular, the minimum-muscle-tension-change model is investigated. A dynamic simulator of the monkey's arm, including seventeen single and double joint muscles, is utilized to generate horizontal hand movements. The hand trajectories produced by this algorithm are discussed.

paragraphs: This paper examines optimization-based explanations of arm movement, focusing on the minimum-muscle-tension-change model. The model identifies changes in muscle tension as the quantity to minimize when generating a movement. The study places that proposal alongside other optimization techniques used in arm-control models, asking what movement behavior follows from this particular choice of objective.

The authors use a dynamic simulator of a monkey’s arm containing seventeen muscles. These include muscles acting across one joint and muscles acting across two joints. The simulator generates horizontal hand movements, linking a muscle-level optimization criterion to the resulting motion of the hand through an explicit model of arm dynamics.

The paper discusses the hand trajectories produced by the algorithm. These trajectories are the observable consequences through which the proposed control objective is investigated. The study’s contribution is to make the movement criterion concrete in a multi-muscle simulation: minimizing changes in muscle tension must produce a path through the coordinated action of muscles and joints, rather than specifying the hand path directly.
summary.tldr: A seventeen-muscle monkey-arm simulation explores the hand trajectories generated by minimizing changes in muscle tension.

title: Simulation of Optimal Movements Using the Minimum-Muscle-Tension-Change Model

abstract: \Vhenever an agent learns to control an unknown environment, two oppos(cid:173) ing principles have to be combined, namely: exploration (long-term opti(cid:173) mization) and exploitation (short-term optimization). Many real-valued connectionist approaches to learning control realize exploration by ran(cid:173) domness in action selection. This might be disadvantageous when costs are assigned to "negative experiences" . The basic idea presented in this paper is to make an agent explore unknown regions in a more directed manner. This is achieved by a so-called competence map, which is trained to predict the controller's accuracy, and is used for guiding exploration. Based on this, a bistable system enables smoothly switching attention between two behaviors - exploration and exploitation - depending on ex(cid:173) pected costs and knowledge gain. The appropriateness of this method is demonstrated by a simple robot navigation task.

paragraphs: An agent learning to control an unfamiliar environment must balance gathering knowledge with using what it already knows. Random action selection can encourage exploration, but it can also produce costly negative experiences. This paper proposes directing exploration using an estimate of the controller's own competence.

The central component is a competence map trained to predict how accurately the controller will behave. That prediction provides guidance about unfamiliar regions and helps make exploration purposeful. The agent can consider the prospect of learning alongside the expected cost of acting, rather than relying solely on randomness to encounter informative situations.

A bistable system coordinates exploration and exploitation, allowing attention to switch smoothly between the two behaviors according to expected costs and knowledge gain. The authors demonstrate the approach on a simple robot navigation task. The stated result supports using predicted controller accuracy to guide exploratory behavior in that setting, linking decisions about where to learn with decisions about how to act.
summary.tldr: A learned competence map guides exploration by balancing expected knowledge gain against the costs of uncertain actions.

title: Active Exploration in Dynamic Environments

abstract: Previously, we have introduced the idea of neural network transfer, where learning on a target problem is sped up by using the weights obtained from a network trained for a related source task. Here, we present a new algorithm. called Discriminability-Based Transfer (DBT), which uses an information measure to estimate the utility of hyperplanes defined by source weights in the target network, and rescales transferred weight magnitudes accordingly. Several experiments demonstrate that target networks initialized via DBT learn significantly faster than networks initialized randomly.

Here, we present a new algorithm. called Discriminability-Based Transfer (DBT), which uses an information measure to estimate the utility of hyperplanes defined by source weights in the target network, and rescales transferred weight magnitudes accordingly. Several experiments demonstrate that target networks initialized via DBT learn significantly faster than networks initialized randomly.

paragraphs: This paper addresses how training on one task can speed up learning on a related task. The starting point is neural network transfer: weights learned by a source network are used to initialize a target network. The new question is how to adjust those transferred weights according to their usefulness for the target problem.

The proposed algorithm, Discriminability-Based Transfer, uses an information measure to assess the utility of hyperplanes defined by the source weights. These hyperplanes describe divisions of the input space associated with those weights. The algorithm then rescales transferred weight magnitudes based on that assessment, making initialization responsive to the target task rather than simply copying the source weights unchanged.

Across several experiments, networks initialized with this procedure learn significantly faster than networks initialized randomly. The finding supports the value of evaluating transferred structure before using it to begin training. The contribution combines reuse of previously learned weights with a target-oriented estimate of how strongly those weights should influence the new network.
summary.tldr: Discriminability-Based Transfer rescales source-network weights according to their target-task usefulness and speeds learning relative to random initialization.

title: Discriminability-Based Transfer between Neural Networks

abstract: The vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) is a compensatory eye movement that stabilizes images on the retina during head turns. Its magnitude, or gain, can be modified by visual experience during head movements. Possible learning mechanisms for this adaptation have been explored in a model of the oculomotor system based on anatomical and physiological con(cid:173) straints. The local correlational learning rules in our model reproduce the adaptation and behavior of the VOR under certain parameter conditions. From these conditions, predictions for the time course of adaptation at the learning sites are made.

paragraphs: The vestibulo-ocular reflex moves the eyes to compensate for head movement, helping keep images stable on the retina. Its gain describes the magnitude of that compensation, and visual experience during head movement can change it. This paper asks what learning mechanisms could account for that adjustment within the biological eye movement system.

The authors investigate local correlational learning rules in a model constrained by anatomy and physiology. These rules make adaptation depend on correlations available at the learning sites. The model therefore links a proposed mechanism for local change to the larger behavior of the reflex, while retaining constraints drawn from the organization of the system.

Under particular parameter conditions, the rules reproduce the reflex's behavior and adaptation. Those conditions also yield predictions about how adaptation should unfold over time at the learning sites. The result is conditional on the model parameters, and its value includes both reproducing behavior and deriving a temporal prediction from the mechanism responsible for that behavior.
summary.tldr: A biologically constrained model shows how local correlational learning can reproduce vestibulo-ocular reflex adaptation under specific parameter conditions.

title: Biologically Plausible Local Learning Rules for the Adaptation of the Vestibulo-Ocular Reflex

abstract: In many vision based tasks, the ability to focus attention on the important portions of a scene is crucial for good performance on the tasks. In this paper we present a simple method of achieving spatial selective attention through the use of a saliency map. The saliency map indicates which regions of the input retina are important for performing the task. The saliency map is cre(cid:173) ated through predictive auto-encoding. The performance of this method is demonstrated on two simple tasks which have multiple very strong distract(cid:173) ing features in the input retina. Architectural extensions and application directions for this model are presented.

paragraphs: The paper presents a method for directing visual attention toward regions that matter for a task. Its central representation is a saliency map over the input retina. Each region's importance is understood in relation to the task being performed, making spatial selection part of how the system handles visual information.

The map is created through predictive auto-encoding. This connects the learned predictive representation to the decision about where attention should be focused. The map supplies a spatial indication of useful input, allowing the attention mechanism to identify relevant portions of a scene even when other features compete strongly for attention.

The authors demonstrate the method on two simple tasks containing multiple strong distracting features. These demonstrations address whether the attention approach can function in the presence of conspicuous competing information. The paper also presents possible architectural extensions and application directions. Its stated contribution is an implemented, simple mechanism for task-relevant spatial attention, supported by initial demonstrations in deliberately distracting visual inputs.
summary.tldr: Predictive auto-encoding creates a task-relevant saliency map that guides visual attention in demonstrations with strong distractors.

title: Using a Saliency Map for Active Spatial Selective Attention: Implementation & Initial Results

abstract: We investigate the computational power of a formal model for net(cid:173) works of spiking neurons, both for the assumption of an unlimited timing precision, and for the case of a limited timing precision. We also prove upper and lower bounds for the number of examples that are needed to train such networks. 1 Introduction and Basic Definitions There exists substantial evidence that timing phenomena such as temporal differ(cid:173) ences between spikes and frequencies of oscillating subsystems are integral parts of various information processing mechanisms in biological neural systems (for a survey and references see e.g. Abeles, 1991; Churchland and Sejnowski, 1992; Aert(cid:173) sen, 1993). Some aspects of these models have also been studied analytically, but almost nothing is known about their computational complexity (see Judd and Aihara, 1993, for some first results in this direction). paragraphs: The paper investigates what networks of spiking neurons can compute and how much training data they require. Its starting point is that the timing of neural events can participate in information processing. The authors introduce a formal network model intended to capture important timing phenomena, including synaptic modulation, so these questions can be studied mathematically.

A central distinction is between unlimited and limited timing precision. Unlimited precision allows arbitrarily fine distinctions in event times, whereas limited precision restricts those distinctions. Analyzing both cases makes the timing assumption explicit when assessing computational power, rather than treating precision as an unspecified property of the model.

The authors prove upper and lower bounds on computational power and on the number of examples needed for training. These results address both capability and learning complexity within the formal framework. The contribution is an analytical account of spiking computation that places mathematical bounds on what timing-based networks can achieve and what their learning requirements can be.
summary.tldr: A formal spiking-network model yields bounds on computational power and training-example requirements under different timing-precision assumptions.

title: On the Computational Complexity of Networks of Spiking Neurons

abstract: A significant limitation of neural networks is that the represen(cid:173) tations they learn are usually incomprehensible to humans. We present a novel algorithm , TREPAN, for extracting comprehensible, symbolic representations from trained neural networks. Our algo(cid:173) rithm uses queries to induce a decision tree that approximates the concept represented by a given network. Our experiments demon(cid:173) strate that TREPAN is able to produce decision trees that maintain a high level of fidelity to their respective networks while being com(cid:173) prehensible and accurate. Unlike previous work in this area, our algorithm is general in its applicability and scales well to large net(cid:173) works and problems with high-dimensional input spaces.

paragraphs: Neural networks can learn useful decision rules that are difficult for people to understand. This paper introduces TREPAN, an algorithm that turns the behavior of a trained network into a symbolic decision tree. The goal is to give people a comprehensible representation of the concept the network has learned.

TREPAN uses queries to construct a tree that approximates the network. The trained network supplies the behavior to be represented, while the tree provides an explicit structure for expressing decisions. This creates two relevant standards of success: the tree should agree with its source network and should remain accurate as a predictor in its own right.

The experiments report trees that combine strong agreement with their networks, comprehensibility, and predictive accuracy. The authors also report broad applicability and good scaling to large networks and high-dimensional inputs. These findings support extracting a readable model after neural training. The result is an approximation of the learned concept, with fidelity to the original network serving as a central measure of its usefulness.
summary.tldr: TREPAN queries trained neural networks to construct readable decision trees that closely reproduce their predictions.

title: Extracting Tree-Structured Representations of Trained Networks

abstract: We train recurrent networks to control chemotaxis in a computer model of the nematode C. elegans. The model presented is based closely on the body mechanics, behavioral analyses, neuroanatomy and neurophysiology of C. elegans, each imposing constraints rel(cid:173) evant for information processing. Simulated worms moving au(cid:173) tonomously in simulated chemical environments display a variety of chemotaxis strategies similar to those of biological worms.

Simulated worms moving au(cid:173) tonomously in simulated chemical environments display a variety of chemotaxis strategies similar to those of biological worms.

paragraphs: This paper trains recurrent neural networks to control chemotaxis in a simulated C. elegans worm. Chemotaxis is movement guided by the chemical environment. The task places the network inside a model of an acting organism, so its outputs must support movement through a changing sequence of sensory situations.

The simulation is closely informed by the worm's body mechanics, observed behavior, neural anatomy, and neural physiology. Each source of biological information constrains the model's information processing. This links the controller to the physical and neural organization of the animal rather than treating navigation as a decision problem detached from the body.

The simulated worms move autonomously in simulated chemical environments and develop several strategies resembling those of biological worms. The result shows that recurrent controllers operating within these biological constraints can produce relevant navigation behavior. Its explanatory value lies in connecting neural processing, body mechanics, and environmental interaction within a single model that generates behavior.
summary.tldr: Biologically constrained recurrent networks guide simulated C. elegans through chemical environments using strategies resembling those of real worms.

title: Neural Network Models of Chemotaxis in the Nematode Caenorhabditis Elegans

abstract: We have investigated the possibility that rapid processing in the visual system could be achieved by using the order of firing in different neurones as a code, rather than more conventional firing rate schemes. Using SPIKENET, a neural net simulator based on integrate-and-fire neurones and in which neurones in the input layer function as analog(cid:173) to-delay converters, we have modeled the initial stages of visual processing. Initial results are extremely promising. Even with activity in retinal output cells limited to one spike per neuron per image (effectively ruling out any form of rate coding), sophisticated processing based on asynchronous activation was nonetheless possible.

Using SPIKENET, a neural net simulator based on integrate-and-fire neurones and in which neurones in the input layer function as analog(cid:173) to-delay converters, we have modeled the initial stages of visual processing. Initial results are extremely promising. Even with activity in retinal output cells limited to one spike per neuron per image (effectively ruling out any form of rate coding), sophisticated processing based on asynchronous activation was nonetheless possible.

paragraphs: Rapid visual processing raises a question about how neurons convey information before many spikes have occurred. This paper investigates a code based on the order in which different neurons fire. In that scheme, relative timing across cells carries information that would otherwise need to be represented through firing rates.

The authors model early visual processing with SPIKENET, a simulator built from integrate-and-fire neurons. Input neurons convert analog values into firing delays, making stimulus information available through the sequence of activations. The network can then process those asynchronous events as they arrive, with firing order forming part of the representation.

In the reported initial results, retinal output cells were limited to one spike per neuron for each image. Despite this restriction, sophisticated processing remained possible. Because repeated firing was unavailable, the result supports the computational usefulness of timing across neurons. It establishes a promising simulated example of visual processing under a tightly constrained spike budget, with temporal order doing substantive work.
summary.tldr: A spiking visual simulation performs sophisticated processing using firing order even when each retinal output neuron emits only one spike per image.

title: Rapid Visual Processing using Spike Asynchrony

abstract: In this paper, we discuss regularisation in online/sequential learn(cid:173) ing algorithms. In environments where data arrives sequentially, techniques such as cross-validation to achieve regularisation or model selection are not possible. Further, bootstrapping to de(cid:173) termine a confidence level is not practical. To surmount these problems, a minimum variance estimation approach that makes use of the extended Kalman algorithm for training multi-layer percep(cid:173) trons is employed. The novel contribution of this paper is to show the theoretical links between extended Kalman filtering, Sutton's variable learning rate algorithms and Mackay's Bayesian estima(cid:173) tion framework. In doing so, we propose algorithms to overcome the need for heuristic choices of the initial conditions and noise covariance matrices in the Kalman approach.

To surmount these problems, a minimum variance estimation approach that makes use of the extended Kalman algorithm for training multi-layer percep(cid:173) trons is employed. paragraphs: The paper addresses regularization when training data arrive sequentially. In the setting described, cross-validation is unavailable for regularization or model selection, and bootstrapping is impractical for estimating confidence. This creates a need for training methods that manage estimation uncertainty within the sequential learning process itself.

The authors use a minimum-variance estimation approach based on the extended Kalman algorithm to train multilayer perceptrons. Their main theoretical contribution is to connect this approach with variable learning-rate algorithms and a Bayesian estimation framework. These links bring together methods that describe adaptation from different perspectives: estimation uncertainty, changing update rates, and probabilistic learning.

Using these connections, the paper proposes algorithms intended to remove heuristic choices of initial conditions and noise covariance matrices in Kalman-based training. Those choices determine how the estimation process starts and represents uncertainty. The contribution is therefore both an explanation of relationships among learning frameworks and a route toward more principled configuration of sequential neural-network training.
summary.tldr: Links between Kalman filtering, adaptive learning rates, and Bayesian estimation support more principled regularization in sequential learning.

title: Regularisation in Sequential Learning Algorithms

abstract: Tangential hand velocity proﬁles of rapid human arm movements of- ten appear as sequences of several bell-shaped acceleration-deceleration phases called submovements or movement units. This suggests how the nervous system might efﬁciently control a motor plant in the presence of noise and feedback delay. Another critical observation is that stochastic- ity in a motor control problem makes the optimal control policy essen- tially different from the optimal control policy for the deterministic case. We use a simpliﬁed dynamic model of an arm and address rapid aimed arm movements. We use reinforcement learning as a tool to approximate the optimal policy in the presence of noise and feedback delay. Using a simpliﬁed model we show that multiple submovements emerge as an optimal policy in the presence of noise and feedback delay. The optimal policy in this situation is to drive the arm’s end point close to the target by one fast submovement and then apply a few slow submovements to accu- rately drive the arm’s end point into the target region. In our simulations, the controller sometimes generates corrective submovements before the initial fast submovement is completed, much like the predictive correc- tions observed in a number of psychophysical experiments.

paragraphs: Rapid human arm movements often contain several bell-shaped phases of speeding up and slowing down. The paper asks whether these submovements can arise from effective control when movements are noisy and feedback arrives late. It emphasizes that introducing randomness can change the optimal control policy fundamentally relative to a deterministic problem.

The authors use a simplified dynamic arm model and reinforcement learning to approximate an optimal policy for rapid aimed movements. In this setting, multiple submovements emerge as optimal behavior under noise and feedback delay. The policy first moves the arm's endpoint quickly toward the target, then uses several slower movements to bring it accurately into the target region.

In some simulations, corrective movements begin before the initial fast movement has finished. The authors relate this behavior to predictive corrections reported in psychophysical experiments. The result offers a computational explanation for movement segmentation: within the simplified model, a sequence of movement units can follow from the demands of noisy, delayed control, including corrections that overlap the initial motion.
summary.tldr: In a simplified arm model, noise and delayed feedback make fast initial movements followed by slower corrections emerge as optimal control.

title: The Emergence of Multiple Movement Units in the Presence of Noise and Feedback Delay

abstract: We present a probabilistic generative model for timing deviations in expressive music. performance. The structure of the proposed model is equivalent to a switching state space model. We formu(cid:173) late two well known music recognition problems, namely tempo tracking and automatic transcription (rhythm quantization) as fil(cid:173) tering and maximum a posteriori (MAP) state estimation tasks. The inferences are carried out using sequential Monte Carlo in(cid:173) tegration (particle filtering) techniques. For this purpose, we have derived a novel Viterbi algorithm for Rao-Blackwellized particle fil(cid:173) ters, where a subset of the hidden variables is integrated out. The resulting model is suitable for realtime tempo tracking and tran(cid:173) scription and hence useful in a number of music applications such as adaptive automatic accompaniment and score typesetting.

paragraphs: The paper models timing deviations in expressive musical performances using a probabilistic generative model. Its structure is equivalent to a switching state-space model, providing a shared framework for tempo tracking and rhythm quantization. These tasks concern following the changing performance tempo and recovering a rhythmic transcription from the performed timing.

The authors formulate the recognition problems as filtering and maximum a posteriori state estimation. Inference uses sequential Monte Carlo methods, also called particle filtering. They additionally derive a Viterbi algorithm for Rao-Blackwellized particle filters, in which some hidden variables are integrated out. This combines particle-based inference with a method for identifying a preferred hidden-state sequence.

The resulting model is described as suitable for real-time tempo tracking and transcription. The authors identify adaptive automatic accompaniment and score typesetting as applications that could use these capabilities. The contribution brings expressive timing, tempo estimation, and rhythmic transcription into one probabilistic treatment, together with an inference method suited to processing the musical performance as it unfolds.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic timing model and particle-filter inference support real-time tempo tracking and rhythm transcription.

title: Tempo tracking and rhythm quantization by sequential Monte Carlo

abstract: With the optimization of pattern discrimination as a goal, graph partitioning approaches often lack the capability to integrate prior knowledge to guide grouping. In this paper, we consider priors from unitary generative models, partially labeled data and spatial attention. These priors are modelled as constraints in the solution space. By imposing uniformity condition on the constraints, we restrict the feasible space to one of smooth solutions. A subspace projection method is developed to solve this constrained eigenprob(cid:173) lema We demonstrate that simple priors can greatly improve image segmentation results.

A subspace projection method is developed to solve this constrained eigenprob(cid:173) lema We demonstrate that simple priors can greatly improve image segmentation results.

paragraphs: The paper addresses how prior knowledge can guide grouping in graph-based image segmentation. Graph partitioning approaches aimed at separating patterns often lack a way to incorporate such knowledge. The authors consider three sources of guidance: unitary generative models, partially labeled data, and spatial attention. These provide information that can influence which groupings should be considered acceptable.

The method expresses those priors as constraints on the space of possible solutions. It then imposes a uniformity condition on the constraints, restricting the feasible space to smooth solutions. This turns prior knowledge into a mathematical part of the grouping problem, so the resulting segmentation is determined jointly by the partitioning objective and the imposed guidance.

To solve the resulting constrained eigenproblem, the authors develop a subspace projection method. Their demonstrations show that even simple priors can greatly improve image segmentation results. The contribution is therefore both a formulation and a solution method: it explains how to introduce guidance into graph partitioning and reports that this guidance can materially improve the resulting image groups.
summary.tldr: Encoding prior knowledge as constraints in graph partitioning can greatly improve image segmentation.

title: Grouping with Bias

abstract: Theories of visual attention commonly posit that early parallel processes extract con- spicuous features such as color contrast and motion from the visual field. These features are then combined into a saliency map, and attention is directed to the most salient regions first. Top-down attentional control is achieved by modulating the contribution of different feature types to the saliency map. A key source of data concerning attentional control comes from behavioral studies in which the effect of recent experience is exam- ined as individuals repeatedly perform a perceptual discrimination task (e.g., “what shape is the odd-colored object?”). The robust finding is that repetition of features of recent trials (e.g., target color) facilitates performance. We view this facilitation as an adaptation to the statistical structure of the environment. We propose a probabilistic model of the environment that is updated after each trial. Under the assumption that attentional control operates so as to make performance more efficient for more likely environmental states, we obtain parsimonious explanations for data from four different experiments. Further, our model provides a rational explanation for why the influence of past experience on attentional control is short lived.

Under the assumption that attentional control operates so as to make performance more efficient for more likely environmental states, we obtain parsimonious explanations for data from four different experiments. Further, our model provides a rational explanation for why the influence of past experience on attentional control is short lived.

paragraphs: People often perform a visual discrimination task more easily when relevant features repeat from recent trials. This paper explains that facilitation as adaptation to the statistical structure of the environment. It places the effect within an account of attention in which different visual features contribute to a saliency map that guides selection.

The authors propose a probabilistic model of the environment that is updated after every trial. Their key assumption is that attentional control makes performance more efficient for environmental states that are more likely. Recent experience therefore influences attention by changing what the model expects to encounter, rather than serving only as a record of earlier stimuli.

Under this assumption, the model provides compact explanations for results from four experiments. It also explains why the influence of past experience fades quickly. The contribution is a rational account linking short-lived attentional adjustments to environmental expectations. Its explanatory force depends on the stated relationship between probability and efficient performance, rather than establishing that every attentional effect follows from this principle.
summary.tldr: A trial-updated probabilistic model explains repetition benefits and their short duration as adaptive control of visual attention.

title: Top-Down Control of Visual Attention: A Rational Account

abstract: We describe a neuromorphic chip that uses binary synapses with spike timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) to learn stimulated patterns of activ- ity and to compensate for variability in excitability. Speciﬁcally, STDP preferentially potentiates (turns on) synapses that project from excitable neurons, which spike early, to lethargic neurons, which spike late. The additional excitatory synaptic current makes lethargic neurons spike ear- lier, thereby causing neurons that belong to the same pattern to spike in synchrony. Once learned, an entire pattern can be recalled by stimulating a subset. 1 Variability in Neural Systems Evidence suggests precise spike timing is important in neural coding, speciﬁcally, in the hippocampus. The hippocampus uses timing in the spike activity of place cells (in addition to rate) to encode location in space [1]. Place cells employ a phase code: the timing at which a neuron spikes relative to the phase of the inhibitory theta rhythm (5-12Hz) conveys information. As an animal approaches a place cell’s preferred location, the place cell not only increases its spike rate, but also spikes at earlier phases in the theta cycle. To implement a phase code, the theta rhythm is thought to prevent spiking until the input synaptic current exceeds the sum of the neuron threshold and the decreasing inhibition on the downward phase of the cycle [2]. However, even with identical inputs and common theta inhibition, neurons do not spike in synchrony. Variability in excitability spreads the activity in phase. Lethargic neurons (such as those with high thresholds) spike late in the theta cycle, since their input exceeds the sum of the neuron threshold and theta inhibition only after the theta inhibition has had time to decrease. Conversely, excitable neurons (such as those with low thresholds) spike early in the theta cycle. Consequently, variability in excitability translates into variability in timing. We hypothesize that the hippocampus achieves its precise spike timing (about 10ms) through plasticity enhanced phase-coding (PEP). paragraphs: The paper describes a neuromorphic chip that learns patterns of neural activity using binary synapses and spike-timing-dependent plasticity. A practical challenge is that neurons differ in excitability: some spike early, while others respond later even under comparable stimulation. The chip uses learning to compensate for these timing differences.

The learning rule preferentially switches on synapses from early-spiking, more excitable neurons to late-spiking, less excitable neurons. The resulting additional excitatory current helps the slower neurons fire earlier. Through this adjustment, neurons belonging to the same learned pattern come to spike together, making synchronization part of the stored pattern.

After learning, stimulating only part of a pattern can recall the whole pattern. The work therefore links timing correction with associative recall in hardware. It also motivates a hypothesis that plasticity could help the hippocampus maintain precise timing despite neuronal variability. The chip demonstrates the proposed compensation principle, while the account of hippocampal timing is presented as a biological hypothesis rather than an established explanation.
summary.tldr: A neuromorphic chip uses spike timing to compensate for excitability differences, synchronize learned patterns, and recall them from partial stimulation.

title: Learning in Silicon: Timing is Everything

abstract: It has been established that the second-order stochastic gradient descent (2SGD) method can potentially achieve generalization performance as well as empirical optimum in a single pass (i.e., epoch) through the training examples. However, 2SGD requires computing the inverse of the Hessian matrix of the loss function, which is prohibitively expensive. This paper presents Periodic Step-size Adaptation (PSA), which approximates the Jacobian matrix of the mapping function and explores a linear relation between the Jacobian and Hessian to approximate the Hessian periodically and achieve near-optimal results in experiments on a wide variety of models and tasks.
originalAbstract: It has been established that the second-order stochastic gradient descent (2SGD) method can potentially achieve generalization performance as well as empirical optimum in a single pass (i.e., epoch) through the training examples. However, 2SGD requires computing the inverse of the Hessian matrix of the loss function, which is prohibitively expensive. This paper presents Periodic Step-size Adaptation (PSA), which approximates the Jacobian matrix of the mapping function and explores a linear relation between the Jacobian and Hessian to approximate the Hessian periodically and achieve near-optimal results in experiments on a wide variety of models and tasks.

paragraphs: The paper addresses learning effectively from a single pass through training examples. Second-order stochastic gradient descent can potentially achieve generalization performance comparable to the empirical optimum in that setting. Its practical obstacle is computing the inverse Hessian of the loss, a matrix calculation the authors describe as prohibitively expensive.

Periodic Step-size Adaptation seeks useful second-order information through an approximation. It estimates the Jacobian of a mapping function and uses a linear relationship between that Jacobian and the Hessian. The Hessian approximation is updated periodically, making the timing and construction of curvature information central to the approach.

Experiments across a wide variety of models and tasks report near-optimal results. These findings support the possibility of obtaining much of the benefit associated with second-order learning through periodic approximation. The contribution is a practical adaptation strategy for the single-pass setting; the reported experimental success does not turn the potential of second-order methods into an unconditional guarantee for every learning problem.
summary.tldr: Periodic Step-size Adaptation approximates Hessian information through a Jacobian relationship and achieves near-optimal single-pass results in experiments.

title: Periodic Step Size Adaptation for Single Pass On-line Learning

abstract: Training conditional maximum entropy models on massive data requires significant time and computational resources. In this paper, we investigate three common distributed training strategies: distributed gradient, majority voting ensembles, and parameter mixtures. We analyze the worst-case runtime and resource costs of each and present a theoretical foundation for the convergence of parameters under parameter mixtures, the most efficient strategy. We present large-scale experiments comparing the different strategies and demonstrate that parameter mixtures over independent models use fewer resources and achieve comparable loss as compared to standard approaches.
originalAbstract: Training conditional maximum entropy models on massive data requires significant time and computational resources. In this paper, we investigate three common distributed training strategies: distributed gradient, majority voting ensembles, and parameter mixtures. We analyze the worst-case runtime and resource costs of each and present a theoretical foundation for the convergence of parameters under parameter mixtures, the most efficient strategy. We present large-scale experiments comparing the different strategies and demonstrate that parameter mixtures over independent models use fewer resources and achieve comparable loss as compared to standard approaches.

paragraphs: Training conditional maximum entropy models on very large datasets can demand substantial computing time and resources. This paper studies how distributing the training work changes those costs. It compares three common strategies: distributing gradient computation, combining predictions through majority voting, and combining the parameters of independently trained models.

These strategies combine work at different levels. Distributed gradients contribute to optimization, voting combines model decisions, and parameter mixtures combine learned model parameters. The authors analyze worst-case runtime and resource requirements for all three approaches. They identify parameter mixtures as the most efficient strategy in this comparison and provide a theoretical foundation for convergence of the resulting parameters.

Large-scale experiments compare the approaches and show that mixtures of independent models use fewer resources while obtaining comparable loss to standard methods. The result matters because it connects computational savings with the quality of the trained model: efficiency is evaluated alongside loss. The paper thus supports parameter mixing as an effective distributed training strategy in the studied setting, with both a cost analysis and convergence theory behind the empirical comparison.
summary.tldr: Combining independently trained model parameters uses fewer resources while achieving comparable loss in large-scale conditional maximum entropy experiments.

title: Efficient Large-Scale Distributed Training of Conditional Maximum Entropy Models

abstract: Probabilistic grammars are generative statistical models that are useful for compositional and sequential structures. We present a framework, reminiscent of structural risk minimization, for empirical risk minimization of the parameters of a fixed probabilistic grammar using the log-loss. We derive sample complexity bounds in this framework that apply both to the supervised setting and the unsupervised setting.
originalAbstract: Probabilistic grammars are generative statistical models that are useful for compositional and sequential structures. We present a framework, reminiscent of structural risk minimization, for empirical risk minimization of the parameters of a fixed probabilistic grammar using the log-loss. We derive sample complexity bounds in this framework that apply both to the supervised setting and the unsupervised setting.

paragraphs: Probabilistic grammars describe how structured observations can be generated, making them useful for data with sequential or compositional organization. Learning such a model involves choosing parameters that determine the probabilities it assigns. This paper studies that learning problem for a fixed grammar, placing parameter estimation within a framework for empirical risk minimization.

The learning objective uses log-loss, which evaluates the probabilities the grammar assigns to observed data. The framework uses approximations of probabilistic grammars and resembles structural risk minimization, linking the learning procedure to questions of model complexity and statistical reliability. Its focus is the estimation of parameters within the specified grammar rather than the selection of a new grammatical structure.

The authors derive sample-complexity bounds for both supervised and unsupervised learning in this framework. Such bounds address how the amount of training data relates to the statistical demands of learning. Covering both settings gives the analysis relevance to different forms of available supervision and provides a theoretical basis for studying grammar estimation through empirical risk minimization.
summary.tldr: The paper gives a log-loss framework for learning fixed probabilistic grammars and derives sample-complexity bounds with and without supervision.

title: Empirical Risk Minimization with Approximations of Probabilistic Grammars

abstract: Several motor related Brain Computer Interfaces (BCIs) have been developed over the years that use activity decoded from the contralateral hemisphere to operate devices. Many recent studies have also talked about the importance of ipsilateral activity in planning of motor movements. For successful upper limb BCIs, it is important to decode finger movements from brain activity. This study uses ipsilateral cortical signals from humans (using ECoG) to decode finger movements. We demonstrate, for the first time, successful finger movement detection using machine learning algorithms. Our results show high decoding accuracies in all cases which are always above chance. We also show that significant accuracies can be achieved with the use of only a fraction of all the features recorded and that these core features also make sense physiologically. The results of this study have a great potential in the emerging world of motor neuroprosthetics and other BCIs.

paragraphs: This study investigates whether human finger movements can be detected using cortical signals from the hemisphere on the same side as the movement. These are ipsilateral signals. The question complements brain-computer interface approaches that decode activity from the opposite hemisphere and connects with evidence that ipsilateral activity contributes to planning movements.

The researchers use electrocorticography, or ECoG, recordings and machine learning algorithms to decode finger movements. They report successful detection, with high decoding accuracy above chance in every evaluated case. The authors present this as the first successful demonstration of finger movement detection in the ipsilateral ECoG setting they study.

The study also examines how much of the recorded feature information is needed. Significant decoding accuracy remains achievable using only a fraction of the features, and the selected core features have physiological meaning. This suggests that the useful signal can be concentrated in a smaller, interpretable subset of the recordings. The findings indicate potential for motor neuroprosthetics and other brain-computer interfaces, rather than establishing a completed device application.
summary.tldr: Machine learning detects finger movements from same-side cortical ECoG signals, including with a reduced set of physiologically meaningful features.

title: Decoding Ipsilateral Finger Movements from ECoG Signals in Humans

abstract: When stimulated with complex action potential sequences synapses exhibit spike timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) with attenuated and enhanced pre- and postsynaptic contributions to long-term synaptic modifications. In order to investigate the functional consequences of these contribution dynamics (CD) we propose a minimal model formulated in terms of differential equations. We find that our model reproduces a wide range of experimental results with a small number of biophysically interpretable parameters. The model allows to investigate the susceptibility of STDP to arbitrary time courses of pre- and postsynaptic activities, i.e. its nonlinear filter properties. We demonstrate this for the simple example of small periodic modulations of pre- and postsynaptic firing rates for which our model can be solved. It predicts synaptic strengthening for synchronous rate modulations. For low baseline rates modifications are dominant in the theta frequency range, a result which underlines the well known relevance of theta activities in hippocampus and cortex for learning. We also find emphasis of low baseline spike rates and suppression for high baseline rates. The latter suggests a mechanism of network activity regulation inherent in STDP. Furthermore, our novel formulation provides a general framework for investigating the joint dynamics of neuronal activity and the CD of STDP in both spike-based as well as rate-based neuronal network models.

paragraphs: Spike timing-dependent plasticity links changes in synaptic strength to neural activity timing. With complex spike sequences, the contributions of presynaptic and postsynaptic activity can themselves be weakened or enhanced. The paper models these changing contributions using a small system of differential equations with biophysically interpretable parameters.

The model reproduces a wide range of experimental findings and provides a way to study plasticity as a nonlinear filter of activity over time. For small periodic changes in firing rates, the authors can solve the model and examine its predictions. Synchronous rate changes produce strengthening, while at low baseline firing rates the strongest modifications occur in the theta frequency range.

The model also emphasizes low baseline spike rates and suppresses high ones. The latter finding suggests a possible mechanism for regulating network activity within plasticity itself. More broadly, the formulation provides a framework for studying interactions between neural activity and changing plasticity contributions in both spike-based and rate-based networks, connecting local synaptic dynamics with network-level modeling.
summary.tldr: A compact dynamical model treats synaptic plasticity as a nonlinear activity filter and predicts frequency- and baseline-dependent changes.

title: Spike timing-dependent plasticity as dynamic filter

abstract: We combine three important ideas present in previous work for building classi- ﬁers: the semi-supervised hypothesis (the input distribution contains information about the classiﬁer), the unsupervised manifold hypothesis (data density concen- trates near low-dimensional manifolds), and the manifold hypothesis for classiﬁ- cation (different classes correspond to disjoint manifolds separated by low den- sity). We exploit a novel algorithm for capturing manifold structure (high-order contractive auto-encoders) and we show how it builds a topological atlas of charts, each chart being characterized by the principal singular vectors of the Jacobian of a representation mapping. This representation learning algorithm can be stacked to yield a deep architecture, and we combine it with a domain knowledge-free version of the TangentProp algorithm to encourage the classiﬁer to be insensitive to local directions changes along the manifold. Record-breaking classiﬁcation results are obtained.
originalAbstract: We combine three important ideas present in previous work for building classi- ﬁers: the semi-supervised hypothesis (the input distribution contains information about the classiﬁer), the unsupervised manifold hypothesis (data density concen- trates near low-dimensional manifolds), and the manifold hypothesis for classiﬁ- cation (different classes correspond to disjoint manifolds separated by low den- sity). We exploit a novel algorithm for capturing manifold structure (high-order contractive auto-encoders) and we show how it builds a topological atlas of charts, each chart being characterized by the principal singular vectors of the Jacobian of a representation mapping. This representation learning algorithm can be stacked to yield a deep architecture, and we combine it with a domain knowledge-free version of the TangentProp algorithm to encourage the classiﬁer to be insensitive to local directions changes along the manifold. Record-breaking classiﬁcation results are obtained.

paragraphs: The paper combines three hypotheses about classification: the distribution of inputs contains useful information about labels, data concentrate near low-dimensional manifolds, and different classes occupy separate manifolds divided by low-density regions. Together, these assumptions suggest that learning the shape of the input distribution can help determine which local changes should leave a prediction stable.

High-order contractive auto-encoders learn that local geometry. The authors describe the representation as an atlas of local charts, with each chart characterized by principal singular vectors of the representation mapping's Jacobian. In plain language, these vectors identify local directions associated with the learned manifold. The representation learners can also be stacked into a deep architecture.

A version of TangentProp then encourages the classifier to remain insensitive to changes along those learned directions, without requiring domain-specific knowledge to supply them. The authors report record-breaking classification results. The contribution links unsupervised geometry learning to supervised prediction through an explicit invariance objective, using learned local structure to guide how the classifier responds to nearby inputs.
summary.tldr: The manifold tangent classifier learns local manifold directions and encourages prediction stability along them, reporting record-breaking classification results.

title: The Manifold Tangent Classifier

abstract: Continuous relaxations play an important role in discrete optimization, but have not seen much use in approximate probabilistic inference. Here we show that a general form of the Gaussian Integral Trick makes it possible to transform a wide class of discrete variable undirected models into fully continuous systems. The continuous representation allows the use of gradient-based Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for inference, results in new ways of estimating normalization constants (partition functions), and in general opens up a number of new avenues for inference in difficult discrete systems. We demonstrate some of these continuous relaxation inference algorithms on a number of illustrative problems.
originalAbstract: Continuous relaxations play an important role in discrete optimization, but have not seen much use in approximate probabilistic inference. Here we show that a general form of the Gaussian Integral Trick makes it possible to transform a wide class of discrete variable undirected models into fully continuous systems. The continuous representation allows the use of gradient-based Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for inference, results in new ways of estimating normalization constants (partition functions), and in general opens up a number of new avenues for inference in difficult discrete systems. We demonstrate some of these continuous relaxation inference algorithms on a number of illustrative problems.

paragraphs: The paper explores how to use continuous mathematical representations for probabilistic inference in models whose variables are discrete. Continuous relaxations already have a role in discrete optimization, but the authors identify approximate inference as a less explored application. Their contribution is a transformation that makes a wide class of discrete undirected models accessible to continuous inference techniques.

The transformation uses a general form of the Gaussian Integral Trick to construct fully continuous systems. This representation allows gradient-based Hamiltonian Monte Carlo to be used for inference. The key benefit is methodological: changing the representation makes a different collection of computational tools available for studying the original discrete system.

The continuous formulation also provides new approaches to estimating partition functions, the normalization constants needed to turn model weights into probabilities. The authors demonstrate some of the resulting inference algorithms on illustrative problems. These demonstrations support the usefulness of the connection, while the broader contribution is the set of inference possibilities created by moving between discrete models and continuous representations.
summary.tldr: A Gaussian integral transformation enables continuous inference methods, including Hamiltonian Monte Carlo, for a wide class of discrete undirected models.

title: Continuous Relaxations for Discrete Hamiltonian Monte Carlo

abstract: While long term human visual memory can store a remarkable amount of visual information, it tends to degrade over time. Recent works have shown that image memorability is an intrinsic property of an image that can be reliably estimated using state-of-the-art image features and machine learning algorithms. However, the class of features and image information that is forgotten has not been explored yet. In this work, we propose a probabilistic framework that models how and which local regions from an image may be forgotten using a data-driven approach that combines local and global images features. The model automatically discov- ers memorability maps of individual images without any human annotation. We incorporate multiple image region attributes in our algorithm, leading to improved memorability prediction of images as compared to previous works.

However, the class of features and image information that is forgotten has not been explored yet. In this work, we propose a probabilistic framework that models how and which local regions from an image may be forgotten using a data-driven approach that combines local and global images features. The model automatically discov- ers memorability maps of individual images without any human annotation. paragraphs: An image’s overall memorability can be estimated from visual features, but that leaves a more local question: which parts of the image are likely to be forgotten? The paper moves from predicting a single property of an entire image toward modeling how memory relates to its individual regions.

The authors propose a probabilistic, data-driven framework that combines local information with features of the image as a whole. It models which regions may be forgotten and automatically produces memorability maps for individual images without human annotation. These maps express regional differences while allowing the surrounding image to contribute to the prediction.

The algorithm incorporates multiple attributes of image regions, and the resulting model improves overall image memorability prediction relative to previous work. This connects the regional analysis to a measurable benefit for the broader prediction task. The findings suggest that local and global image information together help explain memorability, while the probabilistic formulation preserves the distinction between a predicted tendency to forget a region and a certain outcome for every viewer.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic model learns regional memorability maps from local and global image features and improves overall memorability prediction.

title: Memorability of Image Regions

abstract: Graph matching is a challenging problem with very important applications in a wide range of fields, from image and video analysis to biological and biomedical problems. We propose a robust graph matching algorithm inspired in sparsity-related techniques. We cast the problem, resembling group or collaborative sparsity formulations, as a non-smooth convex optimization problem that can be efficiently solved using augmented Lagrangian techniques. The method can deal with weighted or unweighted graphs, as well as multimodal data, where different graphs represent different types of data. The proposed approach is also naturally integrated with collaborative graph inference techniques, solving general network inference problems where the observed variables, possibly coming from different modalities, are not in correspondence. The algorithm is tested and compared with state-of-the-art graph matching techniques in both synthetic and real graphs. We also present results on multimodal graphs and applications to collaborative inference of brain connectivity from alignment-free functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data.

We propose a robust graph matching algorithm inspired in sparsity-related techniques. We cast the problem, resembling group or collaborative sparsity formulations, as a non-smooth convex optimization problem that can be efficiently solved using augmented Lagrangian techniques. We also present results on multimodal graphs and applications to collaborative inference of brain connectivity from alignment-free functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data.

paragraphs: Graph matching seeks correspondence between nodes in different graphs, a problem that appears in visual analysis and biological applications. This paper develops a robust matching method inspired by sparsity techniques. It supports weighted and unweighted graphs, as well as multimodal settings where different graphs describe different types of data.

The authors formulate matching as a nonsmooth convex optimization problem resembling group or collaborative sparsity formulations. Augmented Lagrangian techniques provide an efficient solution approach. The method also integrates with collaborative graph inference, allowing network estimation to proceed when the observed variables across datasets or modalities do not already have established correspondences.

Evaluation includes comparisons with leading graph-matching methods on synthetic and real graphs, along with multimodal examples. A further application jointly infers brain connectivity from functional magnetic resonance imaging data without requiring prior alignment. The stated contribution is therefore both a graph-matching formulation and its integration with network inference; the abstract reports these evaluations without specifying a universal performance advantage over the comparison methods.
summary.tldr: A sparsity-inspired convex formulation supports robust multimodal graph matching and collaborative network inference without pre-established variable correspondences.

title: Robust Multimodal Graph Matching: Sparse Coding Meets Graph Matching

abstract: Many methods have been proposed to recover the intrinsic scene properties such as shape, reflectance and illumination from a single image. However, most of these models have been applied on laboratory datasets. In this work we explore the synergy effects between intrinsic scene properties recovered from an image, and the objects and attributes present in the scene. We cast the problem in a joint energy minimization framework; thus our model is able to encode the strong correlations between intrinsic properties (reflectance, shape, illumination), objects (table, tv-monitor), and materials (wooden, plastic) in a given scene. We tested our approach on the NYU and Pascal datasets, and observe both qualitative and quantitative improvements in the overall accuracy.
originalAbstract: Many methods have been proposed to recover the intrinsic scene properties such as shape, reflectance and illumination from a single image. However, most of these models have been applied on laboratory datasets. In this work we explore the synergy effects between intrinsic scene properties recovered from an image, and the objects and attributes present in the scene. We cast the problem in a joint energy minimization framework; thus our model is able to encode the strong correlations between intrinsic properties (reflectance, shape, illumination), objects (table, tv-monitor), and materials (wooden, plastic) in a given scene. We tested our approach on the NYU and Pascal datasets, and observe both qualitative and quantitative improvements in the overall accuracy.

paragraphs: A single image contains intertwined evidence about a scene's shape, reflectance, illumination, objects, and materials. Recovering these properties is challenging because the visible image reflects their combined effects. The paper explores whether estimating them together can exploit relationships that would be missed when the tasks are handled separately.

The authors formulate a joint energy minimization problem. This provides a shared objective for intrinsic scene properties, object identities such as tables and monitors, and material attributes such as wood and plastic. By encoding correlations among these quantities, the model allows evidence about one aspect of a scene to help constrain estimates of the others.

The motivation includes moving beyond the laboratory datasets used by many earlier intrinsic-image models. Tests on the NYU and Pascal datasets show both qualitative and quantitative improvements in overall accuracy. These results support the proposed synergy between physical scene interpretation and object or material recognition: their relationships can be useful information within a single estimation framework.
summary.tldr: Jointly estimating intrinsic scene properties, objects, and materials improves overall accuracy by modeling their correlations.

title: Higher Order Priors for Joint Intrinsic Image, Objects, and Attributes Estimation

abstract: We consider a number of classical and new computational problems regarding marginal distributions, and inference in models specifying a full joint distribution. We prove general and efficient reductions between a number of these problems, which demonstrate that algorithmic progress in inference automatically yields progress for “pure data” problems. Our main technique involves formulating the problems as linear programs, and proving that the dual separation oracle for the Ellipsoid Method is provided by the target problem. This technique may be of independent interest in probabilistic inference.
originalAbstract: We consider a number of classical and new computational problems regarding marginal distributions, and inference in models specifying a full joint distribution. We prove general and efficient reductions between a number of these problems, which demonstrate that algorithmic progress in inference automatically yields progress for “pure data” problems. Our main technique involves formulating the problems as linear programs, and proving that the dual separation oracle for the Ellipsoid Method is provided by the target problem. This technique may be of independent interest in probabilistic inference.

paragraphs: A marginal distribution describes only part of a collection of variables, whereas a joint distribution describes them together. This paper studies computational connections between problems involving marginals and inference problems in models that specify a full joint distribution. Its aim is to show when methods for one kind of problem can help solve another.

The authors prove general, efficient reductions among several classical and new problems. A reduction translates the task being solved into calls to another computational problem. Their results show that advances in model-based inference can automatically yield advances for the corresponding “pure data” problems connected by these reductions.

The main construction expresses problems as linear programs and uses the target problem to provide a dual separation oracle for the Ellipsoid Method. In this role, the target computation supplies the information needed by the optimization procedure. Beyond the individual reductions, the authors suggest that this technique may have independent value for probabilistic inference, offering a reusable way to establish computational relationships.
summary.tldr: Efficient reductions connect marginal-distribution problems to joint-model inference, allowing algorithmic advances to transfer between them.

title: Marginals-to-Models Reducibility

abstract: Consider an unweighted k-nearest neighbor graph on n points that have been sampled i.i.d. from some unknown density p on R^d. We prove how one can estimate the density p just from the unweighted adjacency matrix of the graph, without knowing the points themselves or their distance or similarity scores. The key insights are that local differences in link numbers can be used to estimate some local function of p, and that integrating this function along shortest paths leads to an estimate of the underlying density.

paragraphs: Suppose a dataset is available only as a graph recording which points are nearest neighbors. The original coordinates are missing, and the edges carry no distances or similarity scores. This paper asks whether that reduced representation still contains enough information to estimate the probability density from which the points were sampled.

The setting assumes that the points are independent samples from a common unknown density in a Euclidean space. The authors prove a way to estimate that density using only the graph’s unweighted adjacency matrix. Their first insight is that local differences in link counts reveal a local function of the underlying density, even though the graph does not explicitly record geometric distances.

The second step integrates the estimated local function along shortest paths through the graph to obtain a density estimate. The contribution thus links local connectivity information to a broader description of where probability mass is concentrated. It establishes that, in the stated sampling setting, discarding coordinates and edge weights does not eliminate all information useful for density estimation.
summary.tldr: The paper proves how to estimate an underlying sampling density from an unweighted nearest-neighbor graph using local link differences and shortest paths.

title: Density estimation from unweighted k-nearest neighbor graphs: a roadmap

abstract: Motivated by generating personalized recommendations using ordinal (or preference) data, we study the question of learning a mixture of MultiNomial Logit (MNL) model, a parameterized class of distributions over permutations, from partial ordinal or preference data (e.g. pair-wise comparisons). Despite its long standing importance across disciplines including social choice, operations research and revenue management, little is known about this question. In case of single MNL models (no mixture), computationally and statistically tractable learning from pair-wise comparisons is feasible. However, even learning mixture of two MNL model is infeasible in general. Given this state of affairs, we seek conditions under which it is feasible to learn the mixture model in both computationally and statistically efficient manner. To that end, we present a sufficient condition as well as an efficient algorithm for learning mixed MNL models from partial preferences/comparisons data. In particular, a mixture of $r$ MNL components over $n$ objects can be learnt using samples whose size scales polynomially in $n$ and $r$ (concretely, $n^3 r^{3.5} \log^4 n$, with $r \ll n^{2/7}$ when the model parameters are sufficiently {\em incoherent}). The algorithm has two phases: first, learn the pair-wise marginals for each component using tensor decomposition; second, learn the model parameters for each component using RankCentrality introduced by Negahban et al. In the process of proving these results, we obtain a generalization of existing analysis for tensor decomposition to a more realistic regime where only partial information about each sample is available.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to learn a mixture of preference models from incomplete rankings, such as pairwise comparisons. Each multinomial logit component describes a distribution over object orderings, while the mixture represents multiple preference patterns. Although learning a single component from comparisons is tractable, even a two-component mixture is infeasible in general.

The authors therefore seek sufficient conditions for efficient learning. Their algorithm first uses tensor decomposition to recover each component's pairwise preference probabilities, then applies RankCentrality to estimate its model parameters. This separates identifying the component-specific comparison behavior from fitting the preference model for each component.

Under sufficiently incoherent model parameters and with the number of components r much smaller than n raised to the 2/7 power, the stated sample requirement scales as n cubed times r to the 3.5 power times the fourth power of log n. The result establishes conditional computational and statistical tractability, not a general solution to arbitrary mixtures. The analysis also extends tensor-decomposition guarantees to samples containing only partial information.
summary.tldr: A two-stage algorithm efficiently learns mixed multinomial logit models from partial preferences under sufficient incoherence and component-count conditions.

title: Learning Mixed Multinomial Logit Model from Ordinal Data

abstract: We present region-based, fully convolutional networks for accurate and efficient object detection. In contrast to previous region-based detectors such as Fast/Faster R-CNN that apply a costly per-region subnetwork hundreds of times, our region-based detector is fully convolutional with almost all computation shared on the entire image. To achieve this goal, we propose position-sensitive score maps to address a dilemma between translation-invariance in image classification and translation-variance in object detection. Our method can thus naturally adopt fully convolutional image classifier backbones, such as the latest Residual Networks (ResNets), for object detection. We show competitive results on the PASCAL VOC datasets (e.g., 83.6% mAP on the 2007 set) with the 101-layer ResNet. Meanwhile, our result is achieved at a test-time speed of 170ms per image, 2.5-20 times faster than the Faster R-CNN counterpart. Code is made publicly available at: https://github.com/daijifeng001/r-fcn.

To achieve this goal, we propose position-sensitive score maps to address a dilemma between translation-invariance in image classification and translation-variance in object detection. paragraphs: Region-based object detectors can spend substantial computation repeatedly processing candidate regions from the same image. R-FCN addresses this cost with a fully convolutional design that shares almost all computation across the image. The goal is to preserve accurate detection while reducing expensive work repeated separately for each region.

The central mechanism is a set of position-sensitive score maps. These address a tension between image classification, which benefits from recognizing an object despite changes in location, and detection, which must retain information about location. This design allows fully convolutional classification backbones, including Residual Networks, to be used naturally for object detection.

With a 101-layer ResNet, the paper reports competitive PASCAL VOC results, including 83.6% mean average precision on the 2007 dataset. It reports a test time of 170 milliseconds per image and speeds 2.5 to 20 times faster than the Faster R-CNN counterpart. These findings demonstrate the practical benefit of sharing computation while retaining position-sensitive information for detection.
summary.tldr: R-FCN shares nearly all image computation and uses position-sensitive score maps to deliver competitive detection accuracy with substantially faster testing.

title: R-FCN: Object Detection via Region-based Fully Convolutional Networks

abstract: Generalized linear models (GLMs)---such as logistic regression, Poisson regression, and robust regression---provide interpretable models for diverse data types. Probabilistic approaches, particularly Bayesian ones, allow coherent estimates of uncertainty, incorporation of prior information, and sharing of power across experiments via hierarchical models. In practice, however, the approximate Bayesian methods necessary for inference have either failed to scale to large data sets or failed to provide theoretical guarantees on the quality of inference. We propose a new approach based on constructing polynomial approximate sufficient statistics for GLMs (PASS-GLM). We demonstrate that our method admits a simple algorithm as well as trivial streaming and distributed extensions that do not compound error across computations. We provide theoretical guarantees on the quality of point (MAP) estimates, the approximate posterior, and posterior mean and uncertainty estimates. We validate our approach empirically in the case of logistic regression using a quadratic approximation and show competitive performance with stochastic gradient descent, MCMC, and the Laplace approximation in terms of speed and multiple measures of accuracy---including on an advertising data set with 40 million data points and 20,000 covariates.

paragraphs: Bayesian generalized linear models offer uncertainty estimates and a way to include prior information, but inference can become expensive on large datasets. Existing approximations can face a tradeoff between scalability and guarantees about their quality. PASS-GLM addresses this through polynomial approximate sufficient statistics: compact summaries designed to support approximate inference.

The resulting method has a simple algorithm and straightforward streaming and distributed extensions. The abstract states that these extensions do not compound error across computations. The authors also give theoretical guarantees covering maximum a posteriori point estimates, the approximate posterior distribution, and posterior estimates of means and uncertainty.

Experiments focus on logistic regression using a quadratic approximation. They show competitive speed and accuracy against stochastic gradient descent, Markov chain Monte Carlo, and the Laplace approximation, including on an advertising dataset with forty million examples and twenty thousand covariates. The contribution links large-scale computation to guarantees on several inferential outputs, including uncertainty, rather than assessing scalability only through a single fitted parameter estimate.
summary.tldr: PASS-GLM uses polynomial data summaries for scalable Bayesian inference with guarantees on point estimates, posterior approximations, and uncertainty.

title: PASS-GLM: polynomial approximate sufficient statistics for scalable Bayesian GLM inference

abstract: We formulate and study a general family of (continuous-time) stochastic dynamics for accelerated first-order minimization of smooth convex functions. Building on an averaging formulation of accelerated mirror descent, we propose a stochastic variant in which the gradient is contaminated by noise, and study the resulting stochastic differential equation. We prove a bound on the rate of change of an energy function associated with the problem, then use it to derive estimates of convergence rates of the function values (almost surely and in expectation), both for persistent and asymptotically vanishing noise. We discuss the interaction between the parameters of the dynamics (learning rate and averaging rates) and the covariation of the noise process. In particular, we show how the asymptotic rate of covariation affects the choice of parameters and, ultimately, the convergence rate.
