paragraphs: Accelerated optimization methods aim to reduce an objective quickly, but noisy gradients complicate their behavior. This paper studies that interaction for smooth convex functions through a family of continuous-time stochastic dynamics. Starting from an averaging formulation of accelerated mirror descent, the authors introduce gradient noise and describe the resulting evolution with a stochastic differential equation.

The analysis uses an energy function associated with the optimization problem. By bounding how this energy changes, the authors obtain convergence-rate estimates for objective values. They consider both noise that persists and noise that diminishes over time, and provide results in expectation as well as almost surely. These describe average behavior and behavior along random trajectories, respectively.

A central finding is that learning and averaging rates must be understood together with the noise process. In particular, the long-run growth of noise covariation influences parameter choices and the resulting convergence rates. The contribution is a continuous-time theoretical account of how acceleration, averaging, and stochastic disturbances interact, with rates tied to the behavior of the noise.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes how gradient noise and averaging choices shape convergence in continuous-time accelerated optimization.

title: Acceleration and Averaging in Stochastic Descent Dynamics

abstract: Discovering a correlation from one variable to another variable is of fundamental scientific and practical interest. While existing correlation measures are suitable for discovering average correlation, they fail to discover hidden or potential correlations. To bridge this gap, (i) we postulate a set of natural axioms that we expect a measure of potential correlation to satisfy; (ii) we show that the rate of information bottleneck, i.e., the hypercontractivity coefficient, satisfies all the proposed axioms; (iii) we provide a novel estimator to estimate the hypercontractivity coefficient from samples; and (iv) we provide numerical experiments demonstrating that this proposed estimator discovers potential correlations among various indicators of WHO datasets, is robust in discovering gene interactions from gene expression time series data, and is statistically more powerful than the estimators for other correlation measures in binary hypothesis testing of canonical examples of potential correlations.
originalAbstract: Discovering a correlation from one variable to another variable is of fundamental scientific and practical interest. To bridge this gap, (i) we postulate a set of natural axioms that we expect a measure of potential correlation to satisfy; (ii) we show that the rate of information bottleneck, i.e., the hypercontractivity coefficient, satisfies all the proposed axioms; (iii) we provide a novel estimator to estimate the hypercontractivity coefficient from samples; and (iv) we provide numerical experiments demonstrating that this proposed estimator discovers potential correlations among various indicators of WHO datasets, is robust in discovering gene interactions from gene expression time series data, and is statistically more powerful than the estimators for other correlation measures in binary hypothesis testing of canonical examples of potential correlations.

paragraphs: A measure designed to summarize average association can miss a relationship that is hidden or only potentially apparent. This paper treats discovering such potential correlations as a distinct measurement problem. It begins by proposing a set of natural properties that a suitable measure should satisfy, making the intended behavior explicit before choosing an estimator.

The authors show that the hypercontractivity coefficient, described through the rate of information bottleneck, satisfies all their proposed axioms. They then develop a method for estimating that coefficient from samples. This connects a theoretical characterization of potential correlation to a procedure that can be applied to observed data.

Numerical experiments find potential correlations among World Health Organization indicators and show robustness in discovering gene interactions from expression time series. In binary hypothesis tests on canonical potential-correlation examples, the estimator has greater statistical power than estimators of other correlation measures. These results support the proposed measure and estimator for the studied forms of hidden association, with the axioms specifying what the method is designed to capture.
summary.tldr: An estimator of the hypercontractivity coefficient detects potential correlations that average-association measures can miss.

title: Discovering Potential Correlations via Hypercontractivity

abstract: We aim to obtain an interpretable, expressive, and disentangled scene representation that contains comprehensive structural and textural information for each object. Previous scene representations learned by neural networks are often uninterpretable, limited to a single object, or lacking 3D knowledge. In this work, we propose 3D scene de-rendering networks (3D-SDN) to address the above issues by integrating disentangled representations for semantics, geometry, and appearance into a deep generative model. Our scene encoder performs inverse graphics, translating a scene into a structured object-wise representation. Our decoder has two components: a differentiable shape renderer and a neural texture generator. The disentanglement of semantics, geometry, and appearance supports 3D-aware scene manipulation, e.g., rotating and moving objects freely while keeping the consistent shape and texture, and changing the object appearance without affecting its shape. Experiments demonstrate that our editing scheme based on 3D-SDN is superior to its 2D counterpart.

paragraphs: Editing an image in a way that respects three-dimensional objects requires a representation of what those objects are, how they are shaped, and how they look. This paper introduces 3D scene de-rendering networks, or 3D-SDN, to separate these aspects while representing multiple objects within a scene.

The encoder performs inverse graphics: it translates a scene into a structured description organized around individual objects. The decoder reconstructs the scene using two components, a differentiable shape renderer and a neural texture generator. Together, these components connect explicit information about geometry with learned appearance generation, making the representation useful for controlled edits.

Separating semantics, geometry, and appearance supports operations such as moving or rotating an object while preserving its shape and texture, or changing its appearance without changing its shape. Experiments report better editing results than a corresponding two-dimensional approach. The contribution is a scene representation whose separate parts correspond to meaningful editing controls, with three-dimensional information helping those controls produce consistent changes.
summary.tldr: 3D-SDN separates object semantics, geometry, and appearance to support consistent three-dimensional scene editing.

title: 3D-Aware Scene Manipulation via Inverse Graphics

abstract: In this work we study the problem of using machine-learned predictions to improve performance of online algorithms. We consider two classical problems, ski rental and non-clairvoyant job scheduling, and obtain new online algorithms that use predictions to make their decisions. These algorithms are oblivious to the performance of the predictor, improve with better predictions, but do not degrade much if the predictions are poor.
originalAbstract: In this work we study the problem of using machine-learned predictions to improve performance of online algorithms. We consider two classical problems, ski rental and non-clairvoyant job scheduling, and obtain new online algorithms that use predictions to make their decisions. These algorithms are oblivious to the performance of the predictor, improve with better predictions, but do not degrade much if the predictions are poor.

paragraphs: Online algorithms must make decisions while information is still arriving. Machine-learned predictions offer a way to inform those decisions, but their usefulness depends on how accurate they are. This paper studies how an online algorithm can benefit from predictions while remaining resilient when the predictor provides poor guidance.

The authors develop new algorithms for two classical problems: ski rental and non-clairvoyant job scheduling. In both settings, predictions influence the choices the algorithm makes. A central property is that the algorithms do not need to know the predictor's performance in advance. Their operation therefore does not require a supplied assessment of prediction quality.

The stated results combine two desirable behaviors: performance improves as predictions improve, and poor predictions cause only limited degradation. The contribution is a way to connect predictive learning with online decision-making while accounting for unreliable forecasts. Its significance lies in that combination: the algorithms can use better information when it is available without requiring the predictor to be consistently accurate.
summary.tldr: Prediction-assisted algorithms for ski rental and job scheduling improve with better forecasts while limiting degradation from poor ones.

title: Improving Online Algorithms via ML Predictions

abstract: Optimization of parameterized policies for reinforcement learning (RL) is an important and challenging problem in artificial intelligence. Among the most common approaches are algorithms based on gradient ascent of a score function representing discounted return. In this paper, we examine the role of these policy gradient and actor-critic algorithms in partially-observable multiagent environments. We show several candidate policy update rules and relate them to a foundation of regret minimization and multiagent learning techniques for the one-shot and tabular cases, leading to previously unknown convergence guarantees. We apply our method to model-free multiagent reinforcement learning in adversarial sequential decision problems (zero-sum imperfect information games), using RL-style function approximation. We evaluate on commonly used benchmark Poker domains, showing performance against fixed policies and empirical convergence to approximate Nash equilibria in self-play with rates similar to or better than a baseline model-free algorithm for zero-sum games, without any domain-specific state space reductions.

paragraphs: Learning a policy becomes harder when other agents influence outcomes and some information remains hidden. This paper examines policy gradient and actor-critic methods in that setting. These approaches adjust a parameterized decision rule to improve a score based on discounted rewards, but their behavior also depends on how interacting agents learn.

The authors connect several candidate policy updates to regret minimization and established multiagent learning techniques. These connections yield previously unknown convergence guarantees for one-shot and tabular cases. The distinction matters: the theoretical results concern those settings, while the paper also explores function approximation in more complex sequential games.

The experimental application is model-free learning in zero-sum games with imperfect information, using benchmark Poker domains. The authors evaluate play against fixed opponents and learning through self-play. They report empirical convergence toward approximate Nash equilibria at rates similar to or better than a baseline model-free algorithm for zero-sum games. This was achieved without domain-specific reductions of the state space, supporting the practical relevance of the proposed updates beyond the simpler theoretical cases.
summary.tldr: The paper connects actor-critic policy updates to regret minimization, establishing guarantees in simpler settings and demonstrating approximate equilibrium learning in Poker.

title: Actor-Critic Policy Optimization in Partially Observable Multiagent Environments

abstract: Known finite-sample concentration bounds for the Wasserstein distance between the empirical and true distribution of a random variable are used to derive a two-sided concentration bound for the error between the true conditional value-at-risk (CVaR) of a (possibly unbounded) random variable and a standard estimate of its CVaR computed from an i.i.d. sample. The bound applies under fairly general assumptions on the random variable, and improves upon previous bounds which were either one sided, or applied only to bounded random variables. Specializations of the bound to sub-Gaussian and sub-exponential random variables are also derived. A similar procedure is followed to derive concentration bounds for the error between the true and estimated Cumulative Prospect Theory (CPT) value of a random variable, in cases where the random variable is bounded or sub-Gaussian. These bounds are shown to match a known bound in the bounded case, and improve upon the known bound in the sub-Gaussian case. The usefulness of the bounds is illustrated through an algorithm, and corresponding regret bound for a stochastic bandit problem, where the underlying risk measure to be optimized is CVaR.

These bounds are shown to match a known bound in the bounded case, and improve upon the known bound in the sub-Gaussian case. The usefulness of the bounds is illustrated through an algorithm, and corresponding regret bound for a stochastic bandit problem, where the underlying risk measure to be optimized is CVaR.

paragraphs: Risk measures estimated from data can differ from their population values. This paper studies how large those errors can be for conditional value-at-risk, or CVaR, and Cumulative Prospect Theory values. Its central strategy is to translate existing bounds on distributional estimation error, measured by Wasserstein distance, into bounds on errors in these risk measures.

For CVaR, the authors derive a two-sided concentration bound from an independent, identically distributed sample. It covers errors in both directions and can apply to unbounded random variables under the stated distributional assumptions. They also obtain specialized results for sub-Gaussian and sub-exponential variables, extending beyond earlier results restricted to bounded variables or one-sided errors.

For Cumulative Prospect Theory, the analysis covers bounded and sub-Gaussian variables. The resulting bounds match a known result in the bounded case and improve a known result in the sub-Gaussian case. A stochastic bandit algorithm that optimizes CVaR, together with its regret bound, demonstrates how these estimation guarantees can inform sequential decisions.
summary.tldr: Wasserstein concentration bounds yield stronger guarantees for estimating risk measures and support a CVaR-based bandit algorithm.

title: Concentration of risk measures: A Wasserstein distance approach

abstract: In this work, we consider one challenging training time attack by modifying training data with bounded perturbation, hoping to manipulate the behavior (both targeted or non-targeted) of any corresponding trained classifier during test time when facing clean samples. To achieve this, we proposed to use an auto-encoder-like network to generate such adversarial perturbations on the training data together with one imaginary victim differentiable classifier. The perturbation generator will learn to update its weights so as to produce the most harmful noise, aiming to cause the lowest performance for the victim classifier during test time. This can be formulated into a non-linear equality constrained optimization problem. Unlike GANs, solving such problem is computationally challenging, we then proposed a simple yet effective procedure to decouple the alternating updates for the two networks for stability. By teaching the perturbation generator to hijacking the training trajectory of the victim classifier, the generator can thus learn to move against the victim classifier step by step. The method proposed in this paper can be easily extended to the label specific setting where the attacker can manipulate the predictions of the victim classifier according to some predefined rules rather than only making wrong predictions. Experiments on various datasets including CIFAR-10 and a reduced version of ImageNet confirmed the effectiveness of the proposed method and empirical results showed that, such bounded perturbations have good transferability across different types of victim classifiers.

paragraphs: This paper studies an attack that modifies training examples with bounded perturbations so a trained classifier behaves incorrectly on clean test inputs. The intended manipulation can be untargeted, reducing performance generally, or targeted toward particular prediction rules. The focus is on influencing what a classifier learns through altered training data.

The method trains an autoencoder-like perturbation generator alongside an imagined differentiable victim classifier. The generator learns changes intended to steer the victim’s training trajectory toward poor test performance. The resulting optimization has nonlinear equality constraints, and the authors propose decoupling alternating updates of the two networks to make the procedure more stable.

The method can also be extended to label-specific manipulation, where predictions follow predefined attacker objectives. Experiments on several datasets, including CIFAR-10 and a reduced ImageNet dataset, support its effectiveness. The reported perturbations also transfer well across different victim classifier types. This empirical transfer is significant because the generator is learned with an imagined victim, while the intended effects extend to other tested classifiers.
summary.tldr: An autoencoder-like generator learns bounded training-data perturbations that impair clean-test predictions and transfer across tested classifiers.

title: Learning to Confuse: Generating Training Time Adversarial Data with Auto-Encoder

abstract: Training of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) is notoriously fragile, requiring to maintain a careful balance between the generator and the discriminator in order to perform well. To mitigate this issue we introduce a new regularization technique - progressive augmentation of GANs (PA-GAN). The key idea is to gradually increase the task difficulty of the discriminator by progressively augmenting its input or feature space, thus enabling continuous learning of the generator. We show that the proposed progressive augmentation preserves the original GAN objective, does not compromise the discriminator's optimality and encourages a healthy competition between the generator and discriminator, leading to the better-performing generator. We experimentally demonstrate the effectiveness of PA-GAN across different architectures and on multiple benchmarks for the image synthesis task, on average achieving 3 point improvement of the FID score.
originalAbstract: Training of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) is notoriously fragile, requiring to maintain a careful balance between the generator and the discriminator in order to perform well. To mitigate this issue we introduce a new regularization technique - progressive augmentation of GANs (PA-GAN). The key idea is to gradually increase the task difficulty of the discriminator by progressively augmenting its input or feature space, thus enabling continuous learning of the generator. We show that the proposed progressive augmentation preserves the original GAN objective, does not compromise the discriminator's optimality and encourages a healthy competition between the generator and discriminator, leading to the better-performing generator. paragraphs: Training a generative adversarial network depends on maintaining a useful balance between its generator and discriminator. If their competition becomes poorly balanced, training can become fragile. This paper introduces progressive augmentation of GANs, or PA-GAN, as a regularization technique intended to keep that competition productive while the generator continues learning.

The method gradually increases the discriminator's task difficulty by augmenting its input space or feature space. This progression adjusts the challenge facing the discriminator over training. The authors show that the augmentation preserves the original GAN objective and does not compromise the discriminator's optimality. Thus, the technique changes the learning conditions while retaining the intended objective and its optimal discriminator.

Image synthesis experiments cover different architectures and multiple benchmarks. Across those experiments, PA-GAN produces an average improvement of three points in FID. The findings support progressive discriminator augmentation as a way to improve generator performance in the evaluated settings. The reported average describes the experimental results rather than a guaranteed improvement for every architecture or dataset.
summary.tldr: PA-GAN progressively increases discriminator difficulty while preserving the GAN objective, improving image synthesis performance in the reported experiments.

title: Progressive Augmentation of GANs

abstract: We present Matrix Krasulina, an algorithm for online k-PCA, by gen- eralizing the classic Krasulina’s method (Krasulina, 1969) from vector to matrix case. We show, both theoretically and empirically, that the algorithm naturally adapts to data low-rankness and converges exponentially fast to the ground-truth principal subspace. Notably, our result suggests that despite various recent efforts to accelerate the convergence of stochastic-gradient based methods by adding a O(n)-time variance reduction step, for the k- PCA problem, a truly online SGD variant suffices to achieve exponential convergence on intrinsically low-rank data.

paragraphs: The paper introduces Matrix Krasulina, an algorithm for learning a principal subspace from data arriving online. Principal component analysis seeks a compact set of directions that captures the data's main variation. The authors extend the classic vector-based Krasulina method to a matrix formulation that handles multiple principal directions.

The central finding is that the algorithm adapts naturally to data with low-rank structure. Theoretical analysis and empirical results show exponential convergence toward the ground-truth principal subspace in the intrinsically low-rank setting. This ties the speed of learning to the structure of the data, rather than describing exponential convergence as a guarantee for every possible input distribution.

The result matters because other acceleration efforts add a variance-reduction step requiring time proportional to the number of examples. Here, the stated fast convergence is achieved by a genuinely online stochastic-gradient variant without that additional step. For the setting studied, this shows that exploiting low-rank structure can make such variance reduction unnecessary for exponential convergence.
summary.tldr: Matrix Krasulina achieves exponential convergence for online principal-subspace learning on intrinsically low-rank data without an added variance-reduction step.

title: Exponentially convergent stochastic k-PCA without variance reduction

abstract: The performance of many network learning applications crucially hinges on the success of network embedding algorithms, which aim to encode rich network information into low-dimensional vertex-based vector representations. This paper considers a novel variational formulation of network embeddings, with special focus on textual networks. Different from most existing methods that optimize a discriminative objective, we introduce Variational Homophilic Embedding (VHE), a fully generative model that learns network embeddings by modeling the semantic (textual) information with a variational autoencoder, while accounting for the structural (topology) information through a novel homophilic prior design. Homophilic vertex embeddings encourage similar embedding vectors for related (connected) vertices. The VHE encourages better generalization for downstream tasks, robustness to incomplete observations, and the ability to generalize to unseen vertices. Extensive experiments on real-world networks, for multiple tasks, demonstrate that the proposed method achieves consistently superior performance relative to competing state-of-the-art approaches.

paragraphs: Network embeddings represent vertices as compact vectors that retain useful information for later tasks. In textual networks, that information includes both text associated with vertices and the links between them. This paper proposes Variational Homophilic Embedding, or VHE, as a generative framework for bringing these two sources of information into the same representation.

VHE models textual meaning with a variational autoencoder and incorporates network structure through a specially designed prior. The prior expresses homophily by encouraging connected vertices to have similar embedding vectors. Text and connectivity therefore shape the learned representations through different, coordinated parts of the probabilistic model.

The design encourages generalization to downstream tasks, robustness when observations are incomplete, and the ability to represent previously unseen vertices. Experiments on real-world networks across multiple tasks report consistently better performance than competing state-of-the-art approaches. These results support the usefulness of combining generative text modeling with a structural prior, while the generalization and robustness benefits are presented as properties encouraged by that formulation.
summary.tldr: VHE combines generative text modeling with a prior favoring similar embeddings for connected vertices to improve textual network learning.

title: Improving Textual Network Learning with Variational Homophilic Embeddings

abstract: While graph kernels (GKs) are easy to train and enjoy provable theoretical guarantees, their practical performances are limited by their expressive power, as the kernel function often depends on hand-crafted combinatorial features of graphs. Compared to graph kernels, graph neural networks (GNNs) usually achieve better practical performance, as GNNs use multi-layer architectures and non-linear activation functions to extract high-order information of graphs as features. However, due to the large number of hyper-parameters and the non-convex nature of the training procedure, GNNs are harder to train. Theoretical guarantees of GNNs are also not well-understood. Furthermore, the expressive power of GNNs scales with the number of parameters, and thus it is hard to exploit the full power of GNNs when computing resources are limited. The current paper presents a new class of graph kernels, Graph Neural Tangent Kernels (GNTKs), which correspond to \emph{infinitely wide} multi-layer GNNs trained by gradient descent. GNTKs enjoy the full expressive power of GNNs and inherit advantages of GKs. Theoretically, we show GNTKs provably learn a class of smooth functions on graphs. Empirically, we test GNTKs on graph classification datasets and show they achieve strong performance.

paragraphs: Graph kernels and graph neural networks offer different strengths for learning from graphs. Kernels are relatively straightforward to train and support theoretical guarantees, but handcrafted graph features can restrict their expressive power. Graph neural networks extract more complex information through multiple nonlinear layers, while introducing difficult optimization and many hyperparameters.

The paper constructs Graph Neural Tangent Kernels, which correspond to infinitely wide multilayer graph neural networks trained by gradient descent. This correspondence brings the graph-processing capabilities of those networks into a kernel formulation. The approach aims to retain neural-network expressiveness while obtaining the training and analytical advantages associated with graph kernels, connecting two methods that otherwise appear quite different.

The authors prove that these kernels can learn a class of smooth functions on graphs. They also report strong empirical results on graph classification datasets. The theoretical and experimental findings address separate questions: the proof establishes learnability for a particular function class, while the classification results demonstrate practical performance on the tested datasets.
summary.tldr: Graph Neural Tangent Kernels connect infinitely wide graph neural networks with kernel learning, yielding learnability guarantees and strong graph-classification results.

title: Graph Neural Tangent Kernel: Fusing Graph Neural Networks with Graph Kernels

abstract: State representation learning, or the ability to capture latent generative factors of an environment is crucial for building intelligent agents that can perform a wide variety of tasks. Learning such representations in an unsupervised manner without supervision from rewards is an open problem. We introduce a method that tries to learn better state representations by maximizing mutual information across spatially and temporally distinct features of a neural encoder of the observations. We also introduce a new benchmark based on Atari 2600 games where we evaluate representations based on how well they capture the ground truth state. We believe this new framework for evaluating representation learning models will be crucial for future representation learning research. Finally, we compare our technique with other state-of-the-art generative and contrastive representation learning methods.

We also introduce a new benchmark based on Atari 2600 games where we evaluate representations based on how well they capture the ground truth state. We believe this new framework for evaluating representation learning models will be crucial for future representation learning research. Finally, we compare our technique with other state-of-the-art generative and contrastive representation learning methods.

paragraphs: An intelligent agent benefits from representations that capture the underlying state of its environment rather than only the appearance of an observation. This paper investigates learning those representations without reward supervision. It contributes both a learning method and a benchmark for checking how much true state information a representation preserves.

The method maximizes mutual information between features from a neural observation encoder at different spatial locations and times. This encourages information to be shared across features that describe distinct parts or moments of the observations. The training signal comes from those relationships, allowing representation learning without a task reward specifying which features matter.

The benchmark uses Atari 2600 games and evaluates representations by how well they capture ground-truth state. The authors compare their method with generative and contrastive representation learning approaches. The abstract does not state a winning method; its reported contribution is an approach and evaluation framework centered on recovering environment state, with the authors arguing that this framework can support future research.
summary.tldr: The paper learns reward-free Atari representations through spatial and temporal mutual information and evaluates how well they capture true environment state.

title: Unsupervised State Representation Learning in Atari

abstract: Temporal prediction is critical for making intelligent and robust decisions in complex dynamic environments. Motion prediction needs to model the inherently uncertain future which often contains multiple potential outcomes, due to multi-agent interactions and the latent goals of others. Towards these goals, we introduce a probabilistic framework that efficiently learns latent variables to jointly model the multi-step future motions of agents in a scene. Our framework is data-driven and learns semantically meaningful latent variables to represent the multimodal future, without requiring explicit labels. Using a dynamic attention-based state encoder, we learn to encode the past as well as the future interactions among agents, efficiently scaling to any number of agents. Finally, our model can be used for planning via computing a conditional probability density over the trajectories of other agents given a hypothetical rollout of the ego agent. We demonstrate our algorithms by predicting vehicle trajectories of both simulated and real data, demonstrating the state-of-the-art results on several vehicle trajectory datasets.

Finally, our model can be used for planning via computing a conditional probability density over the trajectories of other agents given a hypothetical rollout of the ego agent. We demonstrate our algorithms by predicting vehicle trajectories of both simulated and real data, demonstrating the state-of-the-art results on several vehicle trajectory datasets.

paragraphs: Predicting motion requires allowing for several plausible futures, especially when multiple agents interact and their goals are hidden. A vehicle’s future trajectory depends partly on what surrounding vehicles do. This paper develops a probabilistic framework that jointly models agents’ motion over multiple future steps instead of reducing that uncertainty to one outcome.

The framework learns latent variables that represent distinct possible futures without explicit labels for those variables. The authors report that the learned variables have meaningful interpretations. A dynamic attention-based state encoder represents interactions involving agents’ past and future motion, and the architecture is designed to scale efficiently to varying numbers of agents.

The model can also support planning by calculating a probability density over other agents’ trajectories conditional on a hypothetical trajectory for the ego agent. This provides a way to evaluate how predicted behavior depends on a contemplated action sequence. Experiments on simulated and real vehicle trajectories report state-of-the-art results on several datasets, supporting the framework’s ability to model uncertain, interacting motion.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic motion model learns multiple joint futures without explicit latent labels and can condition predictions on an ego agent’s hypothetical plan.

title: Multiple Futures Prediction

abstract: Flexible variational distributions improve variational inference but are harder to optimize. In this work we present a control variate that is applicable for any reparameterizable distribution with known mean and covariance, e.g. Gaussians with any covariance structure. The control variate is based on a quadratic approximation of the model, and its parameters are set using a double-descent scheme. We empirically show that this control variate leads to large improvements in gradient variance and optimization convergence for inference with non-factorized variational distributions.
originalAbstract: Flexible variational distributions improve variational inference but are harder to optimize. In this work we present a control variate that is applicable for any reparameterizable distribution with known mean and covariance, e.g. Gaussians with any covariance structure. The control variate is based on a quadratic approximation of the model, and its parameters are set using a double-descent scheme. We empirically show that this control variate leads to large improvements in gradient variance and optimization convergence for inference with non-factorized variational distributions.

paragraphs: Variational inference uses an adjustable probability distribution to approximate a model's uncertainty. More flexible distributions can improve that approximation, but they can also make optimization harder. This paper addresses that optimization difficulty by reducing the variability of reparameterization gradients, the estimates used to adjust the distribution during learning.

The proposed tool is a control variate built from a quadratic approximation of the model. A control variate provides a structured correction that reduces noise in an estimate. The authors set its parameters through a double-descent scheme. The method applies to reparameterizable distributions whose mean and covariance are known, including Gaussian distributions with different covariance structures.

Experiments show large improvements in gradient variance and optimization convergence for non-factorized variational distributions, which can represent dependencies between variables. The contribution therefore helps make richer approximations more practical to optimize. Its stated applicability depends on reparameterization and known distribution moments; the reported optimization gains are empirical findings for the inference settings studied.
summary.tldr: A quadratic control variate reduces gradient noise and improves optimization in experiments with flexible variational distributions.

title: Approximation Based Variance Reduction for Reparameterization Gradients

abstract: Offering prediction APIs for fee is a fast growing industry and is an important aspect of machine learning as a service. While many such services are available, the heterogeneity in their price and performance makes it challenging for users to decide which API or combination of APIs to use for their own data and budget. We take a first step towards addressing this challenge by proposing FrugalML, a principled framework that jointly learns the strength and weakness of each API on different data, and performs an efficient optimization to automatically identify the best sequential strategy to adaptively use the available APIs within a budget constraint. Our theoretical analysis shows that natural sparsity in the formulation can be leveraged to make FrugalML efficient. We conduct systematic experiments using ML APIs from Google, Microsoft, Amazon, IBM, Baidu and other providers for tasks including facial emotion recognition, sentiment analysis and speech recognition. Across various tasks, FrugalML can achieve up to 90% cost reduction while matching the accuracy of the best single API, or up to 5% better accuracy while matching the best API’s cost.

paragraphs: Paid prediction APIs differ in both price and performance, and their strengths can vary across a user's data. FrugalML addresses the resulting decision problem: how to choose an API, or a sequence of APIs, while respecting a budget. Its starting point is that the best service to use need not be the same for every example.

The framework learns where each API performs well or poorly and optimizes an adaptive sequential strategy for using the available services. It therefore treats service selection and budget allocation as a joint learning problem. The theoretical analysis identifies sparsity in the formulation that can be used to make the optimization efficient.

The experiments cover facial emotion recognition, sentiment analysis, and speech recognition using APIs from several providers. Across the evaluated tasks, FrugalML achieves up to 90% lower cost while matching the best single API's accuracy, or up to 5% better accuracy at the best API's cost. These are separate reported tradeoffs and maxima across tasks. They demonstrate that combining services according to their strengths can improve the cost–accuracy balance.
summary.tldr: FrugalML learns budget-aware sequences of prediction APIs, achieving substantial cost savings or accuracy gains in the reported tasks.

title: FrugalML: How to use ML Prediction APIs more accurately and cheaply

abstract: We present a method for learning generalized Hamiltonian decompositions of ordinary differential equations given a set of noisy time series measurements. Our method simultaneously learns a continuous time model and a scalar energy function for a general dynamical system. Learning predictive models in this form allows one to place strong, high-level, physics inspired priors onto the form of the learnt governing equations for general dynamical systems. Moreover, having shown how our method extends and unifies some previous work in deep learning with physics inspired priors, we present a novel method for learning continuous time models from the weak form of the governing equations which is less computationally taxing than standard adjoint methods.

paragraphs: This paper learns continuous-time dynamical models from noisy time-series measurements. Its target is a generalized Hamiltonian decomposition of ordinary differential equations. Alongside the model describing how the system changes, the method learns a scalar energy function, giving the learned dynamics an explicit physics-inspired form.

That form allows strong, high-level prior assumptions to constrain the governing equations. The aim is therefore not only to fit observed trajectories, but to express predictions through a structured description of a general dynamical system. The authors also show how their formulation extends and brings together earlier deep-learning approaches that incorporate physics-inspired priors.

A second contribution is a method for learning continuous-time models from the weak form of the governing equations. The authors describe this approach as less computationally demanding than standard adjoint methods. Together, the contributions address both what structure a dynamical model should learn and how to train it. The result is a framework that jointly learns dynamics and energy while providing a less costly route to continuous-time model fitting.
summary.tldr: The method jointly learns continuous-time dynamics and an energy function from noisy measurements, using weak-form equations to reduce training cost.

title: Weak Form Generalized Hamiltonian Learning

abstract: Many latent-variable applications, including community detection, collaborative filtering, genomic analysis, and NLP, model data as generated by low-rank matrices. Yet despite considerable research, except for very special cases, the number of samples required to efficiently recover the underlying matrices has not been known. We determine the onset of learning in several common latent-variable settings. For all of them, we show that learning $k\times k$, rank-$r$, matrices to normalized $L_1$ distance $\epsilon$ requires $\Omega(\frac{kr}{\epsilon^2})$ samples, and propose an algorithm that uses ${\cal O}(\frac{kr}{\epsilon^2}\log^2\frac r\epsilon)$ samples, a number linear in the high dimension, and nearly linear in the, typically low, rank. The algorithm improves on existing spectral techniques and runs in polynomial time. The proofs establish new results on the rapid convergence of the spectral distance between the model and observation matrices, and may be of independent interest.

paragraphs: Many latent-variable models describe observed data using a low-rank matrix. This structure appears in applications including community detection, collaborative filtering, genomics, and language processing. The paper asks how many samples are needed to recover such matrices efficiently, establishing bounds in several common latent-variable settings where that requirement had remained unresolved.

For a k-by-k matrix of rank r, the authors show that attaining normalized L1 error ε requires at least order kr/ε² samples. Their algorithm uses order (kr/ε²) log²(r/ε) samples. Thus, its sample requirement matches the lower bound apart from a logarithmic factor, scaling linearly with the matrix dimension and nearly linearly with rank.

The algorithm runs in polynomial time and improves on existing spectral techniques. Its proofs also establish new results about how rapidly the spectral distance between model and observation matrices converges. Together, these contributions quantify the sample scale needed for learning in the analyzed settings and provide an efficient procedure that comes close to that statistical requirement.
summary.tldr: A polynomial-time algorithm learns low-rank matrices with sample requirements matching established lower bounds up to logarithmic factors.

title: Linear-Sample Learning of Low-Rank Distributions

abstract: We consider non-convex stochastic optimization using first-order algorithms for which the gradient estimates may have heavy tails. We show that a combination of gradient clipping, momentum, and normalized gradient descent yields convergence to critical points in high-probability with best-known rates for smooth losses when the gradients only have bounded $\mathfrak{p}$th moments for some $\mathfrak{p}\in(1,2]$. We then consider the case of second-order smooth losses, which to our knowledge have not been studied in this setting, and again obtain high-probability bounds for any $\mathfrak{p}$. Moreover, our results hold for arbitrary smooth norms, in contrast to the typical SGD analysis which requires a Hilbert space norm. Further, we show that after a suitable "burn-in" period, the objective value will monotonically decrease for every iteration until a critical point is identified, which provides intuition behind the popular practice of learning rate "warm-up'' and also yields a last-iterate guarantee.

We then consider the case of second-order smooth losses, which to our knowledge have not been studied in this setting, and again obtain high-probability bounds for any $\mathfrak{p}$. Moreover, our results hold for arbitrary smooth norms, in contrast to the typical SGD analysis which requires a Hilbert space norm. paragraphs: Stochastic optimization uses noisy gradient estimates, and heavy-tailed noise can produce unusually large estimates. This paper studies non-convex optimization when gradients have only a bounded pth moment for some p between one and two, including two. That assumption permits noise beyond settings that require a bounded second moment.

The proposed combination uses gradient clipping, momentum, and normalized gradient descent. For smooth losses, the authors prove convergence to critical points with high probability at best-known rates. They also obtain high-probability bounds under second-order smoothness and allow arbitrary smooth norms, extending beyond the Hilbert-space norms typical of stochastic-gradient analyses.

A further result concerns the course of optimization: after an appropriate burn-in period, the objective decreases at every iteration until a critical point is identified, within the stated guarantee. This also yields a guarantee for the last iterate. The authors connect the burn-in behavior to intuition behind learning-rate warm-up; convergence to a critical point does not assert a global minimum.
summary.tldr: Clipping, momentum, and normalized gradient descent yield high-probability convergence guarantees despite heavy-tailed gradient noise.

title: High-probability Bounds for Non-Convex Stochastic Optimization with Heavy Tails

abstract: Score-based generative models (SGMs) have recently demonstrated impressive results in terms of both sample quality and distribution coverage. However, they are usually applied directly in data space and often require thousands of network evaluations for sampling. Here, we propose the Latent Score-based Generative Model (LSGM), a novel approach that trains SGMs in a latent space, relying on the variational autoencoder framework. Moving from data to latent space allows us to train more expressive generative models, apply SGMs to non-continuous data, and learn smoother SGMs in a smaller space, resulting in fewer network evaluations and faster sampling. To enable training LSGMs end-to-end in a scalable and stable manner, we (i) introduce a new score-matching objective suitable to the LSGM setting, (ii) propose a novel parameterization of the score function that allows SGM to focus on the mismatch of the target distribution with respect to a simple Normal one, and (iii) analytically derive multiple techniques for variance reduction of the training objective. LSGM obtains a state-of-the-art FID score of 2.10 on CIFAR-10, outperforming all existing generative results on this dataset. On CelebA-HQ-256, LSGM is on a par with previous SGMs in sample quality while outperforming them in sampling time by two orders of magnitude. In modeling binary images, LSGM achieves state-of-the-art likelihood on the binarized OMNIGLOT dataset.

paragraphs: Score-based generative models can produce strong samples but often need thousands of network evaluations to generate them. This paper moves score-based modeling from the original data into a latent space using a variational autoencoder framework. The smaller, smoother space supports faster sampling, more expressive generative modeling, and applications to non-continuous data.

The latent score-based generative model introduces three ingredients for scalable, stable end-to-end training. A new score-matching objective fits the latent setting. A score parameterization focuses learning on the difference between the target distribution and a simple Normal distribution. Analytically derived variance-reduction techniques make the training objective more manageable. These changes support learning the latent generative model together with the autoencoder.

The reported CIFAR-10 FID is 2.10, surpassing existing generative results in the paper’s comparison. On CelebA-HQ-256, sample quality matches previous score-based models while sampling is faster by two orders of magnitude. State-of-the-art likelihood on binarized OMNIGLOT also demonstrates the approach on binary images. The findings support latent modeling as a route to both strong generation and reduced sampling cost.
summary.tldr: Training score-based generators inside a variational autoencoder’s latent space achieves strong generation results with substantially faster sampling.

title: Score-based Generative Modeling in Latent Space

abstract: Learning how complex dynamical systems evolve over time is a key challenge in system identification. For safety critical systems, it is often crucial that the learned model is guaranteed to converge to some equilibrium point. To this end, neural ODEs regularized with neural Lyapunov functions are a promising approach when states are fully observed. For practical applications however, {\em partial observations} are the norm. As we will demonstrate, initialization of unobserved augmented states can become a key problem for neural ODEs. To alleviate this issue, we propose to augment the system's state with its history. Inspired by state augmentation in discrete-time systems, we thus obtain {\em neural delay differential equations}. Based on classical time delay stability analysis, we then show how to ensure stability of the learned models, and theoretically analyze our approach. Our experiments demonstrate its applicability to stable system identification of partially observed systems and learning a stabilizing feedback policy in delayed feedback control.

Neural ordinary differential equations regularized by neural Lyapunov functions offer a promising route when the full state is observed, but practical measurements often reveal only part of it.

The paper identifies initialization of unobserved augmented states as an important difficulty for neural ordinary differential equations. To alleviate that issue, the authors augment the system with its history, producing neural delay differential equations. Past information becomes part of the dynamics formulation, addressing the problem of modeling a system from incomplete observations.

Using classical stability analysis for time-delay systems, the authors show how to ensure stability of the learned models and theoretically analyze the approach. Experiments demonstrate applications to stable identification of partially observed systems and to learning a stabilizing policy for delayed feedback control. The contribution connects a history-based model representation with stability analysis, so incomplete observation and delayed feedback can be addressed within a theoretically studied framework.
summary.tldr: Neural delay differential equations incorporate state history and time-delay stability analysis to learn stable dynamics from partial observations.

title: Learning Stable Deep Dynamics Models for Partially Observed or Delayed Dynamical Systems

abstract: Conditional generative models of high-dimensional images have many applications, but supervision signals from conditions to images can be expensive to acquire. This paper describes Diffusion-Decoding models with Contrastive representations (D2C), a paradigm for training unconditional variational autoencoders (VAE) for few-shot conditional image generation. D2C uses a learned diffusion-based prior over the latent representations to improve generation and contrastive self-supervised learning to improve representation quality. D2C can adapt to novel generation tasks, conditioned on labels or manipulation constraints, by learning from as few as 100 labeled examples. On conditional generation from new labels, D2C achieves superior performance over state-of-the-art VAEs and diffusion models. On conditional image manipulation, D2C generations are two orders of magnitude faster to produce over StyleGAN2 ones and are preferred by 50% - 60% of the human evaluators in a double-blind study. We release our code at https://github.com/jiamings/d2c.

title: D2C: Diffusion-Decoding Models for Few-Shot Conditional Generation

abstract: Modeling the time evolution of discrete sets of items (e.g., genetic mutations) is a fundamental problem in many biomedical applications. We approach this problem through the lens of continuous-time Markov chains, and show that the resulting learning task is generally underspecified in the usual setting of cross-sectional data. We explore a perhaps surprising remedy: including a number of additional independent items can help determine time order, and hence resolve underspecification. This is in sharp contrast to the common practice of limiting the analysis to a small subset of relevant items, which is followed largely due to poor scaling of existing methods. To put our theoretical insight into practice, we develop an approximate likelihood maximization method for learning continuous-time Markov chains, which can scale to hundreds of items and is orders of magnitude faster than previous methods. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on synthetic and real cancer data.

The authors report that it is orders of magnitude faster than previous approaches and demonstrate effectiveness on synthetic and real cancer data. The theoretical and computational contributions reinforce each other: considering additional items can help identify temporal structure, and the faster method makes that expanded modeling practical.
summary.tldr: Including additional independent items can help identify temporal order, and a scalable Markov-chain learning method makes this strategy practical.

title: Scaling up Continuous-Time Markov Chains Helps Resolve Underspecification

abstract: Recent deep-learning models have achieved impressive prediction performance, but often sacrifice interpretability and computational efficiency. Interpretability is crucial in many disciplines, such as science and medicine, where models must be carefully vetted or where interpretation is the goal itself. Moreover, interpretable models are concise and often yield computational efficiency. Here, we propose adaptive wavelet distillation (AWD), a method which aims to distill information from a trained neural network into a wavelet transform. Specifically, AWD penalizes feature attributions of a neural network in the wavelet domain to learn an effective multi-resolution wavelet transform. The resulting model is highly predictive, concise, computationally efficient, and has properties (such as a multi-scale structure) which make it easy to interpret. In close collaboration with domain experts, we showcase how AWD addresses challenges in two real-world settings: cosmological parameter inference and molecular-partner prediction. In both cases, AWD yields a scientifically interpretable and concise model which gives predictive performance better than state-of-the-art neural networks. Moreover, AWD identifies predictive features that are scientifically meaningful in the context of respective domains. All code and models are released in a full-fledged package available on Github.

AWD learns the transform by penalizing the network’s feature attributions in the wavelet domain. The resulting model is intended to remain predictive while becoming concise and computationally efficient. The authors develop applications in collaboration with domain experts rather than assessing interpretability solely through a generic visualization.

The demonstrations involve cosmological-parameter inference and molecular-partner prediction. In both settings, the distilled models outperform state-of-the-art neural networks and identify features judged scientifically meaningful in the respective domains. The abstract does not quantify the gains or establish that every network can be distilled equally well. Its evidence supports this approach in the two studied scientific applications.
summary.tldr: Adaptive wavelet distillation converts neural-network information into concise multiscale models.

title: Adaptive wavelet distillation from neural networks through interpretations

abstract: The attention module, which is a crucial component in Transformer, cannot scale efficiently to long sequences due to its quadratic complexity. Many works focus on approximating the dot-then-exponentiate softmax function in the original attention, leading to sub-quadratic or even linear-complexity Transformer architectures. However, we show that these methods cannot be applied to more powerful attention modules that go beyond the dot-then-exponentiate style, e.g., Transformers with relative positional encoding (RPE). Since in many state-of-the-art models, relative positional encoding is used as default, designing efficient Transformers that can incorporate RPE is appealing. In this paper, we propose a novel way to accelerate attention calculation for Transformers with RPE on top of the kernelized attention. Based upon the observation that relative positional encoding forms a Toeplitz matrix, we mathematically show that kernelized attention with RPE can be calculated efficiently using Fast Fourier Transform (FFT). With FFT, our method achieves $\mathcal{O}(n\log n)$ time complexity. Interestingly, we further demonstrate that properly using relative positional encoding can mitigate the training instability problem of vanilla kernelized attention. On a wide range of tasks, we empirically show that our models can be trained from scratch without any optimization issues. The learned model performs better than many efficient Transformer variants and is faster than standard Transformer in the long-sequence regime.

Kernelized approximations can reduce that cost, but the approaches discussed in this paper do not directly accommodate richer attention mechanisms such as relative positional encoding. The authors develop an efficient calculation that preserves this positional information.

Across a wide range of tasks, their models train from scratch without observed optimization issues. They report better performance than many efficient Transformer variants and greater speed than a standard Transformer for long sequences, combining computational and empirical benefits.
summary.tldr: Using Toeplitz structure and FFT makes kernelized attention with relative positions efficient and can improve its training stability.

title: Stable, Fast and Accurate: Kernelized Attention with Relative Positional Encoding

abstract: Reliable evaluation of adversarial defenses is a challenging task, currently limited to an expert who manually crafts attacks that exploit the defense’s inner workings, or to approaches based on ensemble of fixed attacks, none of which may be effective for the specific defense at hand. Our key observation is that adaptive attacks are composed from a set of reusable building blocks that can be formalized in a search space and used to automatically discover attacks for unknown defenses. We evaluated our approach on 24 adversarial defenses and show that it outperforms AutoAttack, the current state-of-the-art tool for reliable evaluation of adversarial defenses: our tool discovered significantly stronger attacks by producing 3.0%-50.8% additional adversarial examples for 10 models, while obtaining attacks with slightly stronger or similar strength for the remaining models.

paragraphs: Evaluating an adversarial defense requires attacks capable of exposing its particular weaknesses. A defense can appear effective when the chosen attacks fail to exploit how it works. Existing evaluation approaches depend either on experts crafting attacks for individual defenses or on collections of fixed attacks, whose members may all be poorly suited to a particular model.

The paper proposes automating the discovery of adaptive attacks. Its central observation is that such attacks can be assembled from reusable components. By representing those components and their combinations as a search space, the method can look for attacks suited to an unfamiliar defense. This turns part of the expert's design task into a search problem.

The authors evaluate the approach on 24 defenses and report stronger results than AutoAttack. For 10 models, their tool produces 3.0%–50.8% additional adversarial examples; for the remaining models, attacks are slightly stronger or similar. These findings show that searching over adaptable attack components can reveal weaknesses missed by a strong fixed evaluation tool in the tested defenses.
summary.tldr: Searching combinations of reusable attack components exposes weaknesses that fixed adversarial evaluation attacks can miss.

title: Automated Discovery of Adaptive Attacks on Adversarial Defenses

abstract: We study personalization of supervised learning with user-level differential privacy. Consider a setting with many users, each of whom has a training data set drawn from their own distribution $P_i$. Assuming some shared structure among the problems $P_i$, can users collectively learn the shared structure---and solve their tasks better than they could individually---while preserving the privacy of their data? We formulate this question using joint, user-level differential privacy---that is, we control what is leaked about each user's entire data set. We provide algorithms that exploit popular non-private approaches in this domain like the Almost-No-Inner-Loop (ANIL) method, and give strong user-level privacy guarantees for our general approach. When the problems $P_i$ are linear regression problems with each user's regression vector lying in a common, unknown low-dimensional subspace, we show that our efficient algorithms satisfy nearly optimal estimation error guarantees. We also establish a general, information-theoretic upper bound via an exponential mechanism-based algorithm.

paragraphs: Personalized learning must accommodate users whose data come from different distributions. If their tasks share some structure, learning together could help each user more than learning alone. This paper studies how to exploit that common structure while protecting information about each user's entire dataset through joint, user-level differential privacy.

The authors develop algorithms that adapt established personalization approaches, including Almost-No-Inner-Loop, and provide strong user-level privacy guarantees for their general framework. The unit of protection is important: the formulation controls leakage about a whole user's dataset, rather than treating each individual training example as the only privacy concern.

The strongest stated estimation result concerns linear regression with a specific shared structure. Each user's regression vector must lie in the same unknown low-dimensional subspace. Under that assumption, the efficient algorithms achieve nearly optimal estimation-error guarantees. The paper also gives a general information-theoretic upper bound using an exponential-mechanism-based algorithm. Together, these results establish both an efficient solution for a structured setting and a broader bound on what private personalization can achieve.
summary.tldr: The paper develops private personalization algorithms with nearly optimal estimation guarantees for regression tasks sharing a low-dimensional subspace.

title: Differentially Private Model Personalization

abstract: Neural MMO is a computationally accessible research platform that combines large agent populations, long time horizons, open-ended tasks, and modular game systems. Existing environments feature subsets of these properties, but Neural MMO is the first to combine them all. We present Neural MMO as free and open source software with active support, ongoing development, documentation, and additional training, logging, and visualization tools to help users adapt to this new setting. Initial baselines on the platform demonstrate that agents trained in large populations explore more and learn a progression of skills. We raise other more difficult problems such as many-team cooperation as open research questions which Neural MMO is well-suited to answer. Finally, we discuss current limitations of the platform, potential mitigations, and plans for continued development.

It combines large populations, extended time horizons, open-ended tasks, and modular game systems. The authors present this combination as its distinctive contribution, noting that earlier environments include subsets of these properties.

The platform is designed to be computationally accessible and is released as free, open-source software. Documentation and tools for training, logging, and visualization accompany the environment. These resources support researchers in adapting to a setting where learning involves sustained interaction among large numbers of agents rather than only isolated decision makers.

Initial baseline experiments show that agents trained in large populations explore more and acquire a progression of skills. These observations provide early evidence about learning in the platform. More difficult problems, including cooperation among many teams, remain open research questions that Neural MMO is intended to support. The paper also discusses platform limitations, possible mitigations, and continued development.
summary.tldr: Neural MMO supports large-population, long-horizon agent research, with initial experiments showing increased exploration and progressive skill learning.

title: The Neural MMO Platform for Massively Multiagent Research

abstract: We analyze the convergence rates of stochastic gradient algorithms for smooth finite-sum minimax optimization and show that, for many such algorithms, sampling the data points \emph{without replacement} leads to faster convergence compared to sampling with replacement. For the smooth and strongly convex-strongly concave setting, we consider gradient descent ascent and the proximal point method, and present a unified analysis of two popular without-replacement sampling strategies, namely \emph{Random Reshuffling} (RR), which shuffles the data every epoch, and \emph{Single Shuffling} or \emph{Shuffle Once} (SO), which shuffles only at the beginning. We obtain tight convergence rates for RR and SO and demonstrate that these strategies lead to faster convergence than uniform sampling. Moving beyond convexity, we obtain similar results for smooth nonconvex-nonconcave objectives satisfying a two-sided Polyak-\L{}ojasiewicz inequality. Finally, we demonstrate that our techniques are general enough to analyze the effect of \emph{data-ordering attacks}, where an adversary manipulates the order in which data points are supplied to the optimizer. Our analysis also recovers tight rates for the \emph{incremental gradient} method, where the data points are not shuffled at all.

paragraphs: Stochastic optimization depends on how examples are selected as well as on the update rule. This paper analyzes that choice for smooth finite-sum minimax problems, where one variable is minimized while another is maximized. It shows that sampling without replacement gives faster convergence for many of the algorithms studied.

For strongly convex-strongly concave objectives, the authors analyze gradient descent-ascent and the proximal point method. It also handles adversarial manipulation of data order and recovers tight rates for incremental gradient updates with no shuffling. The results make data order a theoretically consequential algorithmic choice, while tying the faster rates to explicit structural conditions on the objective.
summary.tldr: Without-replacement sampling yields provably faster convergence for several minimax algorithms under the studied structural conditions.

title: Sampling without Replacement Leads to Faster Rates in Finite-Sum Minimax Optimization

abstract: Existing defenses against adversarial examples such as adversarial training typically assume that the adversary will conform to a specific or known threat model, such as $\ell_p$ perturbations within a fixed budget. In this paper, we focus on the scenario where there is a mismatch in the threat model assumed by the defense during training, and the actual capabilities of the adversary at test time. We ask the question: if the learner trains against a specific ``source" threat model, when can we expect robustness to generalize to a stronger unknown ``target" threat model during test-time? Our key contribution is to formally define the problem of learning and generalization with an unforeseen adversary, which helps us reason about the increase in adversarial risk from the conventional perspective of a known adversary. Applying our framework, we derive a generalization bound which relates the generalization gap between source and target threat models to variation of the feature extractor, which measures the expected maximum difference between extracted features across a given threat model. Based on our generalization bound, we propose variation regularization (VR) which reduces variation of the feature extractor across the source threat model during training. We empirically demonstrate that using VR can lead to improved generalization to unforeseen attacks during test-time, and combining VR with perceptual adversarial training (Laidlaw et al., 2021) achieves state-of-the-art robustness on unforeseen attacks. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/inspire-group/variation-regularization.

It asks when robustness learned under a source threat model can generalize to an unknown, stronger target threat model.

Here, variation measures the expected maximum difference between extracted features across a threat model. The significance is a link between a formal account of threat-model mismatch and a concrete training intervention. The empirical result supports improved transfer of robustness in the evaluated settings, while retaining the paper's qualified claim that such improvement can occur.
summary.tldr: A bound relating threat-model generalization to feature variation motivates regularization that can improve robustness to unforeseen attacks.

title: Formulating Robustness Against Unforeseen Attacks

abstract: Learning visual representations from natural language supervision has recently shown great promise in a number of pioneering works. In general, these language-augmented visual models demonstrate strong transferability to a variety of datasets/tasks. However, it remains challenging to evaluate the transferablity of these foundation models due to the lack of easy-to-use toolkits for fair benchmarking. To tackle this, we build ELEVATER (Evaluation of Language-augmented Visual Task-level Transfer), the first benchmark to compare and evaluate pre-trained language-augmented visual models. Several highlights include: (i) Datasets. As downstream evaluation suites, it consists of 20 image classification datasets and 35 object detection datasets, each of which is augmented with external knowledge. (ii) Toolkit. An automatic hyper-parameter tuning toolkit is developed to ensure the fairness in model adaption. To leverage the full power of language-augmented visual models, novel language-aware initialization methods are proposed to significantly improve the adaption performance. (iii) Metrics. A variety of evaluation metrics are used, including sample-efficiency (zero-shot and few-shot) and parameter-efficiency (linear probing and full model fine-tuning). We will publicly release ELEVATER.

paragraphs: Visual models trained with language supervision can transfer to many tasks, but comparing that transfer fairly requires consistent evaluation procedures. ELEVATER addresses this problem with a benchmark and toolkit for pretrained language-augmented visual models. Its evaluation suite includes 20 image-classification datasets and 35 object-detection datasets, each supplemented with external knowledge.

The toolkit automates hyperparameter tuning to support fairer model adaptation. This matters because comparisons can reflect how carefully each model was adapted as well as the quality of its pretrained representation. The authors also introduce initialization methods that use language information and report significant improvements in adaptation performance.

ELEVATER evaluates transfer from several perspectives. Zero-shot and few-shot settings examine performance with no task examples or only a small number, while linear probing and full fine-tuning examine different levels of parameter adaptation. Together, these settings make it possible to compare how models use labeled data and how much adaptation they require. The paper's contribution is a common evaluation framework that connects broad task coverage with practical tools for adapting and comparing models.
summary.tldr: ELEVATER combines diverse visual tasks, automated tuning, and multiple adaptation settings to benchmark language-augmented visual models.

title: ELEVATER: A Benchmark and Toolkit for Evaluating Language-Augmented Visual Models

abstract: Adversarial robustness is a key desirable property of neural networks. It has been empirically shown to be affected by their sizes, with larger networks being typically more robust. Recently, \citet{bubeck2021universal} proved a lower bound on the Lipschitz constant of functions that fit the training data in terms of their number of parameters. This raises an interesting open question, do---and can---functions with more parameters, but not necessarily more computational cost, have better robustness? We study this question for sparse Mixture of Expert models (MoEs), that make it possible to scale up the model size for a roughly constant computational cost. We theoretically show that under certain conditions on the routing and the structure of the data, MoEs can have significantly smaller Lipschitz constants than their dense counterparts. The robustness of MoEs can suffer when the highest weighted experts for an input implement sufficiently different functions. We next empirically evaluate the robustness of MoEs on ImageNet using adversarial attacks and show they are indeed more robust than dense models with the same computational cost. We make key observations showing the robustness of MoEs to the choice of experts, highlighting the redundancy of experts in models trained in practice.

Recently, \citet{bubeck2021universal} proved a lower bound on the Lipschitz constant of functions that fit the training data in terms of their number of parameters. This raises an interesting open question, do---and can---functions with more parameters, but not necessarily more computational cost, have better robustness? We study this question for sparse Mixture of Expert models (MoEs), that make it possible to scale up the model size for a roughly constant computational cost. We theoretically show that under certain conditions on the routing and the structure of the data, MoEs can have significantly smaller Lipschitz constants than their dense counterparts. The robustness of MoEs can suffer when the highest weighted experts for an input implement sufficiently different functions. We next empirically evaluate the robustness of MoEs on ImageNet using adversarial attacks and show they are indeed more robust than dense models with the same computational cost. We make key observations showing the robustness of MoEs to the choice of experts, highlighting the redundancy of experts in models trained in practice.

paragraphs: Larger neural networks are often empirically more resistant to adversarial perturbations, but increasing size can also increase computation. Sparse mixture-of-experts models offer a way to add parameters while keeping computational cost roughly constant. The paper investigates whether this separation can provide robustness benefits without the corresponding expense of a larger dense model.

The theoretical analysis studies Lipschitz constants, which characterize how much a function can change as its input changes. Under particular conditions on routing and data structure, the authors show that mixtures of experts can have substantially smaller constants than dense counterparts. They also identify a vulnerability: robustness can deteriorate when the highest-weighted experts for an input implement sufficiently different functions.

ImageNet experiments with adversarial attacks find the evaluated mixtures more robust than dense models at the same computational cost. Additional observations show robustness to the choice of experts and indicate redundancy among experts in trained models. Together, the results connect conditional theoretical advantages with empirical evidence, while highlighting the importance of expert behavior and routing.
summary.tldr: Sparse mixtures of experts show conditional theoretical and empirical robustness advantages over dense networks with comparable computational cost.

title: On the Adversarial Robustness of Mixture of Experts

abstract: We present a new concentration of measure inequality for sums of independent bounded random variables, which we name a split-kl inequality. The inequality combines the combinatorial power of the kl inequality with ability to exploit low variance. While for Bernoulli random variables the kl inequality is tighter than the Empirical Bernstein, for random variables taking values inside a bounded interval and having low variance the Empirical Bernstein inequality is tighter than the kl. The proposed split-kl inequality yields the best of both worlds. We discuss an application of the split-kl inequality to bounding excess losses. We also derive a PAC-Bayes-split-kl inequality and use a synthetic example and several UCI datasets to compare it with the PAC-Bayes-kl, PAC-Bayes Empirical Bernstein, PAC-Bayes Unexpected Bernstein, and PAC-Bayes Empirical Bennett inequalities.
