The central contribution is the construction of a bound that can exploit distributional structure and low variance together.
summary.tldr: Split-kl combines strengths of kl and variance-sensitive concentration bounds, with a PAC-Bayes extension for learning guarantees.

title: Split-kl and PAC-Bayes-split-kl Inequalities for Ternary Random Variables

abstract: Motivated by the statistical and computational challenges of computing Wasserstein distances in high-dimensional contexts, machine learning researchers have defined modified Wasserstein distances based on computing distances between one-dimensional projections of the measures. Different choices of how to aggregate these projected distances (averaging, random sampling, maximizing) give rise to different distances, requiring different statistical analyses. We define the \emph{Sliced Wasserstein Process}, a stochastic process defined by the empirical Wasserstein distance between projections of empirical probability measures to all one-dimensional subspaces, and prove a uniform distributional limit theorem for this process. As a result, we obtain a unified framework in which to prove sample complexity and distributional limit results for all Wasserstein distances based on one-dimensional projections. We illustrate these results on a number of examples where no distributional limits were previously known.

paragraphs: Comparing probability distributions with Wasserstein distances becomes statistically and computationally challenging in high dimensions. A common alternative projects the distributions onto one-dimensional directions and compares the resulting projections. Averaging these comparisons, sampling directions, or taking the largest comparison produces different distances, each of which has traditionally required its own statistical analysis.

This paper brings those analyses together by defining the Sliced Wasserstein Process. The process tracks empirical Wasserstein comparisons across all one-dimensional subspaces simultaneously. Instead of starting with a particular way of combining directions, the authors first study the collection of projected comparisons from which those different distances are constructed.

The main result is a uniform distributional limit theorem for this process. It supplies a shared framework for establishing sample complexity and limiting distributions for Wasserstein distances built from one-dimensional projections. The authors illustrate the framework with examples whose distributional limits were previously unknown. Its significance is theoretical: understanding the full process provides a common foundation for analyzing multiple projected distance constructions.
summary.tldr: A uniform limit theorem unifies statistical analysis of Wasserstein distances constructed from one-dimensional projections.

title: Distributional Convergence of the Sliced Wasserstein Process

abstract: Phylogenetics is a classical methodology in computational biology that today has become highly relevant for medical investigation of single-cell data, e.g., in the context of development of cancer. The exponential size of the tree space is unfortunately a formidable obstacle for current Bayesian phylogenetic inference using Markov chain Monte Carlo based methods since these rely on local operations. And although more recent variational inference (VI) based methods offer speed improvements, they rely on expensive auto-differentiation operations for learning the variational parameters. We propose VaiPhy, a remarkably fast VI based algorithm for approximate posterior inference in an \textit{augmented tree space}. VaiPhy produces marginal log-likelihood estimates on par with the state-of-the-art methods on real data, and is considerably faster since it does not require auto-differentiation. Instead, VaiPhy combines coordinate ascent update equations with two novel sampling schemes: (i) \textit{SLANTIS}, a proposal distribution for tree topologies in the augmented tree space, and (ii) the \textit{JC sampler}, the, to the best of our knowledge, first ever scheme for sampling branch lengths directly from the popular Jukes-Cantor model. We compare VaiPhy in terms of density estimation and runtime. Additionally, we evaluate the reproducibility of the baselines. We provide our code on GitHub: \url{https://github.com/Lagergren-Lab/VaiPhy}.

paragraphs: Phylogenetic inference estimates relationships represented as trees, including relationships relevant to single-cell medical research. The number of possible trees grows exponentially, making Bayesian inference difficult. The paper identifies obstacles in both local-search-based Markov chain Monte Carlo methods and variational methods that rely on costly automatic differentiation.

VaiPhy performs approximate posterior inference in an augmented tree space using coordinate-ascent updates instead of automatic differentiation. It combines these updates with two sampling schemes. SLANTIS proposes tree topologies in the augmented space, while the JC sampler draws branch lengths directly from the Jukes-Cantor model. Together, these components address the discrete tree structure and its branch-length parameters.

On real data, VaiPhy produces marginal log-likelihood estimates comparable to state-of-the-art methods while running considerably faster. The authors evaluate density estimation and runtime and also examine the reproducibility of the baselines. The stated result is a favorable balance between inference quality and computation: the method avoids a costly optimization mechanism without sacrificing the reported quality of marginal likelihood estimates.
summary.tldr: VaiPhy combines coordinate-ascent updates with specialized tree and branch-length samplers to accelerate approximate Bayesian phylogenetic inference.

title: VaiPhy: a Variational Inference Based Algorithm for Phylogeny

abstract: Vision-Language Pre-training (VLP) has been shown to be an efficient method to improve the performance of models on different vision-and-language downstream tasks. Substantial studies have shown that neural networks may be able to learn some general rules about language and visual concepts from a large-scale weakly labeled image-text dataset. However, most of the public cross-modal datasets that contain more than 100M image-text pairs are in English; there is a lack of available large-scale and high-quality Chinese VLP datasets. In this work, we propose a new framework for automatic dataset acquisition and cleaning with which we construct a new large-scale and high-quality cross-modal dataset named as TaiSu, containing 166 million images and 219 million Chinese captions. Compared with the recently released Wukong dataset, our dataset is achieved with much stricter restrictions on the semantic correlation of image-text pairs. We also propose to combine texts collected from the web with texts generated by a pre-trained image-captioning model. To the best of our knowledge, TaiSu is currently the largest publicly accessible Chinese cross-modal dataset. Furthermore, we test our dataset on several vision-language downstream tasks. TaiSu outperforms BriVL by a large margin on the zero-shot image-text retrieval task and zero-shot image classification task. TaiSu also shows better performance than Wukong on the image-retrieval task without using image augmentation for training. Results demonstrate that TaiSu can serve as a promising VLP dataset, both for understanding and generative tasks. More information can be referred to https://github.com/ksOAn6g5/TaiSu.

It also combines text collected from the web with captions produced by a pretrained image-captioning model. These choices make the relationship between images and text a central part of the dataset design, alongside the scale of the collection.

TaiSu also performs better than Wukong on image retrieval without training-time image augmentation. Their largest-public-dataset description is explicitly qualified as their knowledge at the time of the work.
summary.tldr: TaiSu provides a large Chinese image-caption dataset built with automatic cleaning and reports strong downstream vision-language results.

title: TaiSu: A 166M Large-scale High-Quality Dataset for Chinese Vision-Language Pre-training

abstract: Many past works aim to improve visual reasoning in models by supervising feature importance (estimated by model explanation techniques) with human annotations such as highlights of important image regions. However, recent work has shown that performance gains from feature importance (FI) supervision for Visual Question Answering (VQA) tasks persist even with random supervision, suggesting that these methods do not meaningfully align model FI with human FI. In this paper, we show that model FI supervision can meaningfully improve VQA model accuracy as well as performance on several Right-for-the-Right-Reason (RRR) metrics by optimizing for four key model objectives: (1) accurate predictions given limited but sufficient information (Sufficiency); (2) max-entropy predictions given no important information (Uncertainty); (3) invariance of predictions to changes in unimportant features (Invariance); and (4) alignment between model FI explanations and human FI explanations (Plausibility). Our best performing method, Visual Feature Importance Supervision (VISFIS), outperforms strong baselines on benchmark VQA datasets in terms of both in-distribution and out-of-distribution accuracy. While past work suggests that the mechanism for improved accuracy is through improved explanation plausibility, we show that this relationship depends crucially on explanation faithfulness (whether explanations truly represent the model’s internal reasoning). Predictions are more accurate when explanations are plausible and faithful, and not when they are plausible but not faithful. Lastly, we show that, surprisingly, RRR metrics are not predictive of out-of-distribution model accuracy when controlling for a model’s in-distribution accuracy, which calls into question the value of these metrics for evaluating model reasoning.

Separately, the studied reasoning metrics do not predict out-of-distribution accuracy after controlling for in-distribution accuracy. These findings support the proposed training objectives while questioning whether those metrics, by themselves, meaningfully assess reasoning relevant to generalization.
summary.tldr: VISFIS improves visual question answering through four evidence-focused objectives while showing that plausible explanations and reasoning metrics require careful interpretation.

title: VisFIS: Visual Feature Importance Supervision with Right-for-the-Right-Reason Objectives

abstract: Machine learning based traffic forecasting models leverage sophisticated spatiotemporal auto-correlations to provide accurate predictions of city-wide traffic states. However, existing methods assume a reliable and unbiased forecasting environment, which is not always available in the wild. In this work, we investigate the vulnerability of spatiotemporal traffic forecasting models and propose a practical adversarial spatiotemporal attack framework. Specifically, instead of simultaneously attacking all geo-distributed data sources, an iterative gradient guided node saliency method is proposed to identify the time-dependent set of victim nodes. Furthermore, we devise a spatiotemporal gradient descent based scheme to generate real-valued adversarial traffic states under a perturbation constraint.Meanwhile, we theoretically demonstrate the worst performance bound of adversarial traffic forecasting attacks. Extensive experiments on two real-world datasets show that the proposed two-step framework achieves up to 67.8% performance degradation on various advanced spatiotemporal forecasting models. Remarkably, we also show that adversarial training with our proposed attacks can significantly improve the robustness of spatiotemporal traffic forecasting models.

paragraphs: Traffic forecasting models learn dependencies across locations and time, but their predictions can become vulnerable when incoming data are manipulated. This paper studies that vulnerability under an attack framework that selects particular data-source nodes rather than requiring simultaneous access to every geographically distributed source.

The framework has two stages. An iterative gradient-guided saliency method identifies victim nodes whose selection can change over time. A spatiotemporal gradient-based procedure then constructs real-valued adversarial traffic states subject to a perturbation constraint. The authors also provide a theoretical bound on worst-case forecasting performance under adversarial attacks.

This is a maximum observed degradation, not a uniform effect across all models or conditions. The authors additionally show that adversarial training with these attacks can significantly improve robustness. The study therefore supplies evidence of vulnerability and a way to use the identified attacks during training to strengthen the evaluated forecasting models.
summary.tldr: Targeted perturbations of selected traffic-data nodes substantially degrade forecasts in experiments and can support robustness-improving adversarial training.

title: Practical Adversarial Attacks on Spatiotemporal Traffic Forecasting Models

abstract: Recent empirical work has shown that hierarchical convolutional kernels inspired by convolutional neural networks (CNNs) signiﬁcantly improve the performance of kernel methods in image classiﬁcation tasks. A widely accepted explanation for their success is that these architectures encode hypothesis classes that are suitable for natural images. However, understanding the precise interplay between approximation and generalization in convolutional architectures remains a challenge. In this paper, we consider the stylized setting of covariates (image pixels) uniformly distributed on the hypercube, and characterize exactly the RKHS of kernels composed of single layers of convolution, pooling, and downsampling operations. We use this characterization to compute sharp asymptotics of the generalization error for any given function in high-dimension. In particular, we quantify the gain in sample complexity brought by enforcing locality with the convolution operation and approximate translation invariance with average pooling. Notably, these results provide a precise description of how convolution and pooling operations trade off approximation with generalization power in one layer convolutional kernels.

paragraphs: Convolutional kernels have improved image classification, but explaining precisely why their architectural choices help remains difficult. This paper studies how convolution, pooling, and downsampling affect both the functions a kernel can represent and the data needed to learn them. It focuses on a single layer in a stylized setting with pixels uniformly distributed on a hypercube.

The authors exactly characterize the associated reproducing kernel Hilbert space, or RKHS: the function space defined by the kernel. They then use that characterization to calculate sharp high-dimensional asymptotics for generalization error for any given target function. This connects the structure imposed by the architecture to both representational ability and prediction error.

The analysis quantifies sample-complexity gains from convolution's locality and from the approximate translation invariance introduced by average pooling. It also describes the tradeoff between approximation and generalization: an architectural constraint changes what can be represented while influencing how efficiently it can be learned. These are precise theoretical results for the specified one-layer, hypercube setting.
summary.tldr: An exact analysis of one-layer convolutional kernels quantifies how locality and pooling trade representational flexibility for improved sample efficiency.

title: Learning with convolution and pooling operations in kernel methods

abstract: The audio-visual video parsing task aims to parse a video into modality- and category-aware temporal segments. Previous work mainly focuses on weakly-supervised approaches, which learn from video-level event labels. During training, they do not know which modality perceives and meanwhile which temporal segment contains the video event. Since there is no explicit grouping in the existing frameworks, the modality and temporal uncertainties make these methods suffer from false predictions. For instance, segments in the same category could be predicted in different event classes. Learning compact and discriminative multi-modal subspaces is essential for mitigating the issue. To this end, in this paper, we propose a novel Multi-modal Grouping Network, namely MGN, for explicitly semantic-aware grouping. Specifically, MGN aggregates event-aware unimodal features through unimodal grouping in terms of learnable categorical embedding tokens. Furthermore, it leverages the cross-modal grouping for modality-aware prediction to match the video-level target. Our simple framework achieves improving results against previous baselines on weakly-supervised audio-visual video parsing. In addition, our MGN is much more lightweight, using only 47.2% of the parameters of baselines (17 MB vs. 36 MB). Code is available at https://github.com/stoneMo/MGN.

paragraphs: Audio-visual video parsing identifies which events occur in different time segments and whether they are perceived through sound, images, or both. With only whole-video labels, training does not reveal either the event's timing or its modality. The paper argues that this ambiguity can produce inconsistent predictions, including assigning different event classes to segments from the same category.

The proposed Multi-modal Grouping Network, or MGN, explicitly groups features according to their event meaning. Within each modality, learnable category embedding tokens aggregate event-related features. A further grouping stage connects modalities and supports predictions that distinguish their contributions while matching the available video-level labels. This gives the model an explicit mechanism for organizing evidence despite weak supervision.

The authors report improved parsing results over previous baselines. They also report a substantially smaller model, using 47.2% of the baseline parameters, with sizes stated as 17 MB versus 36 MB. The findings suggest that explicit semantic grouping can improve both predictive performance and model compactness in the evaluated audio-visual parsing setting.
summary.tldr: MGN explicitly groups event-related audio and visual features to improve weakly supervised video parsing with a smaller model.

title: Multi-modal Grouping Network for Weakly-Supervised Audio-Visual Video Parsing

abstract: Principal Components Analysis (PCA) is a dimension-reduction technique widely used in machine learning and statistics. However, due to the dependence of the principal components on all the dimensions, the components are notoriously hard to interpret. Therefore, a variant known as sparse PCA is often preferred. Sparse PCA learns principal components of the data but enforces that such components must be sparse. This has applications in diverse fields such as computational biology and image processing. To learn sparse principal components, it's well known that standard PCA will not work, especially in high dimensions, and therefore algorithms for sparse PCA are often studied as a separate endeavor. Various algorithms have been proposed for Sparse PCA over the years, but given how fundamental it is for applications in science, the limits of efficient algorithms are only partially understood. In this work, we study the limits of the powerful Sum of Squares (SoS) family of algorithms for Sparse PCA. SoS algorithms have recently revolutionized robust statistics, leading to breakthrough algorithms for long-standing open problems in machine learning, such as optimally learning mixtures of gaussians, robust clustering, robust regression, etc. Moreover, it is believed to be the optimal robust algorithm for many statistical problems. Therefore, for sparse PCA, it's plausible that it can beat simpler algorithms such as diagonal thresholding that have been traditionally used. In this work, we show that this is not the case, by exhibiting strong tradeoffs between the number of samples required, the sparsity and the ambient dimension, for which SoS algorithms, even if allowed sub-exponential time, will fail to optimally recover the component. Our results are complemented by known algorithms in literature, thereby painting an almost complete picture of the behavior of efficient algorithms for sparse PCA. Since SoS algorithms encapsulate many algorithmic techniques such as spectral or statistical query algorithms, this solidifies the message that known algorithms are optimal for sparse PCA. Moreover, our techniques are strong enough to obtain similar tradeoffs for Tensor PCA, another important higher order variant of PCA with applications in topic modeling, video processing, etc.

Finding these sparse components is a separate algorithmic challenge, especially in high dimensions. This paper studies how far the powerful Sum-of-Squares family of algorithms can go in solving it.

The authors establish lower bounds linking sample count, sparsity, and ambient dimension. In the identified regimes, Sum-of-Squares methods fail to recover the component optimally even when given sub-exponential running time. This constrains the possibility that their strength on other statistical problems will translate into better sparse PCA recovery than simpler established methods.

Their reach matters because Sum-of-Squares encompasses many techniques, including spectral and statistical-query approaches. The authors also extend their lower-bound techniques to Tensor PCA, obtaining analogous trade-offs for this higher-order variant.
summary.tldr: Lower bounds show that even sub-exponential-time Sum-of-Squares algorithms cannot optimally solve sparse PCA in specified sample, sparsity, and dimension regimes.

title: Sub-exponential time Sum-of-Squares lower bounds for Principal Components Analysis

abstract: We propose a practical integration of logical state abstraction with AIXI, a Bayesian optimality notion for reinforcement learning agents, to significantly expand the model class that AIXI agents can be approximated over to complex history-dependent and structured environments. The state representation and reasoning framework is based on higher-order logic, which can be used to define and enumerate complex features on non-Markovian and structured environments. We address the problem of selecting the right subset of features to form state abstractions by adapting the $\Phi$-MDP optimisation criterion from state abstraction theory. Exact Bayesian model learning is then achieved using a suitable generalisation of Context Tree Weighting over abstract state sequences. The resultant architecture can be integrated with different planning algorithms. Experimental results on controlling epidemics on large-scale contact networks validates the agent's performance.

paragraphs: This paper develops a practical approximation to AIXI, a Bayesian notion of an optimal reinforcement learning agent. Its focus is on environments with complex structure and dependence on past events. In these settings, choosing a useful description of the current situation is an important part of making effective decisions.

The approach uses higher-order logic to define and enumerate features of an environment. These features can describe structured situations and information from history. The method then adapts a criterion from state abstraction theory to select a subset of features, producing a more manageable state representation for learning.

A generalized Context Tree Weighting method performs exact Bayesian model learning over the resulting abstract state sequences. The architecture can work with different planning algorithms, separating the representation and learning machinery from the choice of planner. Experiments on epidemic control in large contact networks support the agent's performance. The contribution is a way to expand the environments covered by practical AIXI approximations, rather than a claim to implement unrestricted AIXI.
summary.tldr: Logical state abstractions extend a practical AIXI approximation to structured environments whose behavior depends on history.

title: A Direct Approximation of AIXI Using Logical State Abstractions

abstract: Existing subset selection methods for efficient learning predominantly employ discrete combinatorial and model-specific approaches, which lack generalizability--- for each new model, the algorithm has to be executed from the beginning. Therefore, for an unseen architecture, one cannot use the subset chosen for a different model. In this work, we propose $\texttt{SubSelNet}$, a non-adaptive subset selection framework, which tackles these problems. Here, we first introduce an attention-based neural gadget that leverages the graph structure of architectures and acts as a surrogate to trained deep neural networks for quick model prediction. Then, we use these predictions to build subset samplers. This naturally provides us two variants of $\texttt{SubSelNet}$. The first variant is transductive (called Transductive-$\texttt{SubSelNet}$), which computes the subset separately for each model by solving a small optimization problem. Such an optimization is still super fast, thanks to the replacement of explicit model training by the model approximator. The second variant is inductive (called Inductive-$\texttt{SubSelNet}$), which computes the subset using a trained subset selector, without any optimization. Our experiments show that our model outperforms several methods across several real datasets.

paragraphs: Selecting a smaller training dataset can reduce learning costs, but model-specific selection methods often require the selection process to restart for each architecture. SubSelNet addresses this lack of reuse by building a framework that can select data across models without explicitly training every model to guide the selection.

Its central component is an attention-based predictor that uses the graph structure of a neural architecture. This component approximates the predictions of a trained network. Those approximate predictions then guide subset samplers, replacing an expensive source of information for data selection with a learned surrogate.

The framework has two variants with different requirements for a new model. Transductive SubSelNet solves a small optimization problem to choose its subset, using the surrogate to make that step fast. Inductive SubSelNet uses a trained selector and requires no selection-time optimization. Experiments across several real datasets show improvements over several existing methods. The contribution is therefore both a way to approximate model behavior for selection and two ways to turn that approximation into reusable data-selection machinery.
summary.tldr: SubSelNet uses architecture-based prediction surrogates to select training subsets across models through either lightweight optimization or a trained selector.

title: Efficient Data Subset Selection to Generalize Training Across Models: Transductive and Inductive Networks

abstract: In the domain of audio processing, Transfer Learning has facilitated the rise of Self-Supervised Learning and Zero-Shot Learning techniques. These approaches have led to the development of versatile models capable of tackling a wide array of tasks, while delivering state-of-the-art performance. However, current models inherently lack the capacity to produce the requisite language for open-ended tasks, such as Audio Captioning or Audio Question Answering. We introduce Pengi, a novel Audio Language Model that leverages Transfer Learning by framing all audio tasks as text-generation tasks. It takes as input, an audio recording, and text, and generates free-form text as output. The input audio is represented as a sequence of continuous embeddings by an audio encoder. A text encoder does the same for the corresponding text input. Both sequences are combined as a prefix to prompt a pre-trained frozen language model. The unified architecture of Pengi enables open-ended tasks and close-ended tasks without any additional fine-tuning or task-specific extensions. When evaluated on 21 downstream tasks, our approach yields state-of-the-art performance in several of them. Our results show that connecting language models with audio models is a major step towards general-purpose audio understanding.

paragraphs: Audio models can support many tasks through transfer learning, but open-ended tasks require the ability to produce language. Pengi addresses this by expressing audio tasks as text generation. Given an audio recording and a text input, it generates a free-form textual response, bringing tasks such as captioning and audio question answering into one architecture.

An audio encoder converts the recording into a sequence of continuous embeddings, and a text encoder does the same for the accompanying text. The two sequences form a prefix that prompts a pretrained language model whose parameters remain frozen. This connects representations of sound and text to an existing language-generation capability.

The unified model handles both open-ended and closed-ended tasks without additional task-specific fine-tuning or extensions. Evaluation across 21 downstream tasks yields state-of-the-art performance on several of them. The results support the usefulness of connecting audio models with language models as a route toward broader audio understanding, with a common textual output interface spanning tasks that otherwise require different forms of response.
summary.tldr: Pengi connects audio and text encoders to a frozen language model, handling diverse audio tasks through text generation.

title: Pengi: An Audio Language Model for Audio Tasks

abstract: The differential equation (DE) approach for convex optimization, which relates optimization methods to specific continuous DEs with rate-revealing Lyapunov functionals, has gained increasing interest since the seminal paper by Su--Boyd--Candès (2014).However, the approach still lacks a crucial component to make it truly useful: there is no general, consistent way to transition back to discrete optimization methods. Consequently, even if we derive insights from continuous DEs, we still need to perform individualized and tedious calculations for the analysis of each method.This paper aims to bridge this gap by introducing a new concept called ``weak discrete gradient'' (wDG), which consolidates the conditions required for discrete versions of gradients in the DE approach arguments.We then define abstract optimization methods using wDG and provide abstract convergence theories that parallel those in continuous DEs.We demonstrate that many typical optimization methods and their convergence rates can be derived as special cases of this abstract theory.The proposed unified discretization framework for the differential equation approach to convex optimization provides an easy environment for developing new optimization methods and achieving competitive convergence rates with state-of-the-art methods, such as Nesterov's accelerated gradient.

Consequently, even if we derive insights from continuous DEs, we still need to perform individualized and tedious calculations for the analysis of each method.This paper aims to bridge this gap by introducing a new concept called ``weak discrete gradient'' (wDG), which consolidates the conditions required for discrete versions of gradients in the DE approach arguments.We then define abstract optimization methods using wDG and provide abstract convergence theories that parallel those in continuous DEs.We demonstrate that many typical optimization methods and their convergence rates can be derived as special cases of this abstract theory.The proposed unified discretization framework for the differential equation approach to convex optimization provides an easy environment for developing new optimization methods and achieving competitive convergence rates with state-of-the-art methods, such as Nesterov's accelerated gradient.

paragraphs: Differential equations offer a way to understand optimization by treating an algorithm as a continuous process. A Lyapunov functional tracks progress and can reveal how quickly that process approaches a solution. The difficulty is translating this continuous analysis into an algorithm that takes discrete steps: existing approaches often require a separate convergence argument for each method.

The paper introduces a weak discrete gradient, a mathematical concept that collects the conditions needed for discrete gradient expressions to support these arguments. Using this concept, the authors define abstract optimization methods and establish convergence theories that mirror their continuous counterparts. This makes the passage from differential equations to implementable updates more systematic.

Many familiar optimization algorithms and their convergence rates emerge as special cases of the framework. Its contribution is therefore both organizational and constructive: it brings existing analyses under one theory and provides a setting for developing new methods. Within convex optimization, the authors describe competitive convergence rates relative to methods such as Nesterov’s accelerated gradient.
summary.tldr: A weak discrete gradient framework systematically translates continuous differential-equation analyses into discrete convex optimization methods and convergence guarantees.

title: A Unified Discretization Framework for Differential Equation Approach with Lyapunov Arguments for Convex Optimization

abstract: Causality is a central concept in a wide range of research areas, yet there is still no universally agreed axiomatisation of causality. We view causality both as an extension of probability theory and as a study of what happens when one intervenes on a system, and argue in favour of taking Kolmogorov's measure-theoretic axiomatisation of probability as the starting point towards an axiomatisation of causality. To that end, we propose the notion of a causal space, consisting of a probability space along with a collection of transition probability kernels, called causal kernels, that encode the causal information of the space. Our proposed framework is not only rigorously grounded in measure theory, but it also sheds light on long-standing limitations of existing frameworks including, for example, cycles, latent variables and stochastic processes.
originalAbstract: Causality is a central concept in a wide range of research areas, yet there is still no universally agreed axiomatisation of causality. We view causality both as an extension of probability theory and as a study of what happens when one intervenes on a system, and argue in favour of taking Kolmogorov's measure-theoretic axiomatisation of probability as the starting point towards an axiomatisation of causality. To that end, we propose the notion of a causal space, consisting of a probability space along with a collection of transition probability kernels, called causal kernels, that encode the causal information of the space. Our proposed framework is not only rigorously grounded in measure theory, but it also sheds light on long-standing limitations of existing frameworks including, for example, cycles, latent variables and stochastic processes.

paragraphs: The paper asks how causality can be given a precise mathematical foundation. Its starting point is that describing what happens probabilistically and describing what happens after an intervention are closely connected tasks. The authors therefore propose extending the measure-theoretic foundations of probability, rather than treating causal reasoning as a separate mathematical subject.

Their central object is a causal space. It combines an ordinary probability space with a collection of transition probability kernels, which they call causal kernels. The probability space describes uncertainty, while the additional kernels encode causal information. This makes the causal component an explicit part of the mathematical structure instead of leaving it implicit in a probabilistic description.

The contribution is a proposed foundational framework grounded in measure theory. The authors argue that it also clarifies longstanding difficulties involving cycles, hidden variables, and stochastic processes. These are presented as areas where the framework sheds light on existing limitations, rather than as evidence that a universally accepted or final axiomatisation of causality has been achieved.
summary.tldr: The paper proposes a measure-theoretic foundation for causality by augmenting probability spaces with kernels that encode causal information.

title: A Measure-Theoretic Axiomatisation of Causality

abstract: In this paper we offer a new perspective on the well established agglomerative clustering algorithm, focusing on recovery of hierarchical structure. We recommend a simple variant of the standard algorithm, in which clusters are merged by maximum average dot product and not, for example, by minimum distance or within-cluster variance. We demonstrate that the tree output by this algorithm provides a bona fide estimate of generative hierarchical structure in data, under a generic probabilistic graphical model. The key technical innovations are to understand how hierarchical information in this model translates into tree geometry which can be recovered from data, and to characterise the benefits of simultaneously growing sample size and data dimension. We demonstrate superior tree recovery performance with real data over existing approaches such as UPGMA, Ward's method, and HDBSCAN.

We recommend a simple variant of the standard algorithm, in which clusters are merged by maximum average dot product and not, for example, by minimum distance or within-cluster variance. We demonstrate that the tree output by this algorithm provides a bona fide estimate of generative hierarchical structure in data, under a generic probabilistic graphical model. The key technical innovations are to understand how hierarchical information in this model translates into tree geometry which can be recovered from data, and to characterise the benefits of simultaneously growing sample size and data dimension. We demonstrate superior tree recovery performance with real data over existing approaches such as UPGMA, Ward's method, and HDBSCAN.

paragraphs: Hierarchical clustering repeatedly merges groups to produce a tree, but producing a tree is different from recovering a hierarchy that generated the observations. This paper studies that recovery question. It recommends merging clusters according to their maximum average dot product, changing the similarity criterion used by an otherwise familiar agglomerative procedure.

Under a generic probabilistic graphical model, the authors show that the resulting tree estimates the data's generative hierarchy. Their analysis explains how hierarchical information becomes a geometric structure that can be recovered from observations. It also examines the benefits of increasing both the number of samples and the number of data dimensions.

Real-data experiments report better tree recovery than UPGMA, Ward's method, and HDBSCAN. The significance is that a simple change to the merging rule receives both a model-based recovery justification and empirical support. The theoretical interpretation depends on the stated generative model, while the experiments show that the proposed criterion can also be useful when comparing clustering methods on real observations.
summary.tldr: Merging clusters by average dot product recovers generative tree structure under the studied model and improves reported real-data tree recovery.

title: Hierarchical clustering with dot products recovers hidden tree structure

abstract: We consider a fundamental problem where there are multiple groups whose data distributions are unknown, and an analyst would like to learn the mean of each group. We consider an active learning framework to sequentially collect $T$ samples with bandit, each period observing a sample from a chosen group. After observing a sample, the analyst may update their estimate of the mean and variance of that group and choose the next group accordingly. The objective is to dynamically collect samples to minimize the $p$-norm of the vector of variances of our mean estimators after $T$ rounds. We propose an algorithm, Variance-UCB, that selects groups according to a an upper bound on the variance estimate adjusted to the $p$-norm chosen. We show that the regret of Variance-UCB is $O(T^{-2})$ for finite $p$, and prove that no algorithm can do better. When $p$ is infinite, we recover the $O(T^{-1.5})$ obtained in \cite{activelearning, carpentier2011upper} and provide a new lower bound showing that no algorithm can do better.

paragraphs: When an analyst needs average values for several groups, a limited sampling budget raises a practical question: which group should be measured next? This paper studies a sequential setting where each observation comes from one chosen group. The groups’ distributions are unknown, so the analyst must learn their means and variances while deciding how to allocate observations.

The proposed Variance-UCB algorithm selects groups using upper bounds on their estimated variances. Its choices also depend on a parameter, p, that determines how the uncertainties across groups are combined into one objective. For finite p, the objective aggregates those uncertainties; at infinite p, it focuses on the largest one. Sampling decisions therefore respond both to observed variability and to the chosen evaluation criterion.

The authors prove regret rates of O(T^-2) for finite p and O(T^-1.5) for infinite p, where T is the sampling budget. Matching lower bounds establish that these rates cannot be improved in the studied setting. These are guarantees about regret in sample allocation, rather than claims that every mean estimate has error decreasing at those rates.
summary.tldr: Variance-UCB adaptively allocates observations across groups and achieves optimal regret rates for the studied mean-estimation objectives.

title: An active learning framework for multi-group mean estimation

abstract: Generating high-fidelity time series data using generative adversarial networks (GANs) remains a challenging task, as it is difficult to capture the temporal dependence of joint probability distributions induced by time-series data. Towards this goal, a key step is the development of an effective discriminator to distinguish between time series distributions. We propose the so-called PCF-GAN, a novel GAN that incorporates the path characteristic function (PCF) as the principled representation of time series distribution into the discriminator to enhance its generative performance. On the one hand, we establish theoretical foundations of the PCF distance by proving its characteristicity, boundedness, differentiability with respect to generator parameters, and weak continuity, which ensure the stability and feasibility of training the PCF-GAN. On the other hand, we design efficient initialisation and optimisation schemes for PCFs to strengthen the discriminative power and accelerate training efficiency. To further boost the capabilities of complex time series generation, we integrate the auto-encoder structure via sequential embedding into the PCF-GAN, which provides additional reconstruction functionality. Extensive numerical experiments on various datasets demonstrate the consistently superior performance of PCF-GAN over state-of-the-art baselines, in both generation and reconstruction quality.

paragraphs: Generating realistic time series requires capturing how values depend on one another across time. For a generative adversarial network, this places a substantial burden on the discriminator that distinguishes real and generated sequence distributions. PCF-GAN strengthens that component using the path characteristic function as a representation of a time-series distribution.

The authors establish several properties of the resulting distance, including its ability to distinguish distributions, boundedness, differentiability with respect to generator parameters, and weak continuity. These results provide mathematical foundations for feasible and stable training. They also design initialization and optimization schemes intended to make the representation more discriminative and training more efficient.

The model further incorporates an autoencoder through sequential embeddings, adding reconstruction functionality to its generation capabilities. Across the numerical experiments, PCF-GAN consistently outperforms the compared state-of-the-art baselines in generation and reconstruction quality. The contribution links a mathematically grounded comparison of sequence distributions with practical training mechanisms and a model that supports both tasks.
summary.tldr: PCF-GAN uses path characteristic functions to compare time-series distributions and reports improved generation and reconstruction over tested baselines.

title: PCF-GAN: generating sequential data via the characteristic function of measures on the path space

abstract: Recent advancements in dense out-of-distribution (OOD) detection have primarily focused on scenarios where the training and testing datasets share a similar domain, with the assumption that no domain shift exists between them. However, in real-world situations, domain shift often exits and significantly affects the accuracy of existing out-of-distribution (OOD) detection models. In this work, we propose a dual-level OOD detection framework to handle domain shift and semantic shift jointly. The first level distinguishes whether domain shift exists in the image by leveraging global low-level features, while the second level identifies pixels with semantic shift by utilizing dense high-level feature maps. In this way, we can selectively adapt the model to unseen domains as well as enhance model's capacity in detecting novel classes. We validate the efficacy of our proposed method on several OOD segmentation benchmarks, including those with significant domain shifts and those without, observing consistent performance improvements across various baseline models. Code is available at https://github.com/gaozhitong/ATTA.

paragraphs: Detecting unfamiliar objects in an image becomes harder when the image’s overall domain also differs from training. These are two distinct changes: a domain shift affects the setting in which familiar content appears, while a semantic shift introduces unfamiliar classes. The paper addresses their joint effect on pixel-level out-of-distribution detection.

ATTA uses two levels of analysis. Global, low-level image features help determine whether the image exhibits a domain shift. Dense, high-level feature maps then identify pixels associated with semantic novelty. Keeping these decisions distinct allows the framework to selectively adapt to unseen domains while strengthening its ability to detect new classes.

The authors evaluate the method on several segmentation benchmarks, including settings with substantial domain changes and settings without them. They report consistent improvements across multiple baseline models. These findings support treating domain adaptation and novel-class detection together: a detector needs to accommodate changes in the image domain while still recognizing that some individual pixels represent content outside its known classes.
summary.tldr: ATTA separates image-level domain shifts from pixel-level semantic novelty to improve out-of-distribution segmentation detection.

title: ATTA: Anomaly-aware Test-Time Adaptation for Out-of-Distribution Detection in Segmentation

abstract: Hardware-specific optimizations in machine learning (ML) frameworks can cause numerical deviations of inference results. Quite surprisingly, despite using a fixed trained model and fixed input data, inference results are not consistent across platforms, and sometimes not even deterministic on the same platform. We study the causes of these numerical deviations for convolutional neural networks (CNN) on realistic end-to-end inference pipelines and in isolated experiments. Results from 75 distinct platforms suggest that the main causes of deviations on CPUs are differences in SIMD use, and the selection of convolution algorithms at runtime on GPUs. We link the causes and propagation effects to properties of the ML model and evaluate potential mitigations. We make our research code publicly available.

We study the causes of these numerical deviations for convolutional neural networks (CNN) on realistic end-to-end inference pipelines and in isolated experiments. Results from 75 distinct platforms suggest that the main causes of deviations on CPUs are differences in SIMD use, and the selection of convolution algorithms at runtime on GPUs. We link the causes and propagation effects to properties of the ML model and evaluate potential mitigations. We make our research code publicly available.

paragraphs: A fixed neural network given fixed input data can produce different numerical inference results on different computing platforms. Sometimes results can even vary across runs on the same platform. This paper investigates that behavior in convolutional neural networks, focusing on how hardware-specific optimizations in machine-learning frameworks contribute to unexpected deviations.

The study combines realistic, end-to-end inference pipelines with isolated experiments. This combination examines the phenomenon both within complete computations and in settings that help identify particular causes. Evidence from 75 distinct platforms suggests that differences in CPU use of single-instruction, multiple-data operations are a main cause, alongside runtime selection of convolution algorithms on GPUs.

The authors also connect the origins and propagation of deviations to properties of the model and evaluate potential mitigations. The contribution is therefore broader than documenting inconsistent outputs: it links observed differences to computational choices and studies how they spread. These findings help explain why keeping model weights and inputs unchanged does not by itself ensure identical numerical inference results.
summary.tldr: A study across 75 platforms links inference deviations mainly to CPU SIMD differences and GPU convolution-algorithm selection.

title: Causes and Effects of Unanticipated Numerical Deviations in Neural Network Inference Frameworks

abstract: We present Pre-trained Machine Reader (PMR), a novel method for retrofitting pre-trained masked language models (MLMs) to pre-trained machine reading comprehension (MRC) models without acquiring labeled data.PMR can resolve the discrepancy between model pre-training and downstream fine-tuning of existing MLMs.To build the proposed PMR, we constructed a large volume of general-purpose and high-quality MRC-style training data by using Wikipedia hyperlinks and designed a Wiki Anchor Extraction task to guide the MRC-style pre-training.Apart from its simplicity, PMR effectively solves extraction tasks, such as Extractive Question Answering and Named Entity Recognition. PMR shows tremendous improvements over existing approaches, especially in low-resource scenarios.When applied to the sequence classification task in the MRC formulation, PMR enables the extraction of high-quality rationales to explain the classification process, thereby providing greater prediction explainability. PMR also has the potential to serve as a unified model for tackling various extraction and classification tasks in the MRC formulation.

paragraphs: Masked language models are pretrained to fill missing text, while many downstream applications require finding information in a passage. Pre-trained Machine Reader, or PMR, adapts existing masked language models toward reading comprehension without acquiring labeled data. The aim is to make pretraining more closely match the extraction tasks the model will later perform.

The authors construct a large collection of reading-comprehension-style examples from Wikipedia hyperlinks. A Wiki Anchor Extraction task guides additional pretraining using that resource. This supplies a way to retrofit an existing model using supervision derived from the text's hyperlink structure, rather than requiring a separately acquired labeled training collection.

The paper reports substantial improvements on extraction tasks, including extractive question answering and named entity recognition, especially when labeled resources are limited. When classification is expressed as reading comprehension, PMR can also extract high-quality rationales that help explain predictions. The authors propose its potential as a unified model for extraction and classification tasks formulated this way, rather than claiming universal coverage of all language tasks.
summary.tldr: PMR uses Wikipedia hyperlinks to adapt masked language models for reading comprehension, improving extraction and enabling explanatory rationales.

title: From Cloze to Comprehension: Retrofitting Pre-trained Masked Language Models to Pre-trained Machine Reader

abstract: Learning-based video compression is currently a popular research topic, offering the potential to compete with conventional standard video codecs. In this context, Implicit Neural Representations (INRs) have previously been used to represent and compress image and video content, demonstrating relatively high decoding speed compared to other methods. However, existing INR-based methods have failed to deliver rate quality performance comparable with the state of the art in video compression. This is mainly due to the simplicity of the employed network architectures, which limit their representation capability. In this paper, we propose HiNeRV, an INR that combines light weight layers with novel hierarchical positional encodings. We employs depth-wise convolutional, MLP and interpolation layers to build the deep and wide network architecture with high capacity. HiNeRV is also a unified representation encoding videos in both frames and patches at the same time, which offers higher performance and flexibility than existing methods. We further build a video codec based on HiNeRV and a refined pipeline for training, pruning and quantization that can better preserve HiNeRV's performance during lossy model compression. The proposed method has been evaluated on both UVG and MCL-JCV datasets for video compression, demonstrating significant improvement over all existing INRs baselines and competitive performance when compared to learning-based codecs (72.3\% overall bit rate saving over HNeRV and 43.4\% over DCVC on the UVG dataset, measured in PSNR).

However, existing INR-based methods have failed to deliver rate quality performance comparable with the state of the art in video compression. This is mainly due to the simplicity of the employed network architectures, which limit their representation capability. paragraphs: Implicit neural representations encode image or video content in a learned model. summary.tldr: HiNeRV improves neural video compression through hierarchical encodings, higher-capacity lightweight architecture, and a refined model-compression pipeline.

title: HiNeRV: Video Compression with Hierarchical Encoding-based Neural Representation

abstract: In variational inference, the benefits of Bayesian models rely on accurately capturing the true posterior distribution. We propose using neural samplers that specify implicit distributions, which are well-suited for approximating complex multimodal and correlated posteriors in high-dimensional spaces. Our approach introduces novel bounds for approximate inference using implicit distributions by locally linearising the neural sampler. This is distinct from existing methods that rely on additional discriminator networks and unstable adversarial objectives. Furthermore, we present a new sampler architecture that, for the first time, enables implicit distributions over tens of millions of latent variables, addressing computational concerns by using differentiable numerical approximations. We empirically show that our method is capable of recovering correlations across layers in large Bayesian neural networks, a property that is crucial for a network's performance but notoriously challenging to achieve. To the best of our knowledge, no other method has been shown to accomplish this task for such large models. Through experiments in downstream tasks, we demonstrate that our expressive posteriors outperform state-of-the-art uncertainty quantification methods, validating the effectiveness of our training algorithm and the quality of the learned implicit approximation.

paragraphs: Bayesian inference depends on approximating a posterior distribution that may contain multiple plausible explanations and strong dependencies among variables. This paper uses neural samplers to represent such distributions implicitly through the samples they generate. The approach targets high-dimensional posteriors whose correlations and multiple modes are difficult to capture with simpler approximations.

The authors derive new inference bounds by locally linearizing the neural sampler. This provides a training approach distinct from methods requiring an additional discriminator and an unstable adversarial objective. They also introduce a sampler architecture using differentiable numerical approximations, enabling implicit distributions over tens of millions of latent variables.

Experiments show that the method can recover correlations across layers in large Bayesian neural networks, a capability the authors identify as important for performance and difficult to obtain at this scale. On downstream tasks, its expressive posterior approximations outperform state-of-the-art uncertainty-quantification methods. The results support both the computational feasibility of the architecture and the value of preserving richer dependencies in learned uncertainty.
summary.tldr: Neural samplers with new inference bounds scale rich implicit posterior approximations to tens of millions of variables.

title: Implicit Variational Inference for High-Dimensional Posteriors

abstract: We introduce GAUCHE, an open-source library for GAUssian processes in CHEmistry. Gaussian processes have long been a cornerstone of probabilistic machine learning, affording particular advantages for uncertainty quantification and Bayesian optimisation. Extending Gaussian processes to molecular representations, however, necessitates kernels defined over structured inputs such as graphs, strings and bit vectors. By providing such kernels in a modular, robust and easy-to-use framework, we seek to enable expert chemists and materials scientists to make use of state-of-the-art black-box optimization techniques. Motivated by scenarios frequently encountered in practice, we showcase applications for GAUCHE in molecular discovery, chemical reaction optimisation and protein design. The codebase is made available at https://github.com/leojklarner/gauche.

These probabilistic models are useful for quantifying uncertainty and supporting Bayesian optimization. The practical obstacle addressed here is representation: molecules may be described as graphs, strings, or bit vectors, so the models need ways to operate on those structured inputs.

The library supplies kernels for such representations within a modular framework. Kernels provide the connection between the chemical input representation and the Gaussian process model. By packaging these components in a robust, accessible system, the authors aim to make advanced black-box optimization methods usable by chemists and materials scientists working with their own scientific problems.

The paper showcases applications in molecular discovery, chemical reaction optimization, and protein design, motivated by situations encountered in practice. These examples demonstrate the intended breadth of the library across different chemical tasks. The contribution is a reusable modeling framework that brings uncertainty-aware prediction and optimization to structured chemical data, with the application demonstrations illustrating how that framework can be put to work.
summary.tldr: GAUCHE supplies Gaussian-process kernels for structured chemical representations to support uncertainty-aware modeling and Bayesian optimization.

title: GAUCHE: A Library for Gaussian Processes in Chemistry

abstract: In this work, we investigate the task of text-to-image (T2I) synthesis under the abstract-to-intricate setting, i.e., generating intricate visual content from simple abstract text prompts. Inspired by human imagination intuition, we propose a novel scene-graph hallucination (SGH) mechanism for effective abstract-to-intricate T2I synthesis. SGH carries out scene hallucination by expanding the initial scene graph (SG) of the input prompt with more feasible specific scene structures, in which the structured semantic representation of SG ensures high controllability of the intrinsic scene imagination. To approach the T2I synthesis, we deliberately build an SG-based hallucination diffusion system. First, we implement the SGH module based on the discrete diffusion technique, which evolves the SG structure by iteratively adding new scene elements. Then, we utilize another continuous-state diffusion model as the T2I synthesizer, where the overt image-generating process is navigated by the underlying semantic scene structure induced from the SGH module. On the benchmark COCO dataset, our system outperforms the existing best-performing T2I model by a significant margin, especially improving on the abstract-to-intricate T2I generation. Further in-depth analyses reveal how our methods advance.

paragraphs: A short, abstract prompt leaves many visual details unspecified. This paper studies how to turn such prompts into intricate images by explicitly expanding the scene before generating its appearance. The proposed scene-graph hallucination mechanism adds feasible detail to a structured representation of the initial prompt.

The system uses two diffusion processes with different roles. A discrete diffusion module develops the scene graph by repeatedly introducing new scene elements. A continuous-state diffusion model then generates the image under the guidance of that expanded semantic structure. Keeping the imagined content in a scene graph provides a structured basis for controlling how the scene is elaborated.

On COCO, the authors report a significant improvement over the existing best-performing text-to-image model, especially for the abstract-to-intricate setting. The result supports an explicit intermediate stage between a sparse prompt and a detailed image: the system first develops what the scene contains, then uses that representation to direct image synthesis. Additional analyses investigate how the proposed components contribute.
summary.tldr: The system expands simple prompts into detailed scene graphs with discrete diffusion, then uses those graphs to guide image generation.

title: Imagine That! Abstract-to-Intricate Text-to-Image Synthesis with Scene Graph Hallucination Diffusion

abstract: Manipulating garments and fabrics has long been a critical endeavor in the development of home-assistant robots. However, due to complex dynamics and topological structures, garment manipulations pose significant challenges. Recent successes in reinforcement learning and vision-based methods offer promising avenues for learning garment manipulation. Nevertheless, these approaches are severely constrained by current benchmarks, which exhibit offer limited diversity of tasks and unrealistic simulation behavior. Therefore, we present GarmentLab, a content-rich benchmark and realistic simulation designed for deformable object and garment manipulation. Our benchmark encompasses a diverse range of garment types, robotic systems and manipulators. The abundant tasks in the benchmark further explores of the interactions between garments, deformable objects, rigid bodies, fluids, and human body. Moreover, by incorporating multiple simulation methods such as FEM and PBD, along with our proposed sim-to-real algorithms and real-world benchmark, we aim to significantly narrow the sim-to-real gap. We evaluate state-of-the-art vision methods, reinforcement learning, and imitation learning approaches on these tasks, highlighting the challenges faced by current algorithms, notably their limited generalization capabilities. Our proposed open-source environments and comprehensive analysis show promising boost to future research in garment manipulation by unlocking the full potential of these methods. We guarantee that we will open-source our code as soon as possible. You can watch the videos in supplementary files to learn more about the details of our work.

paragraphs: Robots have difficulty manipulating garments because fabrics deform and have complex structures and dynamics. Learning-based approaches are promising, but their evaluation is constrained by benchmarks with limited task variety and unrealistic simulated behavior. GarmentLab expands the setting in which researchers can develop and compare methods for garment and deformable-object manipulation.

It also combines simulation methods including FEM and PBD with proposed simulation-to-reality algorithms and a real-world benchmark, aiming to reduce the gap between simulated behavior and physical deployment.

The authors evaluate vision methods, reinforcement learning, and imitation learning across these tasks. Their analysis highlights difficulties for current algorithms, particularly limited generalization. The contribution therefore includes both a broader testing environment and evidence about where existing methods struggle. Its intended role is to make progress measurable across a richer range of manipulation conditions and to support research toward better transfer to real settings.
summary.tldr: GarmentLab broadens garment-manipulation simulation and evaluation, revealing generalization challenges in current robot-learning methods.

title: GarmentLab: A Unified Simulation and Benchmark for Garment Manipulation

abstract: In this work, we observe that model trained on vast general images via masking strategy, has been naturally embedded with their distribution knowledge, thus spontaneously attains the underlying potential for strong image denoising.Based on this observation, we propose a novel zero-shot denoising paradigm, i.e., $\textbf{M}$asked $\textbf{P}$re-train then $\textbf{I}$terative fill ($\textbf{MPI}$).MPI first trains model via masking and then employs pre-trained weight for high-quality zero-shot image denoising on a single noisy image.Concretely, MPI comprises two key procedures:$\textbf{1) Masked Pre-training}$ involves training model to reconstruct massive natural images with random masking for generalizable representations, gathering the potential for valid zero-shot denoising on images with varying noise degradation and even in distinct image types.$\textbf{2) Iterative filling}$ exploits pre-trained knowledge for effective zero-shot denoising. It iteratively optimizes the image by leveraging pre-trained weights, focusing on alternate reconstruction of different image parts, and gradually assembles fully denoised image within limited number of iterations.Comprehensive experiments across various noisy scenarios underscore the notable advances of MPI over previous approaches with a marked reduction in inference time.

paragraphs: This paper explores how learning to reconstruct missing image regions can prepare a model to remove noise. The authors observe that masked training on many natural images gives a model knowledge of image distributions. Their method, Masked Pre-train then Iterative fill, uses that knowledge for zero-shot denoising of a single noisy image.

The first stage trains the model to reconstruct images after random masking. This develops representations intended to generalize across different noise degradations and even different image types. The second stage applies the pretrained weights to the noisy input, repeatedly reconstructing alternating parts of the image and gradually assembling a denoised result within a limited number of iterations.

The approach matters because it connects a general reconstruction task with the specific task of noise removal. Rather than treating masked pretraining only as preparation for representation learning, it uses the acquired image knowledge directly in an iterative restoration procedure. Experiments across multiple noisy scenarios report notable improvements over earlier approaches together with substantially reduced inference time.
summary.tldr: MPI uses masked image pretraining followed by iterative reconstruction to denoise a single noisy image in a zero-shot setting.

title: Masked Pre-training Enables Universal Zero-shot Denoiser

abstract: Offline safe reinforcement learning (RL) aims to find an optimal policy using a pre-collected dataset when data collection is impractical or risky. We propose a novel linear programming (LP) based primal-dual algorithm for convex MDPs that incorporates ``uncertainty'' parameters to improve data efficiency while requiring only partial data coverage assumption. Our theoretical results achieve a sample complexity of $\mathcal{O}(1/(1-\gamma)\sqrt{n})$ under general function approximation, improving the current state-of-the-art by a factor of $1/(1-\gamma)$, where $n$ is the number of data samples in an offline dataset, and $\gamma$ is the discount factor. The numerical experiments validate our theoretical findings, demonstrating the practical efficacy of our approach in achieving improved safety and learning efficiency in safe offline settings.

We propose a novel linear programming (LP) based primal-dual algorithm for convex MDPs that incorporates ``uncertainty'' parameters to improve data efficiency while requiring only partial data coverage assumption. Our theoretical results achieve a sample complexity of $\mathcal{O}(1/(1-\gamma)\sqrt{n})$ under general function approximation, improving the current state-of-the-art by a factor of $1/(1-\gamma)$, where $n$ is the number of data samples in an offline dataset, and $\gamma$ is the discount factor. The numerical experiments validate our theoretical findings, demonstrating the practical efficacy of our approach in achieving improved safety and learning efficiency in safe offline settings.

paragraphs: Offline safe reinforcement learning seeks useful decision policies from an existing dataset when collecting more experience would be impractical or risky. The learning problem must account for safety while making effective use of the observations already available. This paper proposes a method for convex constrained decision problems that requires only a partial data coverage assumption.

The algorithm uses a linear-programming-based primal-dual approach and introduces uncertainty parameters to improve data efficiency. Its theoretical analysis allows general function approximation. The stated coverage assumption matters because the result does not require comprehensive coverage of the decision problem, although it still depends on the partial coverage condition specified by the framework.

The authors report an improvement over the previous state of the art by a factor of one divided by one minus the discount factor. This identifies the discount factor as a central part of the theoretical gain. Numerical experiments support the theoretical findings and demonstrate improvements in safety and learning efficiency in the evaluated offline settings. The contribution combines an uncertainty-aware optimization method with theoretical and empirical evidence for more efficient safe learning from fixed data.
summary.tldr: An uncertainty-aware primal-dual algorithm improves safe offline reinforcement learning under partial data coverage, with theoretical and numerical support.

title: Safe and Efficient: A Primal-Dual Method for Offline Convex CMDPs under Partial Data Coverage

abstract: Existing dynamic scene generation methods mostly rely on distilling knowledge from pre-trained 3D generative models, which are typically fine-tuned on synthetic object datasets.As a result, the generated scenes are often object-centric and lack photorealism. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel pipeline designed for photorealistic text-to-4D scene generation, discarding the dependency on multi-view generative models and instead fully utilizing video generative models trained on diverse real-world datasets. Our method begins by generating a reference video using the video generation model.We then learn the canonical 3D representation of the video using a freeze-time video, delicately generated from the reference video.To handle inconsistencies in the freeze-time video, we jointly learn a per-frame deformation to model these imperfections.We then learn the temporal deformation based on the canonical representation to capture dynamic interactions in the reference video. The pipeline facilitates the generation of dynamic scenes with enhanced photorealism and structural integrity, viewable from multiple perspectives, thereby setting a new standard in 4D scene generation.

paragraphs: 4Real generates dynamic 3D scenes from text, with time supplying the fourth dimension. The paper addresses a limitation of approaches built around pretrained 3D generators: their reliance on synthetic object datasets often produces object-centered scenes with limited photorealism. Its pipeline instead draws on video generators trained on diverse real-world footage, using their visual knowledge to construct scenes that can be viewed from multiple perspectives.

The process starts with a generated reference video. From that reference, the method produces a freeze-time video and learns a canonical 3D representation, which serves as the scene's shared spatial foundation. Because the freeze-time video can contain inconsistencies, the system jointly learns frame-specific deformations to account for these imperfections during reconstruction.

A further temporal deformation model captures the changing interactions in the original reference video. This separates the construction of the shared scene from the modeling of its dynamics. The paper reports improved photorealism and structural integrity, presenting video generation as a useful foundation for dynamic, explorable scenes without requiring a multi-view generative model.
summary.tldr: 4Real turns generated videos into dynamic 3D scenes by learning a shared scene representation and deformations for inconsistencies and motion.

title: 4Real: Towards Photorealistic 4D Scene Generation via Video Diffusion Models

abstract: Current methods for training Binarized Neural Networks (BNNs) heavily rely on the heuristic straight-through estimator (STE), which crucially enables the application of SGD-based optimizers to the combinatorial training problem. Although the STE heuristics and their variants have led to significant improvements in BNN performance, their theoretical underpinnings remain unclear and relatively understudied. In this paper, we propose a theoretically motivated optimization framework for BNN training based on Gaussian variational inference. In its simplest form, our approach yields a non-convex linear programming formulation whose variables and associated gradients motivate the use of latent weights and STE gradients. More importantly, our framework allows us to formulate semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxations to the BNN training task. Such formulations are able to explicitly models pairwise correlations between weights during training, leading to a more accurate optimization characterization of the training problem. As the size of such formulations grows quadratically in the number of weights, quickly becoming intractable for large networks, we apply the Burer-Monteiro approach and only optimize over linear-size low-rank SDP solutions. Our empirical evaluation on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Tiny-ImageNet and ImageNet datasets shows our method consistently outperforming all state-of-the-art algorithms for training BNNs.

paragraphs: Training binary neural networks involves a combinatorial optimization problem. Common methods make gradient-based training possible through the straight-through estimator, but its theoretical basis remains limited. This paper introduces a framework grounded in Gaussian variational inference to better explain existing practices and develop a richer optimization approach.

In its simplest form, the framework produces a non-convex linear-programming formulation whose variables and gradients motivate latent weights and straight-through gradients. It also supports semidefinite-programming relaxations that explicitly model pairwise weight correlations. Those correlations provide a more detailed characterization of the training problem, but a direct formulation grows quadratically with the number of weights.

To address that scaling problem, the authors use the Burer–Monteiro approach and optimize low-rank solutions of linear size. Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, Tiny-ImageNet, and ImageNet show consistent improvements over the compared state-of-the-art binary-network training algorithms. The contribution links a theoretical account of familiar training tools with a practical way to incorporate weight correlations without retaining the full quadratic-size formulation.
summary.tldr: A variational-inference framework motivates binary-network training heuristics and yields a low-rank optimization method that improves evaluated image-classification performance.

title: Training Binary Neural Networks via Gaussian Variational Inference and Low-Rank Semidefinite Programming

abstract: High dynamic range (HDR) novel view synthesis (NVS) aims to create photorealistic images from novel viewpoints using HDR imaging techniques. The rendered HDR images capture a wider range of brightness levels containing more details of the scene than normal low dynamic range (LDR) images. Existing HDR NVS methods are mainly based on NeRF. They suffer from long training time and slow inference speed. In this paper, we propose a new framework, High Dynamic Range Gaussian Splatting (HDR-GS), which can efficiently render novel HDR views and reconstruct LDR images with a user input exposure time. Specifically, we design a Dual Dynamic Range (DDR) Gaussian point cloud model that uses spherical harmonics to fit HDR color and employs an MLP-based tone-mapper to render LDR color. The HDR and LDR colors are then fed into two Parallel Differentiable Rasterization (PDR) processes to reconstruct HDR and LDR views. To establish the data foundation for the research of 3D Gaussian splatting-based methods in HDR NVS, we recalibrate the camera parameters and compute the initial positions for Gaussian point clouds. Comprehensive experiments show that HDR-GS surpasses the state-of-the-art NeRF-based method by 3.84 and 1.91 dB on LDR and HDR NVS while enjoying 1000$\times$ inference speed and only costing 6.3\% training time. Code and data are released at https://github.com/caiyuanhao1998/HDR-GS
