paragraphs: HDR-GS generates new views of a scene while representing a wider brightness range than ordinary low-dynamic-range images. It addresses the training and rendering costs of existing NeRF-based HDR approaches. The framework produces HDR views and can also reconstruct LDR images at an exposure time chosen by the user.

Its scene representation is a Gaussian point cloud supporting both brightness ranges. Spherical harmonics fit HDR color, while a neural tone-mapper produces LDR color. Two parallel differentiable rasterization processes turn these colors into the respective images. The authors also recalibrate camera parameters and compute initial Gaussian positions to establish a data foundation for this approach.

Experiments report improvements of 3.84 dB for LDR and 1.91 dB for HDR novel-view synthesis over the state-of-the-art NeRF-based comparison. They also report 1000 times the inference speed while using 6.3% of the training time. These results indicate that, in the evaluated setting, the dual-range Gaussian representation improves rendering quality while substantially reducing the cost of learning and displaying new views.
summary.tldr: HDR-GS uses a dual-range Gaussian scene representation to improve HDR and LDR view synthesis while greatly reducing reported training and rendering costs.

title: HDR-GS: Efficient High Dynamic Range Novel View Synthesis at 1000x Speed via Gaussian Splatting

abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) have attracted considerable attention due to their diverse applications. However, the scarcity and quality limitations of graph data present challenges to their training process in practical settings. To facilitate the development of effective GNNs, companies and researchers often seek external collaboration. Yet, directly sharing data raises privacy concerns, motivating data owners to train GNNs on their private graphs and share the trained models. Unfortunately, these models may still inadvertently disclose sensitive properties of their training graphs (\textit{e.g.}, average default rate in a transaction network), leading to severe consequences for data owners. In this work, we study graph property inference attack to identify the risk of sensitive property information leakage from shared models.Existing approaches typically train numerous shadow models for developing such attack, which is computationally intensive and impractical. To address this issue, we propose an efficient graph property inference attack by leveraging model approximation techniques. Our method only requires training a small set of models on graphs, while generating a sufficient number of approximated shadow models for attacks.To enhance diversity while reducing errors in the approximated models, we apply edit distance to quantify the diversity within a group of approximated models and introduce a theoretically guaranteed criterion to evaluate each model's error. Subsequently, we propose a novel selection mechanism to ensure that the retained approximated models achieve high diversity and low error.Extensive experiments across six real-world scenarios demonstrate our method's substantial improvement, with average increases of 2.7\% in attack accuracy and 4.1\% in ROC-AUC, while being 6.5$\times$ faster compared to the best baseline.

paragraphs: Sharing a trained graph neural network can reveal sensitive information even when its training graph remains private. This paper studies attacks that infer properties of that graph, such as the average default rate in a transaction network. The privacy concern is about characteristics of the training data that a model may indirectly expose.

Existing attacks often train many shadow models to learn how model behavior relates to graph properties. That process is expensive. The proposed method trains only a small collection of models on graphs and then creates additional approximate shadow models. To make those approximations useful, it measures their diversity using edit distance and evaluates approximation error with a theoretically supported criterion. A selection mechanism retains models that combine variety with low error.

These findings show that approximation can make this form of privacy-risk assessment both cheaper and more effective in the tested settings. They also reinforce that withholding raw graph data alone does not prevent property leakage through shared models.
summary.tldr: Approximated shadow models make attacks that infer private graph properties from shared neural networks faster and more accurate in the reported experiments.

title: Can Graph Neural Networks Expose Training Data Properties? An Efficient Risk Assessment Approach

abstract: While finetuning language models from pairwise preferences has proven remarkably effective, the underspecified nature of natural language presents critical challenges. Direct preference feedback is uninterpretable, difficult to provide where multidimensional criteria may apply, and often inconsistent, either because it is based on incomplete instructions or provided by diverse principals. To address these challenges, we consider the two-step preference modeling procedure that first resolves the under-specification by selecting a context, and then evaluates preference with respect to the chosen context. We decompose reward modeling error according to these two steps, which suggests that supervising context in addition to context-specific preference may be a viable approach to aligning models with diverse human preferences. For this to work, the ability of models to evaluate context-specific preference is critical. To this end, we contribute context-conditioned preference datasets and accompanying experiments that investigate the ability of language models to evaluate context-specific preference. Unlike past datasets, where context-specific preference is highly correlated with general preference, our "preference reversal" datasets disentangle context-specific and general preferences to isolate context-specific capabilities. We use our datasets to (1) show that existing preference models benefit from, but fail to fully consider, added context, (2) finetune a context-aware reward model with context-specific performance exceeding that of GPT-4 and Llama 3 70B, and (3) investigate the potential value of context-aware preference modeling.

paragraphs: A preference between two language-model responses can depend on unstated criteria or the person making the judgment. This makes direct preference feedback hard to interpret and potentially inconsistent. The paper treats preference modeling as two decisions: selecting the relevant context and evaluating the responses according to that context.

The authors decompose reward-modeling error along these two stages. Their analysis suggests that supervising context alongside context-specific preferences may help models accommodate diverse human preferences. To test the second stage, they construct preference-reversal datasets that separate context-specific choices from general preferences. This design makes it harder for a model to succeed simply by repeating its usual preference regardless of the stated context.

Experiments show that existing preference models benefit from context but do not fully use it. The authors also fine-tune a context-aware reward model whose context-specific performance exceeds GPT-4 and Llama 3 70B in their evaluation. The results establish a targeted capability improvement and motivate further investigation of context-aware preference modeling's value for alignment.
summary.tldr: Preference-reversal datasets reveal incomplete context use in reward models and support training models to evaluate context-specific preferences.

title: Improving Context-Aware Preference Modeling for Language Models

abstract: When using large language models (LLMs) in high-stakes applications, we need to know when we can trust their predictions. Some works argue that prompting high-performance LLMs is sufficient to produce calibrated uncertainties, while others introduce sampling methods that can be prohibitively expensive. In this work, we first argue that prompting on its own is insufficient to achieve good calibration and then show that fine-tuning on a small dataset of correct and incorrect answers can create an uncertainty estimate with good generalization and small computational overhead. We show that a thousand graded examples are sufficient to outperform baseline methods and that training through the features of a model is necessary for good performance and tractable for large open-source models when using LoRA. We also investigate the mechanisms that enable reliable LLM uncertainty estimation, finding that many models can be used as general-purpose uncertainty estimators, applicable not just to their own uncertainties but also the uncertainty of other models. Lastly, we show that uncertainty estimates inform human use of LLMs in human-AI collaborative settings through a user study.

paragraphs: Useful uncertainty estimates should help users distinguish answers they can trust from answers likely to be wrong. This paper argues that prompting alone is insufficient for good calibration and examines a training-based alternative. The approach fine-tunes on a small collection of answers marked correct or incorrect, aiming for estimates that generalize with little computational overhead.

The authors show that a thousand graded examples are sufficient to outperform the evaluated baselines. They also find that training through a model’s features is necessary for good performance in their investigation, and that LoRA makes this tractable for large open-source models. The central result is that explicit correctness supervision can support uncertainty estimation without requiring expensive sampling procedures.

The paper further investigates where this ability comes from and finds that many models can estimate uncertainty for other models as well as themselves. A user study shows that the resulting estimates inform how people use language models in collaborative settings. Together, these findings connect calibration training with both transferable uncertainty estimation and its role in human decisions.
summary.tldr: Fine-tuning on a thousand graded answers produces useful, transferable uncertainty estimates that outperform the evaluated baselines.

title: Large Language Models Must Be Taught to Know What They Don’t Know

abstract: Interest in bilevel optimization has grown in recent years, partially due to its relevance for challenging machine-learning problems. Several exciting recent works have been centered around developing efficient gradient-based algorithms that can solve bilevel optimization problems with provable guarantees. However, the existing literature mainly focuses on bilevel problems either without constraints, or featuring only simple constraints that do not couple variables across the upper and lower levels, excluding a range of complex applications. Our paper studies this challenging but less explored scenario and develops a (fully) first-order algorithm, which we term BLOCC, to tackle BiLevel Optimization problems with Coupled Constraints. We establish rigorous convergence theory for the proposed algorithm and demonstrate its effectiveness on two well-known real-world applications - support vector machine (SVM) - based model training and infrastructure planning in transportation networks.

paragraphs: Bilevel optimization describes problems in which one optimization task depends on the solution of another. Constraints become especially challenging when they connect variables from both levels: the two decisions cannot be treated as independently restricted problems. The paper targets this coupled setting, which is excluded by much of the existing work on unconstrained or simply constrained bilevel optimization.

The authors introduce BLOCC, a fully first-order algorithm for bilevel problems with coupled constraints. Its penalty approach is assisted by primal-dual optimization, as reflected in the title. The central contribution is an algorithm that handles the connection between levels while retaining a first-order formulation. This broadens the class of bilevel problems addressed by algorithms with provable guarantees.

The paper establishes convergence theory and demonstrates the method on support-vector-machine model training and transportation infrastructure planning. These applications provide evidence of effectiveness in two different practical settings. Together, the theory and applications show a way to address constraints that cross the boundary between the upper and lower optimization problems.
summary.tldr: BLOCC provides a fully first-order algorithm with convergence guarantees for bilevel optimization whose constraints couple both decision levels.

title: A Primal-Dual-Assisted Penalty Approach to Bilevel Optimization with Coupled Constraints

abstract: Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DPMs) have been recently utilized to deal with various blind image restoration (IR) tasks, where they have demonstrated outstanding performance in terms of perceptual quality. However, the task-specific nature of existing solutions and the excessive computational costs related to their training, make such models impractical and challenging to use for different IR tasks than those that were initially trained for. This hinders their wider adoption especially by those who lack access to powerful computational resources and vast amounts of training data. In this work we aim to address the above issues and enable the successful adoption of DPMs in practical IR-related applications. Towards this goal, we propose a modular diffusion probabilistic IR framework (DP-IR), which allows us to combine the performance benefits of existing pre-trained state-of-the-art IR networks and generative DPMs, while it requires only the additional training of a small module (0.7M params) related to the particular IR task of interest. Moreover, the architecture of our proposed framework allows us to employ a sampling strategy that leads to at least four times reduction of neural function evaluations without any performance loss, while it can also be combined with existing acceleration techniques (e.g. DDIM). We evaluate our model on four benchmarks for the tasks of burst JDD-SR, dynamic scene deblurring, and super-resolution. Our method outperforms existing approaches in terms of perceptual quality while retaining a competitive performance in relation to fidelity metrics.

paragraphs: Image restoration must recover a useful image from damaged or incomplete visual information. Diffusion models can produce perceptually convincing results, but existing restoration systems often require expensive training for each task. DP-IR addresses this practical obstacle by connecting pretrained restoration networks with pretrained generative diffusion models through a small task-specific module.

The additional module has 0.7 million parameters. Its role is to let the framework combine the strengths of existing restoration and generation systems without requiring a newly trained diffusion model for every restoration task. The architecture also supports a sampling strategy that reduces neural function evaluations by at least fourfold without a reported performance loss. This strategy can be combined with acceleration methods such as DDIM.

The authors evaluate DP-IR on four benchmarks covering burst JDD-SR, dynamic scene deblurring, and super-resolution. They report better perceptual quality than existing approaches while remaining competitive on fidelity metrics. The distinction matters: the results support more convincing-looking reconstructions alongside competitive agreement with reference images, rather than claiming the best performance on every measure.
summary.tldr: DP-IR combines pretrained restoration and diffusion models through a small task-specific module, improving perceptual quality while reducing sampling computation.

title: A Modular Conditional Diffusion Framework for Image Reconstruction

abstract: Diffusion policy has shown a strong ability to express complex action distributions in offline reinforcement learning (RL). However, it suffers from overestimating Q-value functions on out-of-distribution (OOD) data points due to the offline dataset limitation. To address it, this paper proposes a novel entropy-regularized diffusion policy and takes into account the confidence of the Q-value prediction with Q-ensembles. At the core of our diffusion policy is a mean-reverting stochastic differential equation (SDE) that transfers the action distribution into a standard Gaussian form and then samples actions conditioned on the environment state with a corresponding reverse-time process. We show that the entropy of such a policy is tractable and that can be used to increase the exploration of OOD samples in offline RL training. Moreover, we propose using the lower confidence bound of Q-ensembles for pessimistic Q-value function estimation. The proposed approach demonstrates state-of-the-art performance across a range of tasks in the D4RL benchmarks, significantly improving upon existing diffusion-based policies. The code is available at https://github.com/ruoqizzz/entropy-offlineRL.

paragraphs: Diffusion policies can represent complicated action distributions, making them useful for offline reinforcement learning. However, a fixed dataset leaves uncertainty about unfamiliar actions, and learned Q-functions can assign those actions overly optimistic values. This paper combines an entropy-regularized diffusion policy with an ensemble of Q-functions to address that problem.

The policy uses a mean-reverting stochastic differential equation to transform the action distribution into a standard Gaussian. A corresponding reverse-time process generates actions conditioned on the environment state. The authors show that this policy has tractable entropy, allowing entropy regularization to encourage exploration of out-of-distribution samples during offline training.

The Q-ensemble supplies a complementary safeguard: action values are estimated pessimistically using a lower confidence bound. The design therefore combines broader action sampling with caution about uncertain value predictions. Across a range of D4RL tasks, the authors report state-of-the-art performance and substantial improvements over existing diffusion policies. These results support the combined policy-and-value design in the evaluated offline reinforcement-learning settings.
summary.tldr: An entropy-regularized diffusion policy paired with pessimistic Q-ensemble estimates improves offline reinforcement-learning performance on D4RL tasks.

title: Entropy-regularized Diffusion Policy with Q-Ensembles for Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Identifying the features learned by neural networks is a core challenge in mechanistic interpretability. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs), which learn a sparse, overcomplete dictionary that reconstructs a network's internal activations, have been used to identify these features. However, SAEs may learn more about the structure of the datatset than the computational structure of the network. There is therefore only indirect reason to believe that the directions found in these dictionaries are functionally important to the network. We propose end-to-end (e2e) sparse dictionary learning, a method for training SAEs that ensures the features learned are functionally important by minimizing the KL divergence between the output distributions of the original model and the model with SAE activations inserted. Compared to standard SAEs, e2e SAEs offer a Pareto improvement: They explain more network performance, require fewer total features, and require fewer simultaneously active features per datapoint, all with no cost to interpretability. We explore geometric and qualitative differences between e2e SAE features and standard SAE features. E2e dictionary learning brings us closer to methods that can explain network behavior concisely and accurately. We release our library for training e2e SAEs and reproducing our analysis athttps://github.com/ApolloResearch/e2e_sae.

paragraphs: Sparse autoencoders try to explain neural-network activations using a large collection of features, only a few of which are active for any input. Reconstructing activations accurately, however, provides only indirect evidence that those features matter to the network's computation. The paper argues that conventional training may capture structure in the dataset more strongly than structure responsible for the model's behavior.

End-to-end sparse dictionary learning changes the training objective to focus on the model's outputs. It inserts the autoencoder's reconstructed activations into the network and minimizes the KL divergence between the resulting output distribution and the original model's distribution. This makes preserving the network's behavior the direct criterion for learning functionally important features.

Compared with standard sparse autoencoders, the authors report a Pareto improvement: more network performance is explained using fewer total features and fewer active features per input, without a loss of interpretability. They also examine geometric and qualitative differences between the learned dictionaries. The findings support using downstream behavior to train more concise explanations of network computation, rather than relying solely on activation reconstruction.
summary.tldr: Training sparse autoencoders to preserve model outputs produces more compact, functionally relevant feature dictionaries without a reported loss of interpretability.

title: Identifying Functionally Important Features with End-to-End Sparse Dictionary Learning

abstract: Pairwise dot-product self-attention is key to the success of transformers that achieve state-of-the-art performance across a variety of applications in language and vision. This dot-product self-attention computes attention weights among the input tokens using Euclidean distance, which makes the model prone to representation collapse and vulnerable to contaminated samples. In this paper, we propose using a Mahalanobis distance metric for computing the attention weights to stretch the underlying feature space in directions of high contextual relevance. In particular, we define a hyper-ellipsoidal neighborhood around each query to increase the attention weights of the tokens lying in the contextually important directions. We term this novel class of attention Elliptical Attention. Our Elliptical Attention provides two benefits: 1) reducing representation collapse and 2) enhancing the model's robustness as the Elliptical Attention pays more attention to contextually relevant information, rather than focusing on some small subset of informative features. We empirically demonstrate the advantages of Elliptical Attention over the baseline dot-product attention and state-of-the-art attention methods on various practical tasks, including object classification, imagesegmentation, and language modeling across different data modalities.

paragraphs: Elliptical Attention changes how a transformer decides which input tokens deserve attention. The paper links conventional dot-product attention to a Euclidean view of similarity and identifies problems with representation collapse and sensitivity to contaminated samples. Its proposed remedy is to make the geometry of attention reflect directions that matter in the current context.

The method computes attention weights using a Mahalanobis distance. This stretches the feature space along contextually relevant directions and creates an ellipsoidal neighborhood around each query. Tokens positioned along those important directions receive greater weight, allowing the attention mechanism to emphasize relevant information through its choice of distance measure.

The authors present two benefits: less representation collapse and greater robustness. Their explanation is that attention can use contextually relevant information more broadly instead of concentrating on a small subset of informative features. Experiments compare the method with dot-product attention and other leading attention approaches on object classification, image segmentation, and language modeling. The reported advantages across these tasks support the usefulness of adapting attention geometry across visual and language data.
summary.tldr: Elliptical Attention uses context-sensitive distance geometry to reduce representation collapse and improve robustness in evaluated vision and language tasks.

title: Elliptical Attention

abstract: The ultimate goal of multi-objective optimization (MO) is to assist human decision-makers (DMs) in identifying solutions of interest (SOI) that optimally reconcile multiple objectives according to their preferences. Preference-based evolutionary MO (PBEMO) has emerged as a promising framework that progressively approximates SOI by involving human in the optimization-cum-decision-making process. Yet, current PBEMO approaches are prone to be inefficient and misaligned with the DM’s true aspirations, especially when inadvertently exploiting mis-calibrated reward models. This is further exacerbated when considering the stochastic nature of human feedback. This paper proposes a novel framework that navigates MO to SOI by directly leveraging human feedback without being restricted by a predefined reward model nor cumbersome model selection. Specifically, we developed a clustering-based stochastic dueling bandits algorithm that strategically scales well to high-dimensional dueling bandits, and achieves a regret of $\mathcal{O}(K^2\log T)$, where $K$ is the number of clusters and $T$ is the number of rounds. The learned preferences are then transformed into a unified probabilistic format that can be readily adapted to prevalent EMO algorithms. This also leads to a principled termination criterion that strategically manages human cognitive loads and computational budget. Experiments on $48$ benchmark test problems, including synthetic problems, RNA inverse design and protein structure prediction, fully demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed approach.

paragraphs: Multi-objective optimization seeks solutions that balance competing goals according to a person's preferences. A difficulty arises when an optimizer follows an inaccurate reward model: it can pursue solutions that score well without matching what the person wants. Human feedback also varies, making preference learning uncertain.

This paper proposes using human comparisons directly through a clustering-based stochastic dueling bandit algorithm. The algorithm organizes the comparison problem into clusters and learns from uncertain feedback without requiring a predefined reward model or extensive model selection. Its stated regret bound is O(K² log T), where K counts clusters and T counts rounds.

The learned preferences are converted into a common probabilistic representation that existing evolutionary multi-objective algorithms can use. The framework also supplies a stopping criterion intended to manage computational resources and the burden of requesting human judgments. Experiments across 48 benchmark problems, including RNA inverse design and protein structure prediction, demonstrate effectiveness. The contribution links preference elicitation, optimization, and stopping decisions within one framework.
summary.tldr: The framework guides multi-objective optimization with uncertain human comparisons, using clustered dueling bandits and a principled stopping criterion.

title: Direct Preference-Based Evolutionary Multi-Objective Optimization with Dueling Bandits

abstract: Most existing image tokenizers encode images into a fixed number of tokens or patches, overlooking the inherent variability in image complexity and introducing unnecessary computate overhead for simpler images. To address this, we propose Content-Adaptive Tokenizer (CAT), which dynamically adjusts representation capacity based on the image content and encodes simpler images into fewer tokens. We design (1) a caption-based evaluation system that leverages LLMs to predict content complexity and determine the optimal compression ratio for an image, and (2) a novel nested VAE architecture that performs variable-rate compression in a single model. Trained on images with varying complexity, CAT achieves an average of 15% reduction in rFID across seven detail-rich datasets containing text, humans, and complex textures. On natural image datasets like ImageNet and COCO, it reduces token usage by 18% while maintaining high-fidelity reconstructions. We further evaluate CAT on two downstream tasks. For image classification, CAT consistently improves top-1 accuracy across five datasets spanning diverse domains. For image generation, it boosts training throughput by 23% on ImageNet, leading to more efficient learning and improved FIDs over fixed-token baselines.

paragraphs: Image tokenizers usually allocate the same number of tokens to every image, even though images differ greatly in complexity. CAT changes that allocation according to content, using fewer tokens for simpler images. The aim is to match representation capacity to the information an image contains, reducing unnecessary computation while retaining useful detail.

The method combines a caption-based complexity assessment with a nested variational autoencoder. A language model uses captions to estimate content complexity and choose a compression ratio. The nested architecture then supports different compression rates within one model, allowing the tokenizer to handle images with varying levels of detail.

Across seven detail-rich datasets, CAT reduces reconstruction FID by an average of 15%. On ImageNet and COCO, it uses 18% fewer tokens while maintaining high-fidelity reconstructions. Downstream experiments report improved classification accuracy across five datasets and a 23% increase in image-generation training throughput on ImageNet, together with improved generation FIDs over fixed-token baselines. The results connect adaptive compression to both representation quality and computational efficiency.
summary.tldr: CAT adjusts image token counts to content complexity, improving reconstruction and downstream results while reducing token use and increasing training throughput.

title: CAT: Content-Adaptive Image Tokenization

abstract: We study the problem of non-stationary Lipschitz bandits, where the number of actions is infinite and the reward function, satisfying a Lipschitz assumption, can change arbitrarily over time. We design an algorithm that adaptively tracks the recently introduced notion of significant shifts, defined by large deviations of the cumulative reward function. To detect such reward changes, our algorithm leverages a hierarchical discretization of the action space. Without requiring any prior knowledge of the non-stationarity, our algorithm achieves a minimax-optimal dynamic regret bound of $\mathcal{\widetilde{O}}(\tilde{L}^{1/3}T^{2/3})$, where $\tilde{L}$ is the number of significant shifts and $T$ the horizon. This result provides the first optimal guarantee in this setting.

paragraphs: The paper studies sequential decision-making with infinitely many possible actions and rewards that can change arbitrarily over time. A Lipschitz assumption provides structure by controlling how much reward can differ between nearby actions. The challenge is to exploit that structure while adapting to changes whose timing and extent are unknown.

The proposed algorithm tracks significant shifts, defined through large deviations in cumulative rewards. It uses a hierarchical discretization of the action space to detect these changes. This gives the algorithm a way to work with an infinite action set while monitoring reward changes at multiple levels of resolution, without needing advance knowledge of the non-stationarity.

The resulting dynamic regret bound scales as the cube root of the number of significant shifts times the two-thirds power of the time horizon, up to logarithmic factors. Dynamic regret measures the cost of decisions relative to a changing benchmark. The authors establish minimax optimality and describe this as the first optimal guarantee in the setting, connecting adaptation difficulty to significant shifts rather than requiring their schedule as input.
summary.tldr: A hierarchical bandit algorithm adapts to unknown reward changes and achieves minimax-optimal dynamic regret governed by the number of significant shifts.

title: Non-Stationary Lipschitz Bandits

abstract: LibriBrain represents the largest single-subject MEG dataset to date for speech decoding, with over 50 hours of recordings---5$\times$ larger than the next comparable dataset and 50$\times$ larger than most. This unprecedented `depth' of within-subject data enables exploration of neural representations at a scale previously unavailable with non-invasive methods. LibriBrain comprises high-quality MEG recordings together with detailed annotations from a single participant listening to naturalistic spoken English, covering nearly the full Sherlock Holmes canon. Designed to support advances in neural decoding, LibriBrain comes with a Python library for streamlined integration with deep learning frameworks, standard data splits for reproducibility, and baseline results for three foundational decoding tasks: speech detection, phoneme classification, and word classification. Baseline experiments demonstrate that increasing training data yields substantial improvements in decoding performance, highlighting the value of scaling up deep, within-subject datasets. By releasing this dataset, we aim to empower the research community to advance speech decoding methodologies and accelerate the development of safe, effective clinical brain-computer interfaces.

summary.tldr: LibriBrain provides over fifty hours of one participant's MEG recordings and shows that more within-subject data substantially improves speech decoding.

title: LibriBrain: Over 50 Hours of Within-Subject MEG to Improve Speech Decoding Methods at Scale

abstract: Graph foundation models (GFMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for learning transferable knowledge across diverse graph-structured data. The inherent heterogeneity in features and graph structures poses significant challenges for building scalable and generalizable GFMs. Existing research has employed mixture-of-experts (MoE) models to handle the challenges, assigning the most suitable expert to each graph. Despite this, the underlying mechanisms of MoE within the context of GFMs remain insufficiently explored. In this work, we conduct an in-depth experimental study on an MoE-based GFM and uncover an intriguing finding: the experts ranked second and third assigned by the router perform better than the top-ranked expert. This insight motivates us to investigate the potential of leveraging knowledge embedded across multiple experts. However, directly ensembling the outputs of multiple experts would incur substantial computational overhead, while applying a standard expert merging strategy risks suboptimal performance. To address these challenges, we introduce two enhanced expert merging strategies that retain the computational efficiency of expert merging, while improving performance to approach the effectiveness of expert ensembling. Specifically, we propose (i) a knowledge distillation-inspired expert merging method that aligns the behavior of parameter-fused experts with expert ensembles, and (ii) a theoretical parameter proximity approach that leverages the similarity of expert parameters to approximate ensemble outputs while preserving diversity. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our methods effectively enhance model performance.

paragraphs: Graph foundation models must handle datasets with different features and connection patterns. In an experimental study, however, the authors find that experts ranked second and third by the router outperform the first-ranked expert. This motivates looking beyond the router’s top choice for useful knowledge.

Combining several experts’ outputs can exploit that knowledge but adds substantial computation. Merging their parameters is more efficient, yet a standard merge can deliver suboptimal results. The paper develops two enhanced merging strategies. One takes inspiration from knowledge distillation, aligning the behavior of the merged expert with an ensemble. The other uses parameter similarity to approximate ensemble outputs while preserving diversity.

Both strategies aim to retain the computational advantages of merging while approaching the effectiveness of evaluating multiple experts. Extensive experiments show improved model performance. The findings identify a routing weakness in the studied model and demonstrate practical ways to incorporate knowledge distributed across experts.
summary.tldr: Two enhanced expert-merging strategies improve graph foundation models while retaining merging’s computational efficiency.

title: Enhanced Expert Merging for Mixture-of-Experts in Graph Foundation Models

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) show remarkable promise for democratizing automated reasoning by generating formal specifications. However, a fundamental tension exists: LLMs are probabilistic, while formal verification demands deterministic guarantees. This paper addresses this epistemological gap by comprehensively investigating failure modes and uncertainty quantification (UQ) in LLM-generated formal artifacts. Our systematic evaluation of five frontier LLMs reveals Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) based autoformalization's domain-specific impact on accuracy (from +34.8\% on logical tasks to -44.5\% on factual ones), with known UQ techniques like the entropy of token probabilities failing to identify these errors. We introduce a probabilistic context-free grammar (PCFG) framework to model LLM outputs, yielding a refined uncertainty taxonomy. We find uncertainty signals are task-dependent (e.g., grammar entropy for logic, AUROC>0.93). Finally, a lightweight fusion of these signals enables selective verification, drastically reducing errors (14-100\%) with minimal abstention, transforming LLM-driven formalization into a reliable engineering discipline.

paragraphs: Language models can translate problems into formal specifications, but a probabilistically generated specification can be wrong even when a formal reasoning system processes it correctly. This paper studies that gap by examining failures and uncertainty measures in artifacts generated by five frontier models. It asks when formalization helps and which signals identify unreliable outputs.

The evaluation finds sharply different effects across domains: SMT-based autoformalization changes accuracy by +34.8% on logical tasks and −44.5% on factual tasks. Familiar uncertainty measures, including token-probability entropy, fail to identify these errors. The authors instead model generated outputs with probabilistic context-free grammars, producing a more differentiated account of uncertainty.

The useful signals depend on the task. For logical tasks, grammar entropy achieves an AUROC above 0.93, indicating strong discrimination in the reported evaluation. Combining signals in a lightweight system enables selective verification, with reported error reductions of 14–100% and minimal abstention. The findings support task-sensitive reliability checks; they do not make every generated formal specification automatically correct.
summary.tldr: Grammar-based, task-dependent uncertainty signals help identify unreliable LLM formalizations and reduce errors through selective verification.

title: Grammars of Formal Uncertainty: When to Trust LLMs in Automated Reasoning Tasks

abstract: Tree ensembles have demonstrated state-of-the-art predictive performance across a wide range of problems involving tabular data. Nevertheless, the black-box nature of tree ensembles is a strong limitation, especially for applications with critical decisions at stake. The Hoeffding or ANOVA functional decomposition is a powerful explainability method, as it breaks down black-box models into a unique sum of lower-dimensional functions, provided that input variables are independent. In standard learning settings, input variables are often dependent, and the Hoeffding decomposition is generalized through hierarchical orthogonality constraints. Such generalization leads to unique and sparse decompositions with well-defined main effects and interactions. However, the practical estimation of this decomposition from a data sample is still an open problem. Therefore, we introduce the TreeHFD algorithm to estimate the Hoeffding decomposition of a tree ensemble from a data sample. We show the convergence of TreeHFD, along with the main properties of orthogonality, sparsity, and causal variable selection. The high performance of TreeHFD is demonstrated through experiments on both simulated and real data, using our treehfd Python package (https://github.com/ThalesGroup/treehfd). Besides, we empirically show that the widely used TreeSHAP method, based on Shapley values, is strongly connected to the Hoeffding decomposition.

paragraphs: Tree ensembles can predict tabular outcomes accurately while remaining difficult to interpret. The Hoeffding functional decomposition offers a way to separate a model into contributions from individual variables and their interactions. With independent inputs, this decomposition is unique. Dependent inputs require a generalization based on hierarchical orthogonality to define those effects distinctly.

Although the generalized decomposition can be unique and sparse, estimating it from sampled data is a practical challenge. TreeHFD addresses this problem specifically for tree ensembles. The authors establish convergence and properties involving orthogonality, sparsity, and causal variable selection, giving theoretical support to the algorithm’s reconstruction of the model’s component effects.

Experiments on simulated and real data demonstrate strong performance using the authors’ Python implementation. The paper also finds an empirical connection between the widely used TreeSHAP method and the Hoeffding decomposition. Together, these contributions provide a practical route to separating main effects from interactions and relate that decomposition-based explanation to an established approach based on Shapley values.
summary.tldr: TreeHFD estimates a tree ensemble’s Hoeffding decomposition, separating main effects and interactions while accommodating dependent inputs.

title: Tree Ensemble Explainability through the Hoeffding Functional Decomposition and TreeHFD Algorithm

abstract: 3D generation from natural language offers significant potential to reduce expert manual modeling efforts and enhance accessibility to 3D assets. However, existing methods often yield unstructured meshes and exhibit poor interactivity, making them impractical for artistic workflows. To address these limitations, we represent 3D assets as shape programs and introduce ShapeCraft, a novel multi-agent framework for text-to-3D generation. At its core, we propose a Graph-based Procedural Shape (GPS) representation that decomposes complex natural language into a structured graph of sub-tasks, thereby facilitating accurate LLM comprehension and interpretation of spatial relationships and semantic shape details. Specifically, LLM agents hierarchically parse user input to initialize GPS, then iteratively refine procedural modeling and painting to produce structured, textured, and interactive 3D assets. Qualitative and quantitative experiments demonstrate ShapeCraft's superior performance in generating geometrically accurate and semantically rich 3D assets compared to existing LLM-based agents. We further show the versatility of ShapeCraft through examples of animated and user-customized editing, highlighting its potential for broader interactive applications.

paragraphs: ShapeCraft addresses a practical problem in text-to-3D generation: a generated object may look useful but remain difficult to edit because its mesh lacks meaningful structure. The paper represents assets as shape programs, aiming to produce objects that support continued modeling, painting, and interaction within artistic workflows rather than ending at an unstructured geometric output.

Its Graph-based Procedural Shape representation organizes a complex language request into a graph of modeling subtasks. Multiple language-model agents parse the request hierarchically to initialize this graph, then iteratively refine the procedural geometry and painting. The structured representation helps the agents interpret spatial relationships and semantic shape details, connecting what the user describes to the operations that build the asset.

Qualitative and quantitative experiments report better geometric accuracy and semantic richness than existing language-model-based agents. The authors also demonstrate animation and user-customized editing. Those examples illustrate why the representation matters beyond initial generation: the asset retains a structure that can support further interaction. The findings establish reported advantages within the evaluated comparisons and demonstrate potential for broader interactive applications.
summary.tldr: ShapeCraft turns text into procedural shape graphs that language-model agents refine into structured, textured, and editable 3D assets.

title: ShapeCraft: LLM Agents for Structured, Textured and Interactive 3D Modeling

abstract: At the core of the Transformer, the softmax normalizes the attention matrix to be right stochastic. Previous research has shown that this often de-stabilizes training and that enforcing the attention matrix to be doubly stochastic (through Sinkhorn’s algorithm) consistently improves performance across different tasks, domains and Transformer flavors. However, Sinkhorn’s algorithm is iterative, approximative, non-parametric and thus inflexible w.r.t. the obtained doubly stochastic matrix (DSM). Recently, it has been proven that DSMs can be obtained with a parametric quantum circuit, yielding a novel quantum inductive bias for DSMs with no known classical analogue. Motivated by this, we demonstrate the feasibility of a hybrid classical-quantum doubly stochastic Transformer (QDSFormer) that replaces the softmax in the self-attention layer with a variational quantum circuit. We study the expressive power of the circuit and find that it yields more diverse DSMs that better preserve information than classical operators. Across multiple small-scale object recognition tasks, we find that our QDSFormer consistently surpasses both a standard ViT and other doubly stochastic Transformers. Beyond the Sinkformer, this comparison includes a novel quantum-inspired doubly stochastic Transformer (based on QR decomposition) that can be of independent interest. Our QDSFormer also shows improved training stability and lower performance variation suggesting that it may mitigate the notoriously unstable training of ViTs on small-scale data.

paragraphs: Transformer attention usually normalizes its matrix in one direction through softmax. Doubly stochastic attention instead constrains both rows and columns, an approach previously associated with improved performance. This paper explores a quantum alternative to Sinkhorn normalization, whose iterative, approximate, and non-parametric construction limits flexibility in the doubly stochastic matrices it produces.

The authors study the circuit’s expressive power and find that it generates more diverse doubly stochastic matrices that preserve information better than classical operators. They also introduce a quantum-inspired classical comparator based on QR decomposition.

On multiple small-scale object-recognition tasks, QDSFormer consistently outperforms a standard vision transformer and other doubly stochastic transformers, including the QR-based model. It also exhibits more stable training and lower performance variation. These observations suggest that the approach may help with unstable vision-transformer training on small datasets; the evidence presented concerns those small-scale recognition settings.
summary.tldr: QDSFormer uses a trainable quantum circuit for doubly stochastic attention, improving performance and training stability on small-scale recognition tasks.

title: Quantum Doubly Stochastic Transformers

abstract: Federated Graph Learning (FGL) has been shown to be particularly effective in enabling collaborative training of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) in decentralized settings. Model-heterogeneous FGL further enhances practical applicability by accommodating client preferences for diverse model architectures. However, existing model-heterogeneous approaches primarily target Euclidean data and fail to account for a crucial aspect of graph-structured data: topological relationships. To address this limitation, we propose **TRUST**, a novel knowledge distillation-based **model-heterogeneous FGL** framework. Specifically, we propose Progressive Curriculum Node Scheduler to progressively introduce challenging nodes based on learning difficulty. In Adaptive Curriculum Distillation Modulator, we propose an adaptive temperature modulator that dynamically adjusts knowledge distillation temperature to accommodate varying client capabilities and graph complexity. Moreover, we leverage Wasserstein‑Driven Affinity Distillation to enable models to capture cross-class structural relationships through optimal transport. Extensive experiments on multiple graph benchmarks and model-heterogeneous settings show that **TRUST** outperforms existing methods, achieving an average 3.6\% $\uparrow$ performance gain, particularly under moderate heterogeneity conditions. The code is available for anonymous access at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/TRUST-NeurIPS2025.

paragraphs: Federated graph learning enables decentralized clients to collaborate, and allowing different model architectures makes that collaboration more flexible. However, methods for heterogeneous models often overlook relationships encoded by graph topology. TRUST addresses this gap through knowledge distillation designed to account for both differences among client models and the structure of the graph data.

Its curriculum scheduler progressively introduces more challenging nodes according to learning difficulty. An adaptive temperature mechanism adjusts distillation to client capabilities and graph complexity, changing how knowledge is transferred. A further component uses Wasserstein-based optimal transport to convey structural relationships across classes, so the shared knowledge includes more than isolated node-level predictions.

Experiments span multiple graph benchmarks and settings with different client architectures. TRUST outperforms existing methods with a reported average performance gain of 3.6%, particularly under moderate heterogeneity. The findings support coordinating task difficulty, distillation behavior, and graph-structural information when transferring knowledge among different models. The emphasis on moderate heterogeneity also preserves the stated qualification about where the gains are especially pronounced.
summary.tldr: TRUST combines curriculum learning and structure-aware distillation to improve federated graph learning across clients with different model architectures.

title: Multi-order Orchestrated Curriculum Distillation for Model-Heterogeneous Federated Graph Learning

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are powerful but static; they lack mechanisms to adapt their weights in response to new tasks, knowledge, or examples. We introduce $\textbf{Se}$lf-$\textbf{A}$dapting $\textbf{L}$LMs (SEAL), a framework that enables LLMs to self-adapt by generating their own finetuning data and update directives. Given a new input, the model produces a $\textit{self-edit}$ --- a generation that may restructure the information in different ways, specify optimization hyperparameters, or invoke tools for data augmentation and gradient-based updates. Through supervised finetuning (SFT), these self-edits result in persistent weight updates, enabling lasting adaptation. To train the model to produce effective self-edits, we use a reinforcement learning loop, using the downstream performance of the updated model as the reward signal. Unlike prior approaches that rely on separate adaptation modules or auxiliary networks, SEAL directly uses the model's generation to parameterize and control its own adaptation process. Experiments on knowledge incorporation and few-shot generalization show that SEAL is a promising step toward language models capable of self-directed adaptation in response to new data. Our website and code is available at https://jyopari.github.io/posts/seal.

paragraphs: A language model can receive new information without changing its underlying weights. SEAL explores how a model can help direct lasting adaptation by generating the material and instructions used to update itself. Given a new input, it produces a self-edit that guides a subsequent learning step.

A self-edit may reorganize information into training data, choose optimization settings, or invoke tools for data augmentation and gradient-based updates. Supervised fine-tuning then turns those generated instructions and examples into persistent weight changes. To teach the model which self-edits are useful, SEAL uses reinforcement learning with the updated model’s downstream performance as the reward.

The adaptation process is therefore controlled through the model’s own generated output, without relying on a separate adaptation module or auxiliary network. Experiments investigate knowledge incorporation and generalization from a few examples, and the authors describe the findings as promising. The contribution is a framework for learning how to prepare and direct useful updates, with initial evidence that self-generated adaptation can improve subsequent performance.
summary.tldr: SEAL trains language models to generate their own fine-tuning data and update instructions, rewarding edits that improve subsequent performance.

title: Self-Adapting Language Models

abstract: We introduce Auto-Connect, a novel approach for automatic rigging that explicitly preserves skeletal connectivity through a connectivity-preserving tokenization scheme. Unlike previous methods that predict bone positions represented as two joints or first predict points before determining connectivity, our method employs special tokens to define endpoints for each joint's children and for each hierarchical layer, effectively automating connectivity relationships. This approach significantly enhances topological accuracy by integrating connectivity information directly into the prediction framework. To further guarantee high-quality topology, we implement a topology-aware reward function that quantifies topological correctness, which is then utilized in a post-training phase through reward-guided Direct Preference Optimization. Additionally, we incorporate implicit geodesic features for latent top-$k$ bone selection, which substantially improves skinning quality. By leveraging geodesic distance information within the model's latent space, our approach intelligently determines the most influential bones for each vertex, effectively mitigating common skinning artifacts. This combination of connectivity-preserving tokenization, reward-guided fine-tuning, and geodesic-aware bone selection enables our model to consistently generate more anatomically plausible skeletal structures with superior deformation properties.

paragraphs: Automatic rigging must produce a connected skeleton and determine how that skeleton influences a model’s surface. Auto-Connect builds skeletal connectivity directly into the sequence it predicts. Special tokens mark the endpoints of each joint’s children and each hierarchical layer, allowing the generated representation to express how joints belong together.

This representation addresses topology alongside joint placement. The method then uses a reward that measures topological correctness to guide a post-training phase with Direct Preference Optimization. Connectivity-aware prediction and reward-guided refinement therefore target the structure of the skeleton at two stages of the process.

Distance information in the latent space helps select the most influential bones for each vertex and reduces common skinning artifacts. The authors report more anatomically plausible skeletal structures and better deformation properties from the combined method. Its contribution spans both constructing the skeletal hierarchy and connecting that hierarchy to surface movement.
summary.tldr: Auto-Connect integrates skeletal connectivity, topology-guided preference optimization, and geodesic-aware bone selection to improve automatic rigging and deformation.

title: Auto-Connect: Connectivity-Preserving RigFormer with Direct Preference Optimization

abstract: We propose HoliGS, a novel deformable Gaussian splatting framework that addresses embodied view synthesis from long monocular RGB videos. Unlike prior 4D Gaussian splatting and dynamic NeRF pipelines, which struggle with training overhead in minute-long captures, our method leverages invertible Gaussian Splatting deformation networks to reconstruct large-scale, dynamic environments accurately. Specifically, we decompose each scene into a static background plus time-varying objects, each represented by learned Gaussian primitives undergoing global rigid transformations, skeleton-driven articulation, and subtle non-rigid deformations via an invertible neural flow. This hierarchical warping strategy enables robust free-viewpoint novel-view rendering from various embodied camera trajectories by attaching Gaussians to a complete canonical foreground shape (e.g., egocentric or third-person follow), which may involve substantial viewpoint changes and interactions between multiple actors. Our experiments demonstrate that HoliGS achieves superior reconstruction quality on challenging datasets while significantly reducing both training and rendering time compared to state-of-the-art monocular deformable NeRFs. These results highlight a practical and scalable solution for EVS in real-world scenarios. The source code will be released.

The target is embodied view synthesis, where cameras may follow actors or move through a scene from an egocentric perspective. Existing dynamic reconstruction pipelines face substantial training overhead on minute-long recordings, particularly when scenes contain movement and changing viewpoints.

summary.tldr: HoliGS uses hierarchical Gaussian deformation to reconstruct long dynamic monocular videos and efficiently render new embodied viewpoints.

title: HoliGS: Holistic Gaussian Splatting for Embodied View Synthesis

abstract: Modern machine learning often requires training with large batch size, distributed data, and massively parallel compute hardware (like mobile and other edge devices or distributed data centers). Communication becomes a major bottleneck in such settings but methods like Local Stochastic Gradient Descent (Local SGD) show great promise to reduce the global communication need. Local SGD consists of three parts: a local optimization processes, an aggregation mechanism, and an outer optimizer that uses the aggregated updates from the nodes to produce a new model. While there exists an extensive literature on understanding the impact of hyperparameters in the local optimization process, the choice of outer optimizer and its hyperparameters is less clear. We study the role of the outer learning in Local SGD, and prove new convergence guarantees for the algorithm. In particular, we show that tuning the outer learning rate allows us to (a) trade off between optimization error and stochastic gradient noise variance, and (b) make up for ill-tuning of the inner learning rate. Our theory suggests that the outer learning rate should sometimes be set to values greater than $1$. We extend our results to apply to when we use momentum in the outer optimizer, and also introduce a novel data-dependent analysis of Local SGD that yields further insights on outer learning rate tuning. We conduct comprehensive experiments with standard language models and various outer optimizers to validate our theory.

The combined update then passes through an outer optimizer to produce a new shared model. This paper studies that outer step, whose learning rate and optimizer choices are less understood than the local training settings.

Experiments with standard language models and several outer optimizers validate the theoretical findings. The contribution clarifies how local training and global updating interact, while preserving the conditional nature of the recommendation to use larger-than-one outer learning rates.
summary.tldr: The paper shows how Local SGD's outer learning rate balances error and noise, compensates for inner-rate mistuning, and can sometimes exceed one.

title: Understanding Outer Optimizers in Local SGD: Learning Rates, Momentum, and Acceleration

abstract: Motion simulation, prediction and planning are foundational tasks in autonomous driving, each essential for modeling and reasoning about dynamic traffic scenarios. While often addressed in isolation due to their differing objectives, such as generating diverse motion states or estimating optimal trajectories, these tasks inherently depend on shared capabilities: understanding multi-agent interactions, modeling motion behaviors, and reasoning over temporal and spatial dynamics. Despite this underlying commonality, existing approaches typically adopt specialized model designs, which hinders cross-task generalization and system scalability. More critically, this separation overlooks the potential mutual benefits among tasks. Motivated by these observations, we propose **UniMotion**, a unified motion framework that captures shared structures across motion tasks while accommodating their individual requirements. Built on a decoder-only Transformer architecture, UniMotion employs dedicated interaction modes and tailored training strategies to simultaneously support these motion tasks. This unified design not only enables joint optimization and representation sharing but also allows for targeted fine-tuning to specialize in individual tasks when needed. Extensive experiments on the Waymo Open Motion Dataset (WOMD) demonstrate that joint training leads to robust generalization and effective task integration. With further fine-tuning, UniMotion achieves state-of-the-art performance across a range of motion tasks, establishing it as a versatile and scalable solution for autonomous driving.

The paper argues that separate specialized models limit shared learning, cross-task generalization, and scalability.

Experiments on the Waymo Open Motion Dataset report robust generalization and effective integration from joint training. With additional fine-tuning, UniMotion reaches state-of-the-art performance across a range of motion tasks. The distinction between these stages matters: joint training supports a reusable motion representation, while the strongest reported task results involve further specialization. The work provides empirical evidence that related motion tasks can benefit from a common architecture and coordinated training.
summary.tldr: UniMotion shares a Transformer across driving simulation, prediction, and planning, with joint-training benefits and state-of-the-art results after task-specific fine-tuning.

title: UniMotion: A Unified Motion Framework for Simulation, Prediction and Planning

abstract: Performativity of predictions refers to the phenomenon where prediction-informed decisions influence the very targets they aim to predict—a dynamic commonly observed in policy-making, social sciences, and economics. In this paper, we initiate an end-to-end framework of statistical inference under performativity. Our contributions are twofold. First, we establish a central limit theorem for estimation and inference in the performative setting, enabling standard inferential tasks such as constructing confidence intervals and conducting hypothesis tests in policy-making contexts. Second, we leverage this central limit theorem to study prediction-powered inference (PPI) under performativity. This approach yields more precise estimates and tighter confidence regions for the model parameters (i.e., policies) of interest in performative prediction. We validate the effectiveness of our framework through numerical experiments. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to establish a complete statistical inference under performativity, introducing new challenges and inference settings that we believe will provide substantial value to policy-making, statistics, and machine learning.

paragraphs: Predictions can change the outcomes they are intended to forecast when people or institutions act on them. This feedback is called performativity and arises in settings such as policymaking and economics. The paper develops statistical inference for this situation, where evaluating uncertainty must account for the interaction between a prediction-informed decision and its target.

The first contribution is a central limit theorem for estimation in the performative setting. This provides a foundation for familiar inferential tasks, including confidence intervals and hypothesis tests. The goal extends beyond selecting a policy or producing a prediction to quantifying uncertainty about the parameters of interest.

The authors then use the theorem to develop prediction-powered inference under performativity. Their approach yields more precise parameter estimates and tighter confidence regions, and numerical experiments validate the framework's effectiveness. These findings connect a theoretical description of estimation uncertainty with a method for improving statistical precision. The work establishes an end-to-end framework for inference in a setting where decisions influence the data-generating outcomes that subsequent analysis seeks to understand.
summary.tldr: A new inference framework supports uncertainty estimates when prediction-informed decisions change the outcomes being predicted.

title: Statistical Inference under Performativity

abstract: Molecular docking is a fundamental technique in structure-based drug discovery, playing a critical role in predicting the binding poses of protein-ligand complexes. While traditional docking methods are generally reliable, they are often computationally expensive. Recent deep learning (DL) approaches have substantially accelerated docking and improved prediction accuracy; however, they frequently generate conformations that lack physical plausibility due to insufficient integration of physical priors. To deal with these challenges, we propose ForceFM, a novel force-guided model that integrates a force-guided network into the generation process, steering ligand poses toward low-energy, physically realistic conformations. Force guidance also halves inference cost compared with the unguided approaches. Importantly, replacing the guiding potential with diverse energy functions-including Vina, Glide, Gnina, and Confscore-preserves or improves performance, underscoring the method's generality and robustness. These results highlight ForceFM's ability to set new standards in docking accuracy and physical consistency, surpassing the limitations of previous methods. Code is available at \url{https://github.com/Guhuary/ForceFM}.

paragraphs: Molecular docking predicts how a ligand sits within a protein, an important task in structure-based drug discovery. Deep learning can accelerate this prediction, but generated poses may still be physically implausible. ForceFM addresses the gap between producing an accurate-looking arrangement and producing a conformation consistent with physical information about the molecular system.

The model incorporates a force-guided network into the generation process. This guidance steers proposed ligand poses toward lower-energy, physically realistic conformations as they are generated. The key design choice is to make physical priors participate directly in constructing the prediction. The paper also examines whether this guidance remains effective when its underlying energy function changes.

The authors report improved docking accuracy and physical consistency, with force guidance halving inference cost relative to unguided approaches. Replacing the guiding potential with Vina, Glide, Gnina, or Confscore preserves or improves performance in their tests. These results support the method's flexibility across the evaluated energy functions and show that incorporating physical guidance can improve efficiency as well as plausibility.
summary.tldr: ForceFM guides ligand-pose generation with physical forces, improving reported docking quality while halving inference cost versus unguided approaches.

title: ForceFM: Enhancing Protein-Ligand Predictions through Force-Guided Flow Matching

abstract: Text-to-SQL systems translate natural language (NL) questions into SQL queries, enabling non-technical users to interact with structured data. While large language models (LLMs) have shown promising results on the text-to-SQL task, they often produce semantically incorrect yet syntactically valid queries, with limited insight into their reliability. We propose SQLens, an end-to-end framework for fine-grained detection and correction of semantic errors in LLM-generated SQL. SQLens integrates error signals from both the underlying database and the LLM to identify potential semantic errors within SQL clauses. It further leverages these signals to guide query correction. Empirical results on two public benchmarks show that SQLens outperforms the best LLM-based self-evaluation method by 25.78% in F1 for error detection, and improves execution accuracy of out-of-the-box text-to-SQL systems by up to 20%.

paragraphs: Text-to-SQL systems let people ask database questions in ordinary language. A generated query can be valid SQL while still expressing the wrong meaning, making successful execution an incomplete indication of reliability. SQLens addresses this gap by detecting semantic errors in generated queries and using the resulting evidence to guide corrections.

The framework combines error signals from the underlying database with signals from the language model. It uses them to identify possible problems within individual SQL clauses, giving the diagnosis finer granularity than a single judgment about the whole query. Those same signals then inform the correction process, connecting error localization with repair.

On two public benchmarks, SQLens improves error-detection F1 by 25.78% relative to the best language-model self-evaluation method and raises execution accuracy of out-of-the-box text-to-SQL systems by up to 20%. The findings support checking generated queries with both database and model evidence. They also show that detecting meaning-level errors can lead to improvements in the queries ultimately executed.
summary.tldr: SQLens combines database and language-model signals to detect clause-level semantic errors and improve generated SQL queries.

title: SQLens: An End-to-End Framework for Error Detection and Correction in Text-to-SQL

abstract: Understanding the internal mechanisms of transformer-based language models remains challenging. Mechanistic interpretability based on circuit discovery aims to reverse engineer neural networks by analyzing their internal processes at the level of computational subgraphs. In this paper, we revisit existing gradient-based circuit identification methods and find that their performance is either affected by the zero-gradient problem or saturation effects, where edge attribution scores become insensitive to input changes, resulting in noisy and unreliable attribution evaluations for circuit components. To address the saturation effect, we propose Edge Attribution Patching with GradPath (EAP-GP), EAP-GP introduces an integration path, starting from the input and adaptively following the direction of the difference between the gradients of corrupted and clean inputs to avoid the saturated region. This approach enhances attribution reliability and improves the faithfulness of circuit identification. We evaluate EAP-GP on 6 datasets using GPT-2 Small, GPT-2 Medium, and GPT-2 XL. Experimental results demonstrate that EAP-GP outperforms existing methods in circuit faithfulness, achieving improvements up to 17.7\%. Comparisons with manually annotated ground-truth circuits demonstrate that EAP-GP achieves precision and recall comparable to or better than previous approaches, highlighting its effectiveness in identifying accurate circuits.

paragraphs: Circuit discovery tries to explain language models by identifying computational subgraphs that account for their behavior. This paper examines a weakness in gradient-based methods used to score connections within those subgraphs. Zero gradients or saturation can make scores insensitive to changes in the input, producing unreliable judgments about which components matter.

EAP-GP addresses saturation by changing the integration path used for attribution. Starting from the input, the path adapts according to the difference between gradients associated with clean and corrupted inputs. This is designed to avoid saturated regions, producing more reliable edge scores and circuits that more faithfully represent the model’s computation.

The authors evaluate the method on six datasets using GPT-2 Small, Medium, and XL. They report improvements in circuit faithfulness of up to 17.7% over existing methods. Against manually annotated reference circuits, precision and recall are comparable to or better than earlier approaches. These results support adaptive path selection as a way to improve circuit attribution, with the largest reported gain representing an observed maximum.
summary.tldr: EAP-GP uses an adaptive attribution path to reduce saturation and improve the faithfulness of automatically discovered language-model circuits.

title: EAP-GP: Mitigating Saturation Effect in Gradient-based Automated Circuit Identification

abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have shown promising capabilities in reasoning tasks, yet still struggle significantly with complex problems requiring explicit self-reflection and self-correction, especially compared to their unimodal text-based counterparts. Existing reflection methods are simplistic and struggle to generate meaningful, instructive feedback, as the reasoning ability and knowledge limits of pre-trained models are largely fixed during initial training. To overcome these challenges, we propose \textit{multimodal \textbf{S}elf-\textbf{R}eflection enhanced reasoning with Group Relative \textbf{P}olicy \textbf{O}ptimization} \textbf{SRPO}, a two-stage reflection-aware reinforcement learning (RL) framework explicitly designed to enhance multimodal LLM reasoning. In the first stage, we construct a high-quality, reflection-focused dataset under the guidance of an advanced MLLM, which generates reflections based on initial responses to help the policy model to learn both reasoning and self-reflection. In the second stage, we introduce a novel reward mechanism within the GRPO framework that encourages concise and cognitively meaningful reflection while avoiding redundancy. Extensive experiments across multiple multimodal reasoning benchmarks—including MathVista, MathVision, Mathverse, and MMMU-Pro—using Qwen-2.5-VL-7B and Qwen-2.5-VL-32B demonstrate that SRPO significantly outperforms state-of-the-art models, achieving notable improvements in both reasoning accuracy and reflection quality.

paragraphs: SRPO aims to make multimodal language models better at examining and correcting their own reasoning. The paper argues that existing reflection methods often produce feedback that is too simplistic to help with complex problems. Its approach explicitly trains reflection alongside reasoning, then rewards useful reflection during reinforcement learning.

The first stage builds a reflection-focused dataset with guidance from a more advanced multimodal model. That model generates reflections based on initial responses, giving the policy model examples of both reasoning and reviewing its reasoning. The second stage introduces a reward within Group Relative Policy Optimization that encourages concise, meaningful reflection while discouraging redundancy.

Experiments use Qwen-2.5-VL models with 7 billion and 32 billion parameters across MathVista, MathVision, Mathverse, and MMMU-Pro. The authors report significant improvements over state-of-the-art models in reasoning accuracy and reflection quality. The results support treating reflection as a learned and rewarded capability, with the quality of feedback central to the framework rather than simply generating more reflective text.
summary.tldr: SRPO combines reflection-focused training data with reinforcement-learning rewards for concise, useful self-reflection to improve multimodal reasoning.

title: SRPO: Enhancing Multimodal LLM Reasoning via Reflection-Aware Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We study cost-aware routing for large language models across diverse and dynamic pools of models. Existing approaches often overlook prompt-specific context, rely on expensive model profiling, assume a fixed set of experts, or use inefficient trial-and-error strategies. We introduce Cost-Spectrum Contrastive Routing (CSCR), a lightweight framework that maps both prompts and models into a shared embedding space to enable fast, cost-sensitive selection. CSCR uses compact, fast-to-compute logit footprints for open-source models and perplexity fingerprints for black-box APIs. A contrastive encoder is trained to favor the cheapest accurate expert within adaptive cost bands. At inference time, routing reduces to a single $k$‑NN lookup via a FAISS index, requiring no retraining when the expert pool changes and enabling microsecond latency. Across multiple benchmarks, CSCR consistently outperforms baselines, improving the accuracy–cost tradeoff by up to 25\%, while generalizing robustly to unseen LLMs and out-of-distribution prompts.

CSCR uses compact, fast-to-compute logit footprints for open-source models and perplexity fingerprints for black-box APIs.
