paragraphs: When several language models are available, selecting one for a prompt involves balancing response accuracy against cost. Existing routing approaches can require expensive profiling, overlook the particular prompt, or depend on an unchanging model pool. Cost-Spectrum Contrastive Routing addresses these problems by representing prompts and models in a shared embedding space.

The framework characterizes open-source models with compact logit footprints and black-box APIs with perplexity fingerprints. A contrastive encoder learns to favor the cheapest accurate model within adaptive cost bands. At inference time, selecting a model becomes a single nearest-neighbor lookup in a FAISS index, turning the learned relationship between prompts, capabilities, and costs into a fast routing operation.

The authors report microsecond routing latency and support for changes to the expert pool without retraining. Across multiple benchmarks, the method consistently outperforms baselines, with accuracy–cost tradeoff improvements of up to 25 percent. It also generalizes to unseen models and out-of-distribution prompts in the evaluations, supporting its use with diverse, changing collections of language models.
summary.tldr: CSCR uses shared prompt–model embeddings to select accurate, inexpensive language models through a fast nearest-neighbor lookup.

title: Cost-Aware Contrastive Routing for LLMs

abstract: The relative similarity testing aims to determine which of the distributions, $P$ or $Q$, is closer to an anchor distribution $U$. Existing kernel-based approaches often test the relative similarity with a fixed kernel in a manually specified alternative hypothesis, e.g., $Q$ is closer to $U$ than $P$. Although kernel selection is known to be important to kernel-based testing methods, the manually specified hypothesis poses a significant challenge for kernel selection in relative similarity testing: Once the hypothesis is specified first, we can always find a kernel such that the hypothesis is rejected. This challenge makes relative similarity testing ill-defined when we want to select a good kernel after the hypothesis is specified. In this paper, we cope with this challenge via learning a proper hypothesis and a kernel simultaneously, instead of learning a kernel after manually specifying the hypothesis. We propose an anchor-based maximum discrepancy (AMD), which defines the relative similarity as the maximum discrepancy between the distances of $(U, P)$ and $(U, Q)$ in a space of deep kernels. Based on AMD, our testing incorporates two phases. In Phase I, we estimate the AMD over the deep kernel space and infer the potential hypothesis. In Phase II, we assess the statistical significance of the potential hypothesis, where we propose a unified testing framework to derive thresholds for tests over different possible hypotheses from Phase I. Lastly, we validate our method theoretically and demonstrate its effectiveness via extensive experiments on benchmark datasets. Codes are publicly available at: https://github.com/zhijianzhouml/AMD.

paragraphs: Relative similarity testing asks which of two distributions is closer to a reference distribution. Kernel-based methods make this comparison through a chosen mathematical representation. The paper identifies a problem with first declaring which distribution should be closer and then selecting a kernel: kernel selection can produce a rejection of that preselected hypothesis, making the procedure ill-defined.

The proposed anchor-based maximum discrepancy, or AMD, learns the comparison hypothesis together with the kernel. It searches a space of deep kernels for the largest discrepancy between the two distances to the reference. This makes the choice of representation and the direction of the comparison parts of the same learning problem.

Testing then proceeds in two phases. The first estimates AMD and identifies a candidate hypothesis; the second evaluates its statistical significance. A unified framework supplies thresholds for the different hypotheses the first phase might produce. The authors provide theoretical validation and benchmark experiments supporting effectiveness, addressing how to make adaptive similarity comparisons statistically meaningful.
summary.tldr: AMD jointly learns a similarity hypothesis and a deep kernel, then tests the hypothesis’s statistical significance.

title: Anchor-based Maximum Discrepancy for Relative Similarity Testing

abstract: Molecular synthetic space projecting is a critical technique in de novo molecular design, which aims to rectify molecules without synthesizability guarantee by converting them into synthetic postfix notations. However, the vast synthesizable chemical space and the discrete data modalities involved pose significant challenges to postfix notation conversion benchmarking. In this paper, we exploit conditional probability transitions in discrete state space and introduce MoleBridge, a deep generative model built on the Markov bridge approach for designing postfix notations of molecular synthesis pathways. MoleBridge consists of two iterative optimizations: i) Autoregressive extending of notation tokens from molecular graphs, and ii) generation of discrete reaction postfix notations through Markov bridge, where noisy token blocks are progressively denoised over multi-step iterations. For the challenging second iteration, which demands sensitivity to incorrect generative probability paths within intricate chemical spaces, we employ a thinking and denoising separation approach to denoise. Empirically, we find that MoleBridge is capable of accurately predicting synthesis pathways while exhibiting excellent performance in a variety of application scenarios.

MoleBridge tackles this conversion as a discrete generative problem, where the size of chemical space and the sequence of reaction-related tokens make generation challenging.

The other uses a Markov bridge to generate reaction postfix notations by progressively denoising blocks of tokens over multiple steps. This uses conditional transitions between discrete states to move noisy candidate sequences toward a predicted synthesis pathway.

For the denoising stage, the authors separate thinking from denoising to address sensitivity to incorrect generation paths in complex chemical space. They report accurate pathway prediction and strong performance across several application scenarios. The contribution is a structured generation procedure that connects molecular graphs to synthesis descriptions, making pathway prediction part of the process of converting proposed molecules into synthesizable candidates.
summary.tldr: MoleBridge combines autoregressive generation and discrete Markov-bridge denoising to predict synthesis-pathway notations from molecular graphs.

title: MoleBridge: Synthetic Space Projecting with Discrete Markov Bridges

abstract: This position paper argues that the use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) to control, direct, guide or govern any weapon, either in situ or remotely, should be prohibited by government agencies and non-governmental organizations. Such a moratorium should exist until hallucinations can be successfully modeled and predicted. Generative AI is inherently unreliable and not appropriate in environments that could result in the loss of life.

Generative AI is inherently unreliable and not appropriate in environments that could result in the loss of life.

paragraphs: This position paper calls for a prohibition on using generative AI to control, direct, guide, or govern weapons. Its scope includes systems operating locally and remotely. The proposal addresses government agencies and nongovernmental organizations, framing weapon-related use of generative AI as a matter requiring an explicit institutional restriction.

The authors base their position on the unreliability of generative AI and the possibility that its use in these environments could lead to loss of life. Hallucinations are the specific reliability issue identified. The argument connects that issue to the proposed restriction: systems whose hallucinations cannot be successfully modeled and predicted should not have these roles in weapon operation.

The proposed moratorium has a stated endpoint: it should remain until hallucinations can be successfully modeled and predicted. That condition defines the duration the authors advocate; it does not itself establish that satisfying it would make weapon use safe. The paper’s contribution is a policy position about acceptable reliability in potentially lethal settings, rather than an experimental evaluation of a weapon-control system.
summary.tldr: This position paper advocates prohibiting generative AI in weapon control until hallucinations can be successfully modeled and predicted.

title: Prohibiting Generative AI in any Form of Weapon Control

abstract: Generating an interactive visual world from a single image is both challenging and practically valuable, as single-view inputs are easy to acquire and align well with prompt-driven applications such as gaming and virtual reality. This paper introduces a novel unified framework, Image as a World (**IaaW**), which synthesizes high-quality 360-degree videos from a single image that are both controllable and temporally continuable. Our framework consists of three stages: world initialization, which jointly synthesizes spatially complete and temporally dynamic scenes from a single view; world exploration, which supports user-specified viewpoint rotation; and world continuation, which extends the generated scene forward in time with temporal consistency. To support this pipeline, we design a visual world model based on generative diffusion models modulated with spherical 3D positional encoding and multi-view composition to represent geometry and view semantics. Additionally, a vision-language model (IaaW-VLM) is fine-tuned to produce both global and view-specific prompts, improving semantic alignment and controllability. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method produces panoramic videos with superior visual quality, minimal distortion and seamless continuation in both qualitative and quantitative evaluations. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to generate a controllable, consistent, and temporally expandable 360-degree world from a single image.

paragraphs: Image as a World turns a single image into a generated panoramic video environment that users can explore through viewpoint rotation and extend over time. The framework separates this process into initialization, exploration, and continuation. Initialization fills out a spatially complete, dynamic scene; exploration changes the viewing direction; continuation advances the generated scene while maintaining temporal consistency.

These components represent geometry and the meaning of different views within the panoramic scene. Its contribution is the integration of these capabilities into a single pipeline starting from an easily acquired input.
summary.tldr: Image as a World generates controllable 360-degree videos from one image, supporting viewpoint rotation and temporally consistent continuation.

title: Image as a World: Generating Interactive World from Single Image via Panoramic Video Generation

abstract: Direct policy search can effectively scale to high-dimensional systems, but complex policies with hundreds of parameters often present a challenge for such methods, requiring numerous samples and often falling into poor local optima. We present a guided policy search algorithm that uses trajectory optimization to direct policy learning and avoid poor local optima. We show how differential dynamic programming can be used to generate suitable guiding samples, and describe a regularized importance sampled policy optimization that incorporates these samples into the policy search. We evaluate the method by learning neural network controllers for planar swimming, hopping, and walking, as well as simulated 3D humanoid running.

We show how differential dynamic programming can be used to generate suitable guiding samples, and describe a regularized importance sampled policy optimization that incorporates these samples into the policy search. We evaluate the method by learning neural network controllers for planar swimming, hopping, and walking, as well as simulated 3D humanoid running.

paragraphs: Direct policy search adjusts a controller to improve its behavior, but searching over policies with hundreds of parameters can require many samples and lead to poor local solutions. This paper introduces guided policy search, which uses trajectory optimization to provide direction for learning a policy in a high-dimensional control problem.

The approach uses differential dynamic programming to generate guiding samples. These samples represent trajectories that can inform the controller's search. A regularized, importance-sampled policy optimization procedure then incorporates them into policy learning. The key connection is between optimizing trajectories and using the resulting experience to shape a more general controller.

The method is evaluated by learning neural network controllers for planar swimming, hopping, and walking, together with simulated three-dimensional humanoid running. These tasks place the proposed guidance mechanism in varied movement settings. The contribution is a concrete way to steer complex policy learning toward useful behavior and away from poor local optima, addressing difficulties that arise when policy search must discover effective behavior through sampling.
summary.tldr: Guided policy search uses optimized trajectories to steer the learning of complex neural network controllers.

title: Guided Policy Search

abstract: In this paper we propose two constructions of dependent normalized random measures, a class of nonparametric priors over dependent probability measures. Our constructions, which we call mixed normalized random measures (MNRM) and thinned normalized random measures (TNRM), involve (respectively) weighting and thinning parts of a shared underlying Poisson process before combining them together. We show that both MNRM and TNRM are marginally normalized random measures, resulting in well understood theoretical properties. We develop marginal and slice samplers for both models, the latter necessary for inference in TNRM. In time-varying topic modelling experiments, both models exhibit superior performance over related dependent models such as the hierarchical Dirichlet process and the spatial normalized Gamma process.

We show that both MNRM and TNRM are marginally normalized random measures, resulting in well understood theoretical properties. We develop marginal and slice samplers for both models, the latter necessary for inference in TNRM. paragraphs: The paper develops priors for collections of probability distributions that are related to one another. Its two constructions belong to Bayesian nonparametrics and are called mixed normalized random measures and thinned normalized random measures. Both create dependence through a shared underlying Poisson process, giving the resulting distributions a common probabilistic foundation.

The constructions differ in how they use that shared process. One weights its parts before combining them; the other thins those parts before combination. The authors show that each resulting distribution, considered individually, remains a normalized random measure. This marginal property makes established theoretical understanding available even though the distributions are jointly dependent.

The paper also develops marginal and slice sampling methods, with slice sampling needed for inference in the thinned construction. In experiments on topics that change over time, both models outperform related dependent models, including the hierarchical Dirichlet process and spatial normalized Gamma process. The findings support these constructions as useful ways to model related, evolving distributions.
summary.tldr: Two shared-process constructions model dependent probability distributions while preserving normalized-random-measure marginals and performing well in time-varying topic experiments.

title: Dependent Normalized Random Measures

abstract: While MAP inference is typically intractable for many real-world applications, linear programming relaxations have been proven very effective. Dual block-coordinate descent methods are among the most efficient solvers, however, they are prone to get stuck in sub-optimal points. Although subgradient approaches achieve global convergence, they are typically slower in practice. To improve convergence speed, algorithms which compute the steepest ε-descent direction by solving a quadratic program have been proposed. In this paper we suggest to decouple the quadratic program based on the Frank-Wolfe approach. This allows us to obtain an efficient and easy to parallelize algorithm while retaining the global convergence properties. Our method proves superior when compared to existing algorithms on a set of spin-glass models and protein design tasks.

paragraphs: The paper develops a solver for linear programming relaxations of maximum a posteriori, or MAP, inference. These relaxations are useful because the original inference problem is often intractable. Existing solver choices involve a tradeoff: efficient dual block-coordinate descent methods can stop at suboptimal points, while globally convergent subgradient approaches are often slower in practice.

Another approach computes a steepest epsilon-descent direction by solving a quadratic program. The authors build on this idea but use the Frank-Wolfe approach to decouple that quadratic program. This restructuring produces an efficient algorithm that is straightforward to parallelize while preserving global convergence.

The distinction between the relaxed and original problems matters: the convergence claim concerns solving the MAP linear programming relaxation. Experiments on spin-glass models and protein design tasks show superior performance over the compared algorithms. The contribution therefore joins a convergence property with a computational organization suitable for parallel execution, addressing the practical tension between reliable optimization and speed in this class of inference solvers.
summary.tldr: A Frank-Wolfe-based decomposition yields an easily parallelized MAP linear-programming relaxation solver with global convergence.

title: Globally Convergent Parallel MAP LP Relaxation Solver using the Frank-Wolfe Algorithm

abstract: We study the statistical properties of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) using explicit and implicit updates for fitting generalized linear models (GLMs). Initially, we develop a computationally efficient algorithm to implement implicit SGD learning of GLMs. Next, we obtain exact formulas for the bias and variance of both updates which leads to two important observations on their comparative statistical properties. First, in small samples, the estimates from the implicit procedure are more biased than the estimates from the explicit one, but their empirical variance is smaller and they are more robust to learning rate misspecification. Second, the two procedures are statistically identical in the limit: they are both unbiased, converge at the same rate and have the same asymptotic variance. Our set of experiments confirm our theory and more broadly suggest that the implicit procedure can be a competitive choice for fitting large-scale models, especially when robustness is a concern.

paragraphs: This paper compares explicit and implicit stochastic gradient updates for fitting generalized linear models. Its aim is to understand their statistical behavior, including bias, variability, and sensitivity to the learning rate. The authors first develop an efficient algorithm for carrying out the implicit updates in this model family.

They then derive exact formulas for the bias and variance of both procedures. In small samples, the implicit estimates have more bias, but their empirical variance is lower and they are more robust when the learning rate is misspecified. This identifies a trade-off: the implicit method's greater small-sample bias accompanies benefits in variability and robustness.

In the limit, the distinction disappears statistically. Both procedures are unbiased, converge at the same rate, and have the same asymptotic variance. Experiments confirm the theory and suggest that implicit SGD can be competitive for large-scale fitting, especially when robustness matters. The result makes finite-sample behavior a central consideration even when two procedures share the same limiting performance.
summary.tldr: Implicit SGD trades greater small-sample bias for lower empirical variance and learning-rate robustness while matching explicit SGD's asymptotic statistical behavior.

title: Statistical analysis of stochastic gradient methods for generalized linear models

abstract: Given a graph, the Densest k-Subgraph (\DkS) problem asks for the subgraph on k vertices that contains the largest number of edges. In this work, we develop a novel algorithm for \DkS that searches a low-dimensional space for provably good solutions. We obtain provable performance bounds that depend on the graph spectrum. One of our results is that if there exists a k-subgraph that contains a constant fraction of all the edges, we can approximate \DkS within a factor arbitrarily close to two in polynomial time. Our algorithm runs in nearly linear time, under spectral assumptions satisfied by most graphs found in applications. Moreover, it is highly scalable and parallelizable. We demonstrate this by implementing it in MapReduce and executing numerous experiments on massive real-world graphs that have up to billions of edges. We empirically show that our algorithm can find subgraphs of significantly higher density compared to the previous state of the art.

paragraphs: The densest k-subgraph problem asks which set of k vertices contains the most edges. This paper develops an algorithm that searches a low-dimensional space for good solutions. Its theoretical performance bounds depend on the graph spectrum, connecting the quality of the approximation to mathematical properties of the input graph.

One guarantee applies when some k-vertex subgraph contains a constant fraction of all edges in the graph. Under that condition, the algorithm achieves an approximation factor arbitrarily close to two in polynomial time. The authors also establish nearly linear running time under spectral assumptions they describe as holding for most application graphs. Both results retain their stated conditions.

The method is designed to support large-scale parallel computation. A MapReduce implementation is evaluated on real-world graphs containing up to billions of edges, demonstrating its ability to operate at that scale. In those experiments, it finds significantly denser subgraphs than the previous state of the art. The paper thus combines conditional approximation guarantees with empirical evidence of scalability and solution quality on massive graphs.
summary.tldr: A low-dimensional search finds dense subgraphs with spectrum-dependent guarantees and strong empirical results on graphs with billions of edges.

title: Finding Dense Subgraphs via Low-Rank Bilinear Optimization

abstract: Recent studies reveal that a deep neural network can learn transferable features which generalize well to novel tasks for domain adaptation. However, as deep features eventually transition from general to specific along the network, the feature transferability drops significantly in higher layers with increasing domain discrepancy. Hence, it is important to formally reduce the dataset bias and enhance the transferability in task-specific layers. In this paper, we propose a new Deep Adaptation Network (DAN) architecture, which generalizes deep convolutional neural network to the domain adaptation scenario. In DAN, hidden representations of all task-specific layers are embedded in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space where the mean embeddings of different domain distributions can be explicitly matched. The domain discrepancy is further reduced using an optimal multi-kernel selection method for mean embedding matching. DAN can learn transferable features with statistical guarantees, and can scale linearly by unbiased estimate of kernel embedding. Extensive empirical evidence shows that the proposed architecture yields state-of-the-art image classification error rates on standard domain adaptation benchmarks.

paragraphs: The paper addresses transferring a deep network between domains whose data distributions differ. Its motivation is that higher network layers become increasingly specific to the original task, making their features less transferable as domain discrepancy grows. Improving adaptation therefore requires addressing dataset differences within those task-specific layers.

The proposed Deep Adaptation Network embeds the hidden representations of all task-specific layers in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. In that space, it explicitly matches the mean embeddings of the different domain distributions. An optimal multi-kernel selection method further reduces discrepancy, making the choice of comparison functions part of the adaptation mechanism.

The authors provide statistical guarantees for learning transferable features and describe linear scaling through an unbiased estimate of the kernel embedding. Extensive experiments yield state-of-the-art image-classification error rates on standard domain-adaptation benchmarks. These findings support combining deep feature learning with explicit distribution matching, particularly in the layers where the original representation has become most specialized to its source task.
summary.tldr: Deep Adaptation Networks improve feature transfer by matching domain distributions across task-specific layers using multiple kernels.

title: Learning Transferable Features with Deep Adaptation Networks

abstract: We study the K-armed dueling bandit problem which is a variation of the classical Multi-Armed Bandit (MAB) problem in which the learner receives only relative feedback about the selected pairs of arms. We propose a new algorithm called Relative Exponential-weight algorithm for Exploration and Exploitation (REX3) to handle the adversarial utility-based formulation of this problem. This algorithm is a non-trivial extension of the Exponential-weight algorithm for Exploration and Exploitation (EXP3) algorithm. We prove a finite time expected regret upper bound of order O(sqrt(K ln(K)T)) for this algorithm and a general lower bound of order omega(sqrt(KT)). At the end, we provide experimental results using real data from information retrieval applications.
originalAbstract: We study the K-armed dueling bandit problem which is a variation of the classical Multi-Armed Bandit (MAB) problem in which the learner receives only relative feedback about the selected pairs of arms. We propose a new algorithm called Relative Exponential-weight algorithm for Exploration and Exploitation (REX3) to handle the adversarial utility-based formulation of this problem. This algorithm is a non-trivial extension of the Exponential-weight algorithm for Exploration and Exploitation (EXP3) algorithm. We prove a finite time expected regret upper bound of order O(sqrt(K ln(K)T)) for this algorithm and a general lower bound of order omega(sqrt(KT)). At the end, we provide experimental results using real data from information retrieval applications.

paragraphs: In a dueling bandit problem, a learner chooses pairs of options and receives feedback about their relative quality. This differs from observing a separate reward for an individual choice. The paper studies a formulation with K available options and adversarial utilities, asking how effectively a learner can make decisions from these comparisons over T rounds.

The proposed algorithm, REX3, extends the exponential-weight approach used by EXP3. Its task is to balance exploration of options with exploitation of what previous comparisons suggest. Adapting this strategy to relative feedback is the central algorithmic contribution, since the learner must update its choices using comparisons rather than directly observed individual utilities.

The authors prove a finite-time expected regret upper bound of order O(sqrt(K ln(K)T)) and provide a general lower bound expressed in terms of sqrt(KT). These results quantify achievable performance and a fundamental difficulty of the problem. The paper also reports experiments using real information-retrieval data, connecting the theoretical comparison-learning setting to an application where relative preferences are relevant.
summary.tldr: REX3 adapts exponential weighting to adversarial dueling bandits and provides a finite-time expected regret guarantee using relative feedback.

title: A Relative Exponential Weighing Algorithm for Adversarial Utility-based Dueling Bandits

abstract: A fundamental task in machine learning is to compare the performance of multiple algorithms. This is typically performed by frequentist tests (usually the Friedman test followed by a series of multiple pairwise comparisons). This implies dealing with null hypothesis significance tests and p-values, although the shortcomings of such methods are well known. First, we propose a nonparametric Bayesian version of the Friedman test using a Dirichlet process (DP) based prior. Our derivations show that, from a Bayesian perspective, the Friedman test is an inference for a multivariate mean based on an ellipsoid inclusion test. Second, we derive a joint procedure for the analysis of the multiple comparisons which accounts for their dependencies and which is based on the posterior probability computed through the DP. The proposed approach allows verifying the null hypothesis, not only rejecting it. Third, we apply our test to perform algorithms racing, i.e., the problem of identifying the best algorithm among a large set of candidates. We show by simulation that our approach is competitive both in terms of accuracy and speed in identifying the best algorithm.

paragraphs: Comparing several learning algorithms often involves an overall statistical test followed by comparisons between individual pairs. This paper develops a Bayesian alternative to that workflow. It uses a Dirichlet process prior to construct a nonparametric counterpart of the Friedman test, framing algorithm comparison through posterior probabilities rather than only significance tests and p-values.

The analysis also gives a geometric interpretation of the conventional Friedman test: from the proposed Bayesian perspective, it concerns a multivariate mean and whether an ellipsoid is included in a relevant region. For multiple comparisons, the authors develop a joint procedure that accounts for dependencies between comparisons instead of treating each comparison as an isolated inference.

A stated benefit is the ability to assess support for the null hypothesis, beyond merely rejecting it. The authors also apply the procedure to algorithm racing, where the task is to identify the best candidate from a large collection. Simulations show competitive accuracy and speed for that selection task, supporting the approach as a practical comparison procedure.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian approach jointly compares algorithms, accounts for dependent comparisons, and shows competitive performance in selecting the best candidate.

title: A Bayesian nonparametric procedure for comparing algorithms

abstract: Most tasks in natural language processing can be cast into question answering (QA) problems over language input. We introduce the dynamic memory network (DMN), a neural network architecture which processes input sequences and questions, forms episodic memories, and generates relevant answers. Questions trigger an iterative attention process which allows the model to condition its attention on the inputs and the result of previous iterations. These results are then reasoned over in a hierarchical recurrent sequence model to generate answers. The DMN can be trained end-to-end and obtains state-of-the-art results on several types of tasks and datasets: question answering (Facebook’s bAbI dataset), text classification for sentiment analysis (Stanford Sentiment Treebank) and sequence modeling for part-of-speech tagging (WSJ-PTB). The training for these different tasks relies exclusively on trained word vector representations and input-question-answer triplets.

paragraphs: This paper introduces the dynamic memory network, an architecture that treats language tasks as answering questions about an input. It processes both the input sequence and a question, builds episodic memories, and produces an answer. The motivation is that many language problems can share this input-question-answer structure despite asking for different kinds of outputs.

Its central mechanism is repeated, question-directed attention. Each pass can depend on the input and on what earlier passes have already produced. This lets the network revisit information with an updated internal context. A hierarchical recurrent sequence model reasons over the resulting memories to generate the answer, and the full architecture can be trained together.

The paper reports state-of-the-art results on the stated evaluations: bAbI question answering, Stanford Sentiment Treebank sentiment classification, and WSJ-PTB part-of-speech tagging. Training across these tasks uses learned word vectors and input-question-answer triplets. These findings support the usefulness of a shared memory-and-attention architecture across several language tasks, without establishing that every language problem fits equally well.
summary.tldr: Dynamic memory networks use repeated question-directed attention to support several language tasks within one trainable architecture.

title: Ask Me Anything: Dynamic Memory Networks for Natural Language Processing

abstract: Hyperparameter selection generally relies on running multiple full training trials, with selection based on validation set performance. We propose a gradient-based approach for locally adjusting hyperparameters during training of the model. Hyperparameters are adjusted so as to make the model parameter gradients, and hence updates, more advantageous for the validation cost. We explore the approach for tuning regularization hyperparameters and find that in experiments on MNIST, SVHN and CIFAR-10, the resulting regularization levels are within the optimal regions. The additional computational cost depends on how frequently the hyperparameters are trained, but the tested scheme adds only 30% computational overhead regardless of the model size. Since the method is significantly less computationally demanding compared to similar gradient-based approaches to hyperparameter optimization, and consistently finds good hyperparameter values, it can be a useful tool for training neural network models.

We propose a gradient-based approach for locally adjusting hyperparameters during training of the model. Hyperparameters are adjusted so as to make the model parameter gradients, and hence updates, more advantageous for the validation cost. We explore the approach for tuning regularization hyperparameters and find that in experiments on MNIST, SVHN and CIFAR-10, the resulting regularization levels are within the optimal regions. The additional computational cost depends on how frequently the hyperparameters are trained, but the tested scheme adds only 30% computational overhead regardless of the model size. Since the method is significantly less computationally demanding compared to similar gradient-based approaches to hyperparameter optimization, and consistently finds good hyperparameter values, it can be a useful tool for training neural network models.

paragraphs: Hyperparameter selection often requires training a model repeatedly and comparing the resulting validation performance. This paper proposes adjusting continuous hyperparameters locally during training instead. It focuses on regularization settings, making their adjustment part of the ongoing learning process rather than relying entirely on separate completed training trials.

The method uses gradients to change hyperparameters so that the model's parameter gradients, and therefore its updates, become more favorable for validation cost. This ties hyperparameter changes to the direction in which training is currently moving the model. Its local character is central: it seeks useful adjustments during optimization rather than claiming a global hyperparameter optimum.

Experiments on MNIST, SVHN, and CIFAR-10 place the learned regularization levels within optimal regions. The tested scheme adds 30% computational overhead regardless of model size, although overall cost depends on how often hyperparameters are updated. The authors report substantially lower computation than similar gradient-based approaches, supporting the method as a practical way to obtain good regularization settings during neural-network training.
summary.tldr: Local gradient-based hyperparameter updates find good regularization settings during training with modest reported overhead.

title: Scalable Gradient-Based Tuning of Continuous Regularization Hyperparameters

abstract: Motivated by the need for distributed learning and optimization algorithms with low communication cost, we study communication efficient algorithms for distributed mean estimation. Unlike previous works, we make no probabilistic assumptions on the data. We first show that for $d$ dimensional data with $n$ clients, a naive stochastic rounding approach yields a mean squared error (MSE) of $\Theta(d/n)$ and uses a constant number of bits per dimension per client. We then extend this naive algorithm in two ways: we show that applying a structured random rotation before quantization reduces the error to $\mathcal{O}((\log d)/n)$ and a better coding strategy further reduces the error to $\mathcal{O}(1/n)$. We also show that the latter coding strategy is optimal up to a constant in the minimax sense i.e., it achieves the best MSE for a given communication cost. We finally demonstrate the practicality of our algorithms by applying them to distributed Lloyd’s algorithm for k-means and power iteration for PCA.

paragraphs: Distributed mean estimation asks how clients can communicate enough information to estimate an average while sending few bits. This paper studies that tradeoff without probabilistic assumptions about the data. The motivation is to reduce communication costs in distributed learning and optimization while controlling the error introduced by compressed messages.

For n clients with d-dimensional data, a basic stochastic-rounding method uses a constant number of bits per dimension per client and has mean squared error Θ(d/n). Applying a structured random rotation before quantization improves the error to O((log d)/n). A better coding strategy reduces it further to O(1/n), removing the dimension dependence from that stated error rate.

The authors show that the latter strategy is minimax optimal up to a constant: for the given communication cost, its worst-case error matches the best achievable level within that factor. They also demonstrate the algorithms in distributed k-means through Lloyd's algorithm and in PCA through power iteration. These applications connect the mean-estimation guarantees to broader computational procedures that repeatedly aggregate distributed information.
summary.tldr: Random rotation and improved coding reduce distributed mean-estimation error under limited communication, achieving minimax optimality up to a constant.

title: Distributed Mean Estimation with Limited Communication

abstract: We consider influence maximization (IM) in social networks, which is the problem of maximizing the number of users that become aware of a product by selecting a set of “seed” users to expose the product to. While prior work assumes a known model of information diffusion, we propose a novel parametrization that not only makes our framework agnostic to the underlying diffusion model, but also statistically efficient to learn from data. We give a corresponding monotone, submodular surrogate function, and show that it is a good approximation to the original IM objective. We also consider the case of a new marketer looking to exploit an existing social network, while simultaneously learning the factors governing information propagation. For this, we propose a pairwise-influence semi-bandit feedback model and develop a LinUCB-based bandit algorithm. Our model-independent analysis shows that our regret bound has a better (as compared to previous work) dependence on the size of the network. Experimental evaluation suggests that our framework is robust to the underlying diffusion model and can efficiently learn a near-optimal solution.

paragraphs: Influence maximization chooses initial users in a social network to make as many people as possible aware of a product. The challenge becomes harder when the marketer does not know how information spreads. This paper develops a parametrization designed to be statistically efficient to learn without committing to a particular underlying diffusion model.

The authors construct a monotone, submodular surrogate and show that it approximates the original influence objective well. They also study a marketer who must learn about propagation while choosing seed users. For this setting, they introduce pairwise-influence semi-bandit feedback and a LinUCB-based algorithm that combines learning with ongoing decisions.

Their analysis gives a regret bound with improved dependence on network size compared with previous work. Experiments suggest robustness across underlying diffusion models and efficient learning of a near-optimal solution. The contribution joins a model-independent representation of influence with an online learning procedure, addressing both what to optimize and how to learn while acting.
summary.tldr: A model-independent influence framework learns seed-selection decisions online, with improved network-size dependence in its regret bound.

title: Model-Independent Online Learning for Influence Maximization

abstract: We propose a novel approach to parameter estimation for simulator-based statistical models with intractable likelihood. Our proposed method involves recursive application of kernel ABC and kernel herding to the same observed data. We provide a theoretical explanation regarding why the approach works, showing (for the population setting) that, under a certain assumption, point estimates obtained with this method converge to the true parameter, as recursion proceeds. We have conducted a variety of numerical experiments, including parameter estimation for a real-world pedestrian flow simulator, and show that in most cases our method outperforms existing approaches.

paragraphs: Simulator-based models can generate observations even when their likelihood is intractable, making direct likelihood-based parameter estimation difficult. This paper proposes a method for obtaining a point estimate of the simulator's parameters in that setting. The task is to use observed data to identify parameter values without requiring a tractable likelihood.

The procedure recursively applies kernel approximate Bayesian computation, or kernel ABC, together with kernel herding. Each round uses the same observed data. Recursion is therefore central to the method: the estimate is refined through repeated applications of these two components rather than through a requirement to collect new observations at every stage.

The theoretical explanation shows that, in the population setting and under a particular assumption, the resulting estimates converge to the true parameter as recursion continues. Numerical experiments include estimating parameters for a real-world pedestrian-flow simulator. The method outperforms existing approaches in most of the tested cases, providing empirical support alongside a convergence result whose population setting and assumption remain part of the claim.
summary.tldr: Repeated kernel ABC and kernel herding estimate simulator parameters, with conditional population-level convergence and favorable results in most tested cases.

title: Kernel Recursive ABC: Point Estimation with Intractable Likelihood

abstract: In this paper, we propose a listwise approach for constructing user-specific rankings in recommendation systems in a collaborative fashion. We contrast the listwise approach to previous pointwise and pairwise approaches, which are based on treating either each rating or each pairwise comparison as an independent instance respectively. By extending the work of ListNet (Cao et al., 2007), we cast listwise collaborative ranking as maximum likelihood under a permutation model which applies probability mass to permutations based on a low rank latent score matrix. We present a novel algorithm called SQL-Rank, which can accommodate ties and missing data and can run in linear time. We develop a theoretical framework for analyzing listwise ranking methods based on a novel representation theory for the permutation model. Applying this framework to collaborative ranking, we derive asymptotic statistical rates as the number of users and items grow together. We conclude by demonstrating that our SQL-Rank method often outperforms current state-of-the-art algorithms for implicit feedback such as Weighted-MF and BPR and achieve favorable results when compared to explicit feedback algorithms such as matrix factorization and collaborative ranking.

paragraphs: Recommendation systems need rankings tailored to individual users while drawing information from many users together. This paper models whole ranked lists, rather than treating each rating or each pairwise comparison as an independent example. The listwise formulation makes the ordering itself the central object of collaborative learning.

The authors assign probabilities to permutations using a low-rank matrix of latent user-item scores and learn through maximum likelihood. Their SQL-Rank algorithm accommodates tied preferences and missing observations and can run in linear time. These properties make the proposed ranking model applicable when the available preference information is incomplete or does not define a strict ordering.

The paper also develops a representation-based theoretical framework for permutation models and derives asymptotic statistical rates as user and item counts grow together. Empirically, SQL-Rank often outperforms Weighted-MF and BPR on implicit feedback and compares favorably with methods for explicit feedback. The wording matters: these are favorable comparative findings, not a claim of dominance on every recommendation problem.
summary.tldr: SQL-Rank learns collaborative user rankings through a listwise permutation model that supports ties, missing data, and linear-time computation.

title: SQL-Rank: A Listwise Approach to Collaborative Ranking

abstract: Analyzing multivariate time series data is important to predict future events and changes of complex systems in finance, manufacturing, and administrative decisions. The expressiveness power of Gaussian Process (GP) regression methods has been significantly improved by compositional covariance structures. In this paper, we present a new GP model which naturally handles multiple time series by placing an Indian Buffet Process (IBP) prior on the presence of shared kernels. Our selective covariance structure decomposition allows exploiting shared parameters over a set of multiple, selected time series. We also investigate the well-definedness of the models when infinite latent components are introduced. We present a pragmatic search algorithm which explores a larger structure space efficiently. Experiments conducted on five real-world data sets demonstrate that our new model outperforms existing methods in term of structure discoveries and predictive performances.

paragraphs: Multiple time series can contain shared patterns without every series following the same structure. This paper develops a Gaussian process model that learns covariance structure across selected groups of series. Its aim is to use shared information while preserving differences in which components apply to each series.

The model places an Indian Buffet Process prior on the presence of shared kernels. This supports a selective decomposition of covariance structure, with parameters shared across the series that use a particular component. The authors also investigate whether the models remain well defined when infinitely many latent components are introduced. A practical search algorithm explores a larger space of possible structures efficiently.

Experiments on five real datasets show improvements over existing methods in both discovering structure and making predictions. Those findings support the usefulness of selective sharing: relationships across series can inform a model without requiring a single covariance structure for the entire collection. The contribution combines a model for discovering shared components with a search procedure for finding useful compositions.
summary.tldr: A Gaussian process model selectively shares covariance components across time series, improving structure discovery and prediction on five real datasets.

title: Discovering Latent Covariance Structures for Multiple Time Series

abstract: Generative adversarial networks (GANs) represent a zero-sum game between two machine players, a generator and a discriminator, designed to learn the distribution of data. While GANs have achieved state-of-the-art performance in several benchmark learning tasks, GAN minimax optimization still poses great theoretical and empirical challenges. GANs trained using first-order optimization methods commonly fail to converge to a stable solution where the players cannot improve their objective, i.e., the Nash equilibrium of the underlying game. Such issues raise the question of the existence of Nash equilibria in GAN zero-sum games. In this work, we show through theoretical and numerical results that indeed GAN zero-sum games may have no Nash equilibria. To characterize an equilibrium notion applicable to GANs, we consider the equilibrium of a new zero-sum game with an objective function given by a proximal operator applied to the original objective, a solution we call the proximal equilibrium. Unlike the Nash equilibrium, the proximal equilibrium captures the sequential nature of GANs, in which the generator moves first followed by the discriminator. We prove that the optimal generative model in Wasserstein GAN problems provides a proximal equilibrium. Inspired by these results, we propose a new approach, which we call proximal training, for solving GAN problems. We perform several numerical experiments indicating the existence of proximal equilibria in GANs.

The paper asks whether such an equilibrium necessarily exists in the first place, rather than assuming that unsuccessful training only reflects an optimization problem.

title: Do GANs always have Nash equilibria?

abstract: Transformers have increasingly outperformed gated RNNs in obtaining new state-of-the-art results on supervised tasks involving text sequences. Inspired by this trend, we study the question of how Transformer-based models can improve the performance of sequential decision-making agents. We present the Working Memory Graph (WMG), an agent that employs multi-head self-attention to reason over a dynamic set of vectors representing observed and recurrent state. We evaluate WMG in three environments featuring factored observation spaces: a Pathfinding environment that requires complex reasoning over past observations, BabyAI gridworld levels that involve variable goals, and Sokoban which emphasizes future planning. We find that the combination of WMG’s Transformer-based architecture with factored observation spaces leads to significant gains in learning efficiency compared to baseline architectures across all tasks. WMG demonstrates how Transformer-based models can dramatically boost sample efficiency in RL environments for which observations can be factored.

paragraphs: Sequential decision-making requires an agent to connect current observations with information retained from earlier steps. Working Memory Graphs explore whether Transformer-style attention can improve that process. The proposed agent applies multi-head self-attention to a changing collection of vectors representing both observations and recurrent state.

The evaluation covers three environments with factored observations, where inputs are presented as separable components. Pathfinding emphasizes reasoning over past observations, BabyAI gridworld levels introduce variable goals, and Sokoban emphasizes future planning. This collection tests the architecture across different demands on memory and decision-making rather than a single kind of task.

Across all evaluated tasks, the combination of the attention-based architecture and factored observation spaces yields significant gains in learning efficiency over baseline architectures. The finding ties the benefit to both the model and the input structure. It demonstrates that Transformer-based agents can substantially improve sample efficiency in reinforcement-learning environments whose observations can be factored, rather than establishing the same gain for every observation format.
summary.tldr: Working Memory Graphs use attention over observations and recurrent state to improve learning efficiency in environments with factored inputs.

title: Working Memory Graphs

abstract: Detecting semantic anomalies is challenging due to the countless ways in which they may appear in real-world data. While enhancing the robustness of networks may be sufficient for modeling simplistic anomalies, there is no good known way of preparing models for all potential and unseen anomalies that can potentially occur, such as the appearance of new object classes. In this paper, we show that a previously overlooked strategy for anomaly detection (AD) is to introduce an explicit inductive bias toward representations transferred over from some large and varied semantic task. We rigorously verify our hypothesis in controlled trials that utilize intervention, and show that it gives rise to surprisingly effective auxiliary objectives that outperform previous AD paradigms.

paragraphs: Semantic anomalies can differ from familiar data in meaning, such as when a new object class appears. Their variety makes it difficult to prepare a detector for everything it might encounter. This paper investigates whether knowledge transferred from a large and varied semantic task can provide a useful bias for detecting such anomalies.

The proposed strategy explicitly favors representations inherited from that broader task. The underlying idea is to guide anomaly detection using features shaped by varied semantic information. The authors test this hypothesis through controlled trials that use interventions, examining the proposed role of transferred representations in the detector’s behavior.

The findings lead to auxiliary training objectives that outperform previous anomaly-detection paradigms in the reported evaluations. These objectives turn the transfer hypothesis into a practical learning approach. The result supports semantic representation transfer as an effective strategy in the studied settings, while the motivating challenge remains broad: unseen anomalies can take many forms, so success does not amount to preparation for every possible anomaly.
summary.tldr: Biasing anomaly detectors toward representations transferred from broad semantic tasks yields effective auxiliary objectives in controlled evaluations.

title: Transfer-Based Semantic Anomaly Detection

abstract: The performance of modern algorithms on certain computer vision tasks such as object recognition is now close to that of humans. This success was achieved at the price of complicated architectures depending on millions of parameters and it has become quite challenging to understand how particular predictions are made. Interpretability methods propose to give us this understanding. In this paper, we study LIME, perhaps one of the most popular. On the theoretical side, we show that when the number of generated examples is large, LIME explanations are concentrated around a limit explanation for which we give an explicit expression. We further this study for elementary shape detectors and linear models. As a consequence of this analysis, we uncover a connection between LIME and integrated gradients, another explanation method. More precisely, the LIME explanations are similar to the sum of integrated gradients over the superpixels used in the preprocessing step of LIME.

paragraphs: LIME is used to explain predictions from complicated models, but understanding an explanation method requires knowing what its outputs represent. This paper studies LIME mathematically in the image setting. Its focus is on the behavior of the explanation as the number of examples generated by the method becomes large.

The authors prove that, with many generated examples, LIME explanations concentrate around a limiting explanation and provide an explicit expression for that limit. This turns an explanation produced through sampling into an object that can be analyzed directly. They further investigate the behavior for elementary shape detectors and linear models, giving concrete settings in which to understand the formula.

The analysis uncovers a connection to integrated gradients. Specifically, LIME’s explanations resemble integrated-gradient contributions summed over the superpixels used in its preprocessing. This relates LIME’s region-level output to another attribution method while making the image partition part of the interpretation. The result describes a similarity between the explanations, rather than asserting that the two methods produce identical outputs in every setting.
summary.tldr: A theoretical analysis characterizes LIME’s large-sample image explanations and connects them to integrated gradients aggregated over superpixels.

title: What does LIME really see in images?

abstract: We consider the problem of molecular graph generation using deep models. While graphs are discrete, most existing methods use continuous latent variables, resulting in inaccurate modeling of discrete graph structures. In this work, we propose GraphDF, a novel discrete latent variable model for molecular graph generation based on normalizing flow methods. GraphDF uses invertible modulo shift transforms to map discrete latent variables to graph nodes and edges. We show that the use of discrete latent variables reduces computational costs and eliminates the negative effect of dequantization. Comprehensive experimental results show that GraphDF outperforms prior methods on random generation, property optimization, and constrained optimization tasks.

Comprehensive experimental results show that GraphDF outperforms prior methods on random generation, property optimization, and constrained optimization tasks.

paragraphs: Generating a molecule as a graph requires choosing discrete nodes and edges. The paper argues that using continuous latent variables for this task can model those discrete structures inaccurately. GraphDF addresses that mismatch by keeping its latent representation discrete, aligning the variables used for generation with the kind of objects being generated.

The model builds on normalizing flows and uses invertible modulo shift transformations to turn discrete latent variables into graph nodes and edges. Invertibility means these transformations can be reversed. This construction gives GraphDF a way to generate graph structures without relying on the continuous conversion associated with dequantization.

The authors report that discrete latent variables reduce computational costs and remove the negative effect of dequantization. Their experiments find that GraphDF outperforms prior methods in random molecular generation, property optimization, and constrained optimization. Together, these results support the paper's central design choice: directly modeling discrete structure can improve both computational efficiency and empirical performance across several molecular generation tasks.
summary.tldr: GraphDF uses invertible transformations of discrete latent variables to generate molecular graphs, reducing computation and improving results across three generation tasks.

title: GraphDF: A Discrete Flow Model for Molecular Graph Generation

abstract: A recent line of work has analyzed the theoretical properties of deep neural networks via the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK). In particular, the smallest eigenvalue of the NTK has been related to the memorization capacity, the global convergence of gradient descent algorithms and the generalization of deep nets. However, existing results either provide bounds in the two-layer setting or assume that the spectrum of the NTK matrices is bounded away from 0 for multi-layer networks. In this paper, we provide tight bounds on the smallest eigenvalue of NTK matrices for deep ReLU nets, both in the limiting case of infinite widths and for finite widths. In the finite-width setting, the network architectures we consider are fairly general: we require the existence of a wide layer with roughly order of $N$ neurons, $N$ being the number of data samples; and the scaling of the remaining layer widths is arbitrary (up to logarithmic factors). To obtain our results, we analyze various quantities of independent interest: we give lower bounds on the smallest singular value of hidden feature matrices, and upper bounds on the Lipschitz constant of input-output feature maps.

paragraphs: The neural tangent kernel is a tool for analyzing deep networks, and its smallest eigenvalue has been linked to memorization, optimization, and generalization. Earlier results either treated two-layer networks or assumed that the eigenvalues of deeper networks stayed away from zero. This paper derives tight bounds for deep ReLU networks directly.

The results cover both infinite-width limits and finite-width networks. In the finite case, the architecture must contain a layer with roughly as many neurons as there are data samples. The remaining layer widths can scale arbitrarily up to logarithmic factors, making the studied family broader than architectures requiring every layer to be wide.

These intermediate results characterize feature behavior as well as the kernel itself. The main contribution supplies quantitative control over a kernel property that other theoretical analyses rely on.
summary.tldr: The paper tightly bounds the smallest neural tangent kernel eigenvalue for deep ReLU networks, including finite networks with one sufficiently wide layer.

title: Tight Bounds on the Smallest Eigenvalue of the Neural Tangent Kernel for Deep ReLU Networks

abstract: Attribution methods have been shown as promising approaches for identifying key features that led to learned model predictions. While most existing attribution methods rely on a baseline input for performing feature perturbations, limited research has been conducted to address the baseline selection issues. Poor choices of baselines limit the ability of one-vs-one explanations for multi-class classifiers, which means the attribution methods were not able to explain why an input belongs to its original class but not the other specified target class. Achieving one-vs-one explanation is crucial when certain classes are more similar than others, e.g. two bird types among multiple animals, by focusing on key differentiating features rather than shared features across classes. In this paper, we present GANMEX, a novel approach applying Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN) by incorporating the to-be-explained classifier as part of the adversarial networks. Our approach effectively selects the baseline as the closest realistic sample belong to the target class, which allows attribution methods to provide true one-vs-one explanations. We showed that GANMEX baselines improved the saliency maps and led to stronger performance on multiple evaluation metrics over the existing baselines. Existing attribution results are known for being insensitive to model randomization, and we demonstrated that GANMEX baselines led to better outcome under the cascading randomization of the model.

While most existing attribution methods rely on a baseline input for performing feature perturbations, limited research has been conducted to address the baseline selection issues. Poor choices of baselines limit the ability of one-vs-one explanations for multi-class classifiers, which means the attribution methods were not able to explain why an input belongs to its original class but not the other specified target class. Achieving one-vs-one explanation is crucial when certain classes are more similar than others, e.g. two bird types among multiple animals, by focusing on key differentiating features rather than shared features across classes. In this paper, we present GANMEX, a novel approach applying Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN) by incorporating the to-be-explained classifier as part of the adversarial networks. Our approach effectively selects the baseline as the closest realistic sample belong to the target class, which allows attribution methods to provide true one-vs-one explanations. We showed that GANMEX baselines improved the saliency maps and led to stronger performance on multiple evaluation metrics over the existing baselines. Existing attribution results are known for being insensitive to model randomization, and we demonstrated that GANMEX baselines led to better outcome under the cascading randomization of the model.

paragraphs: Feature attribution methods often explain a prediction by comparing an input with a baseline. The baseline choice becomes especially important when the question is why the classifier chose one particular class instead of another. Features shared by both classes may explain the broad category while doing little to explain that specific distinction.

GANMEX uses a generative adversarial network that incorporates the classifier being explained. It selects a baseline as the closest realistic sample belonging to the specified alternative class. This gives the attribution method a comparison tied to the requested contrast, helping it emphasize differentiating features instead of features common to both classes.

The authors report improved saliency maps and stronger results on multiple evaluation metrics compared with existing baselines. They also examine cascading model randomization, addressing the concern that attribution outputs can remain insensitive when the model changes. GANMEX performs better under that evaluation as well. The findings make baseline construction an active part of producing explanations that reflect both the selected alternative class and the classifier.
summary.tldr: GANMEX generates realistic alternative-class baselines to improve explanations of why a classifier chose one class over another.

title: GANMEX: One-vs-One Attributions using GAN-based Model Explainability

abstract: The inductive biases of graph representation learning algorithms are often encoded in the background geometry of their embedding space. In this paper, we show that general directed graphs can be effectively represented by an embedding model that combines three components: a pseudo-Riemannian metric structure, a non-trivial global topology, and a unique likelihood function that explicitly incorporates a preferred direction in embedding space. We demonstrate the representational capabilities of this method by applying it to the task of link prediction on a series of synthetic and real directed graphs from natural language applications and biology. In particular, we show that low-dimensional cylindrical Minkowski and anti-de Sitter spacetimes can produce equal or better graph representations than curved Riemannian manifolds of higher dimensions.

paragraphs: A graph embedding represents nodes as points in a space, and the geometry of that space shapes which relationships are easy to express. Directed graphs add a particular challenge because a connection from one node to another has an orientation. This paper investigates embedding spaces and a likelihood model designed to incorporate that directional structure.

The proposed model combines a pseudo-Riemannian metric, nontrivial global topology, and a likelihood function with an explicit preferred direction. These components jointly determine how the embedding represents relationships. The approach therefore treats the choice of geometry and the way links are modeled as coordinated parts of the representation.

The authors evaluate link prediction on synthetic graphs and real directed graphs from language applications and biology. They show that low-dimensional cylindrical Minkowski and anti-de Sitter spaces can match or improve on representations using higher-dimensional curved Riemannian spaces. The finding suggests that choosing a geometry suited to directionality can be more effective than simply increasing the number of embedding dimensions.
summary.tldr: Direction-aware pseudo-Riemannian embeddings can represent directed graphs as well as or better than higher-dimensional Riemannian alternatives.

title: Directed Graph Embeddings in Pseudo-Riemannian Manifolds

abstract: We address the problem of teaching a deep reinforcement learning (RL) agent to follow instructions in multi-task environments. Instructions are expressed in a well-known formal language {–} linear temporal logic (LTL) {–} and can specify a diversity of complex, temporally extended behaviours, including conditionals and alternative realizations. Our proposed learning approach exploits the compositional syntax and the semantics of LTL, enabling our RL agent to learn task-conditioned policies that generalize to new instructions, not observed during training. To reduce the overhead of learning LTL semantics, we introduce an environment-agnostic LTL pretraining scheme which improves sample-efficiency in downstream environments. Experiments on discrete and continuous domains target combinatorial task sets of up to $\sim10^{39}$ unique tasks and demonstrate the strength of our approach in learning to solve (unseen) tasks, given LTL instructions.

paragraphs: An agent following instructions may need to carry out behavior over time, respond to conditions, or choose among alternative ways to complete a task. LTL2Action expresses such instructions in linear temporal logic, a formal language that can describe these temporally extended requirements. The aim is to learn across many tasks and handle instructions absent from training.

The learning approach uses both the compositional structure of LTL expressions and their meaning. It trains task-conditioned policies, so the instruction helps determine the agent's behavior. The authors also introduce LTL pretraining that is independent of the downstream environment, reducing the overhead of learning the logic's semantics during environment-specific training.

Experiments cover discrete and continuous domains with combinatorial task sets containing up to approximately 10^39 unique tasks. They demonstrate learning to solve unseen tasks from LTL instructions, while the pretraining improves downstream sample efficiency. The large task-set size describes the combinatorial scope of the environments; the reported contribution is generalization through the structured instruction language.
summary.tldr: LTL2Action uses temporal logic structure and environment-independent pretraining to help reinforcement learning agents follow unseen instructions.

title: LTL2Action: Generalizing LTL Instructions for Multi-Task RL

abstract: We propose a reparametrization scheme to address the challenges of applying differentially private SGD on large neural networks, which are 1) the huge memory cost of storing individual gradients, 2) the added noise suffering notorious dimensional dependence. Specifically, we reparametrize each weight matrix with two \emph{gradient-carrier} matrices of small dimension and a \emph{residual weight} matrix. We argue that such reparametrization keeps the forward/backward process unchanged while enabling us to compute the projected gradient without computing the gradient itself. To learn with differential privacy, we design \emph{reparametrized gradient perturbation (RGP)} that perturbs the gradients on gradient-carrier matrices and reconstructs an update for the original weight from the noisy gradients. Importantly, we use historical updates to find the gradient-carrier matrices, whose optimality is rigorously justified under linear regression and empirically verified with deep learning tasks. RGP significantly reduces the memory cost and improves the utility. For example, we are the first able to apply differential privacy on the BERT model and achieve an average accuracy of $83.9%$ on four downstream tasks with $\epsilon=8$, which is within $5%$ loss compared to the non-private baseline but enjoys much lower privacy leakage risk.

This paper introduces a different parameterization intended to reduce both burdens while retaining the original forward and backward computation.

Reparametrized gradient perturbation adds noise to the carrier gradients and then reconstructs an update for the original weights. Historical updates guide the choice of carrier matrices; their optimality is justified for linear regression and examined empirically in deep learning.

The result demonstrates a practical route to private training of a large language model.
summary.tldr: Low-dimensional gradient carriers reduce the memory and utility costs of differentially private training for large neural networks.

title: Large Scale Private Learning via Low-rank Reparametrization

abstract: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is making rapid progress for solving tasks in a grid world and real-world scenarios, in which agents are given different attributes and goals, resulting in different behavior through the whole multi-agent task. In this study, we quantify the agent’s behavior difference and build its relationship with the policy performance via {\bf Role Diversity}, a metric to measure the characteristics of MARL tasks. We define role diversity from three perspectives: action-based, trajectory-based, and contribution-based to fully measure a multi-agent task. Through theoretical analysis, we find that the error bound in MARL can be decomposed into three parts that have a strong relation to the role diversity. The decomposed factors can significantly impact policy optimization in three popular directions including parameter sharing, communication mechanism, and credit assignment. The main experimental platforms are based on {\bf Multiagent Particle Environment (MPE) }and {\bf The StarCraft Multi-Agent Challenge (SMAC)}. Extensive experiments clearly show that role diversity can serve as a robust measurement for the characteristics of a multi-agent cooperation task and help diagnose whether the policy fits the current multi-agent system for better policy performance.

Its value lies in explaining task–policy fit and informing policy optimization through several complementary views of agent differences.
summary.tldr: Role diversity measures differences in agents’ actions, trajectories, and contributions to help diagnose cooperative multi-agent policies.

title: Policy Diagnosis via Measuring Role Diversity in Cooperative Multi-agent RL

abstract: We propose new, more efficient targeted white-box attacks against deep neural networks. Our attacks better align with the attacker’s goal: (1) tricking a model to assign higher probability to the target class than to any other class, while (2) staying within an $\epsilon$-distance of the attacked input. First, we demonstrate a loss function that explicitly encodes (1) and show that Auto-PGD finds more attacks with it. Second, we propose a new attack method, Constrained Gradient Descent (CGD), using a refinement of our loss function that captures both (1) and (2). CGD seeks to satisfy both attacker objectives—misclassification and bounded $\ell_{p}$-norm—in a principled manner, as part of the optimization, instead of via ad hoc post-processing techniques (e.g., projection or clipping). We show that CGD is more successful on CIFAR10 (0.9–4.2%) and ImageNet (8.6–13.6%) than state-of-the-art attacks while consuming less time (11.4–18.8%). Statistical tests confirm that our attack outperforms others against leading defenses on different datasets and values of $\epsilon$.
