paragraphs: A targeted adversarial attack must achieve two things together: make a chosen class more probable than every alternative, and keep the altered input within an allowed distance of the original. This paper develops white-box attacks whose optimization objectives more directly express those requirements. White-box access is part of the setting studied.

The first contribution is a loss function that explicitly represents the target-class ranking objective. Using it with Auto-PGD produces more successful attacks. The authors then refine the loss to incorporate the perturbation bound and introduce Constrained Gradient Descent. CGD handles misclassification and the bounded norm within its optimization, instead of relying on projection or clipping as post-processing.

The reported evaluations find greater attack success on CIFAR10 and ImageNet while using less time than the compared state-of-the-art attacks. Statistical tests also support improvements against leading defenses across different datasets and perturbation allowances. The findings show that aligning the optimization with both attack requirements can improve the efficiency and effectiveness of these evaluated robustness tests.
summary.tldr: Constrained Gradient Descent jointly optimizes targeted misclassification and perturbation bounds, improving attack success and runtime in the reported evaluations.

title: Constrained Gradient Descent: A Powerful and Principled Evasion Attack Against Neural Networks

abstract: Autoencoders are the simplest neural network for unsupervised learning, and thus an ideal framework for studying feature learning. While a detailed understanding of the dynamics of linear autoencoders has recently been obtained, the study of non-linear autoencoders has been hindered by the technical difficulty of handling training data with non-trivial correlations {–} a fundamental prerequisite for feature extraction. Here, we study the dynamics of feature learning in non-linear, shallow autoencoders. We derive a set of asymptotically exact equations that describe the generalisation dynamics of autoencoders trained with stochastic gradient descent (SGD) in the limit of high-dimensional inputs. These equations reveal that autoencoders learn the leading principal components of their inputs sequentially. An analysis of the long-time dynamics explains the failure of sigmoidal autoencoders to learn with tied weights, and highlights the importance of training the bias in ReLU autoencoders. Building on previous results for linear networks, we analyse a modification of the vanilla SGD algorithm which allows learning of the exact principal components. Finally, we show that our equations accurately describe the generalisation dynamics of non-linear autoencoders on realistic datasets such as CIFAR10.

paragraphs: Autoencoders offer a setting for studying how neural networks learn features without labels. This paper analyzes shallow nonlinear autoencoders, where correlated training inputs make the dynamics harder to understand than in linear models. The authors derive equations describing generalization during stochastic gradient descent that become exact asymptotically as input dimensionality grows.

The equations reveal sequential learning of the inputs’ leading principal components. An analysis of long-time behavior also explains why sigmoidal autoencoders fail to learn with tied weights and highlights the importance of training the bias in ReLU autoencoders. They also show that their equations accurately describe nonlinear autoencoder generalization dynamics on realistic datasets, including CIFAR10. The theoretical foundation is the high-dimensional limit, while the dataset results demonstrate that the equations can also describe observed learning behavior beyond an exclusively abstract calculation.
summary.tldr: High-dimensional learning equations explain sequential principal-component learning and key training behaviors in shallow nonlinear autoencoders.

title: The dynamics of representation learning in shallow, non-linear autoencoders

abstract: Active learning has become a prevalent technique for designing label-efficient algorithms, where the central principle is to only query and fit “informative” labeled instances. It is, however, known that an active learning algorithm may incur unfairness due to such instance selection procedure. In this paper, we henceforth study metric-fair active learning of homogeneous halfspaces, and show that under the distribution-dependent PAC learning model, fairness and label efficiency can be achieved simultaneously. We further propose two extensions of our main results: 1) we show that it is possible to make the algorithm robust to the adversarial noise – one of the most challenging noise models in learning theory; and 2) it is possible to significantly improve the label complexity when the underlying halfspace is sparse.

paragraphs: Active learning reduces labeling effort by selecting informative examples rather than requesting labels indiscriminately. That selection process can also introduce unfairness. This paper asks whether an algorithm can preserve label efficiency while meeting metric-fairness requirements, making fairness part of the learning problem rather than treating selection solely as an information-gathering decision.

The analysis concerns homogeneous halfspaces, a particular class of linear classifiers, under a distribution-dependent probably approximately correct learning model. Within that setting, the authors show that fairness and efficient use of labels can be achieved simultaneously. The result establishes compatibility between the two goals for the studied class and learning framework.

The paper extends its main results in two directions. First, it shows that robustness to adversarial noise is possible, addressing a demanding noise model. Second, it shows that label complexity can improve significantly when the underlying halfspace is sparse. These extensions connect the fairness result to both difficult labeling conditions and exploitable structure in the classifier being learned.
summary.tldr: Metric fairness and label efficiency can coexist for active learning of homogeneous halfspaces in the studied distribution-dependent framework.

title: Metric-Fair Active Learning

abstract: We propose an algorithm that uses linear function approximation (LFA) for stochastic shortest path (SSP). Under minimal assumptions, it obtains sublinear regret, is computationally efficient, and uses stationary policies. To our knowledge, this is the first such algorithm in the LFA literature (for SSP or other formulations). Our algorithm is a special case of a more general one, which achieves regret square root in the number of episodes given access to a computation oracle.
originalAbstract: We propose an algorithm that uses linear function approximation (LFA) for stochastic shortest path (SSP). paragraphs: The paper develops a learning algorithm for stochastic shortest-path problems using linear function approximation. Its focus is the combination of statistical performance, computational efficiency, and policy structure. Rather than studying only how much regret can be bounded, it also asks whether the algorithm can be implemented efficiently and use stationary policies.

Under assumptions the authors characterize as minimal, the proposed algorithm achieves sublinear regret while satisfying both additional requirements. Sublinear regret means that the cumulative performance gap grows more slowly than the amount of interaction, so the average gap decreases. The authors identify this combination as the first of its kind in the linear-function-approximation literature, to their knowledge.

The efficient algorithm is also a special case of a broader method. With access to a computation oracle, that general method achieves regret proportional to the square root of the number of episodes. The oracle condition matters: the broader statistical guarantee and the directly computationally efficient construction are related results, but they carry different computational qualifications.
summary.tldr: An efficient algorithm combines linear function approximation, stationary policies, and sublinear regret for stochastic shortest-path problems.

title: Regret Bounds for Stochastic Shortest Path Problems with Linear Function Approximation

abstract: Given a dataset on actions and resulting long-term rewards, a direct estimation approach fits value functions that minimize prediction error on the training data. Temporal difference learning (TD) methods instead fit value functions by minimizing the degree of temporal inconsistency between estimates made at successive time-steps. Focusing on finite state Markov chains, we provide a crisp asymptotic theory of the statistical advantages of this approach. First, we show that an intuitive inverse trajectory pooling coefficient completely characterizes the percent reduction in mean-squared error of value estimates. Depending on problem structure, the reduction could be enormous or nonexistent. Next, we prove that there can be dramatic improvements in estimates of the difference in value-to-go for two states: TD’s errors are bounded in terms of a novel measure – the problem’s trajectory crossing time – which can be much smaller than the problem’s time horizon.

paragraphs: A value function estimates future reward. One approach fits it directly to observed long-term returns; temporal difference learning instead makes estimates at successive times consistent with one another. This paper asks when that temporal consistency produces more statistically accurate estimates, focusing on finite-state Markov chains and asymptotic behavior.

The first result identifies an inverse trajectory pooling coefficient that completely characterizes the percentage reduction in mean-squared estimation error. This makes the advantage depend explicitly on the structure of the problem. Depending on that structure, temporal difference learning can produce an enormous improvement or no improvement at all. The theory therefore explains variation in its benefit rather than asserting a uniform statistical gain.

The second result concerns differences between the values of two states. Such comparisons can improve dramatically under temporal difference learning. The authors bound the associated errors using a new quantity called trajectory crossing time, which can be much shorter than the full time horizon. This separates the difficulty of estimating a value difference from the duration over which rewards accumulate.
summary.tldr: For finite-state Markov chains, the statistical benefits of temporal difference learning depend on trajectory structure and can range from absent to dramatic.

title: On the Statistical Benefits of Temporal Difference Learning

abstract: Retrieval-augmented models have proven to be effective in natural language processing tasks, yet there remains a lack of research on their optimization using variational inference. We introduce the Variational Open-Domain (VOD) framework for end-to-end training and evaluation of retrieval-augmented models, focusing on open-domain question answering and language modelling. The VOD objective, a self-normalized estimate of the Rényi variational bound, approximates the task marginal likelihood and is evaluated under samples drawn from an auxiliary sampling distribution (cached retriever and/or approximate posterior). It remains tractable, even for retriever distributions defined on large corpora. We demonstrate VOD’s versatility by training reader-retriever BERT-sized models on multiple-choice medical exam questions. On the MedMCQA dataset, we outperform the domain-tuned Med-PaLM by +5.3% despite using 2.500$\times$ fewer parameters. Our retrieval-augmented BioLinkBERT model scored 62.9% on the MedMCQA and 55.0% on the MedQA-USMLE. Last, we show the effectiveness of our learned retriever component in the context of medical semantic search.

This paper introduces Variational Open-Domain, or VOD, as a framework for training and evaluating these components end to end. Its focus is optimizing retrieval-augmented systems through variational inference.

summary.tldr: VOD makes variational training of retrieval-augmented models tractable over large corpora and demonstrates strong medical question-answering results.

title: Variational Open-Domain Question Answering

abstract: Concept bottleneck models (CBMs) are a class of interpretable neural network models that predict the target response of a given input based on its high-level concepts. Unlike the standard end-to-end models, CBMs enable domain experts to intervene on the predicted concepts and rectify any mistakes at test time, so that more accurate task predictions can be made at the end. While such intervenability provides a powerful avenue of control, many aspects of the intervention procedure remain rather unexplored. In this work, we develop various ways of selecting intervening concepts to improve the intervention effectiveness and conduct an array of in-depth analyses as to how they evolve under different circumstances. Specifically, we find that an informed intervention strategy can reduce the task error more than ten times compared to the current baseline under the same amount of intervention counts in realistic settings, and yet, this can vary quite significantly when taking into account different intervention granularity. We verify our findings through comprehensive evaluations, not only on the standard real datasets, but also on synthetic datasets that we generate based on a set of different causal graphs. We further discover some major pitfalls of the current practices which, without a proper addressing, raise concerns on reliability and fairness of the intervention procedure.

paragraphs: Concept bottleneck models make predictions through an intermediate set of high-level concepts. This gives domain experts a place to correct the model: they can edit mistaken concept predictions before the final answer is produced. The paper studies how to choose those edits, asking how much the intervention procedure itself affects the benefit of human input.

The authors develop several strategies for selecting concepts to intervene on and examine their behavior across different circumstances. Their evaluations include real datasets and synthetic datasets generated from different causal graphs. These tests explore how intervention effectiveness changes with the relationships underlying the data and with the granularity at which corrections are made.

In realistic settings, an informed strategy can reduce task error more than ten times compared with the current baseline using the same number of interventions. That benefit varies substantially with intervention granularity. The authors also identify pitfalls that raise reliability and fairness concerns, showing that providing an editable concept layer alone does not settle how interventions should be used.
summary.tldr: Choosing which concepts to correct can dramatically improve concept bottleneck models, but intervention granularity and procedural pitfalls affect the benefit.

title: A Closer Look at the Intervention Procedure of Concept Bottleneck Models

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) provides a theoretical framework for continuously improving an agent’s behavior via trial and error. However, efficiently learning policies from scratch can be very difficult, particularly for tasks that present exploration challenges. In such settings, it might be desirable to initialize RL with an existing policy, offline data, or demonstrations. However, naively performing such initialization in RL often works poorly, especially for value-based methods. In this paper, we present a meta algorithm that can use offline data, demonstrations, or a pre-existing policy to initialize an RL policy, and is compatible with any RL approach. In particular, we propose Jump-Start Reinforcement Learning (JSRL), an algorithm that employs two policies to solve tasks: a guide-policy, and an exploration-policy. By using the guide-policy to form a curriculum of starting states for the exploration-policy, we are able to efficiently improve performance on a set of simulated robotic tasks. We show via experiments that it is able to significantly outperform existing imitation and reinforcement learning algorithms, particularly in the small-data regime. In addition, we provide an upper bound on the sample complexity of JSRL and show that with the help of a guide-policy, one can improve the sample complexity for non-optimism exploration methods from exponential in horizon to polynomial.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning can struggle to discover useful behavior from scratch, even when demonstrations, offline data, or an existing policy are available. Simply using that information to initialize learning can work poorly, particularly for value-based methods. Jump-Start Reinforcement Learning offers a different way to organize the help provided by prior behavior.

The algorithm maintains a guide policy and an exploration policy. The guide creates a curriculum of starting states from which the exploration policy learns. This makes existing behavior useful through the states it provides for further learning. The authors present JSRL as a meta-algorithm compatible with any reinforcement-learning approach and able to incorporate the stated forms of prior information.

On simulated robotic tasks, JSRL significantly outperforms the evaluated imitation-learning and reinforcement-learning methods, especially when data is limited. The paper also provides a sample-complexity upper bound. Its theory shows that help from a guide can change the horizon dependence of non-optimistic exploration methods from exponential to polynomial, giving a formal account of how guided starting states can ease exploration.
summary.tldr: JSRL uses a guide policy to create starting-state curricula, improving exploration empirically and yielding stronger sample-complexity guarantees.

title: Jump-Start Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has made significant progress in areas such as Atari games and robotic control, where the agents have perfect sensing capabilities. However, in many real-world sequential decision-making tasks, the observation data could be noisy or incomplete due to the intrinsic low quality of the sensors or unexpected malfunctions; that is, the agent’s perceptions are rarely perfect. The current POMDP RL methods, such as particle-based and Gaussian-based, can only provide a probability estimate of hidden states rather than certain belief regions, which may lead to inefficient and even wrong decision-making. This paper proposes a novel algorithm called Set-membership Belief state-based Reinforcement Learning (SBRL), which consists of two parts: a Set-membership Belief state learning Model (SBM) for learning bounded belief state sets and an RL controller for making decisions based on SBM. We prove that our belief estimation method can provide a series of belief state sets that always contain the true states under the unknown-but-bounded (UBB) noise. The effectiveness of the proposed method is verified on a collection of benchmark tasks, and the results show that our method outperforms the state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning agent may receive incomplete or noisy observations instead of directly seeing the environment’s true state. This paper studies decision-making under that uncertainty using sets of possible hidden states. Its motivation is that probability estimates alone may not provide the definite belief regions useful for reliable decisions.

Set-membership Belief state-based Reinforcement Learning combines two parts. A belief-state learning model estimates bounded sets of possible states, and a reinforcement learning controller makes decisions using those sets. The central theoretical result shows that the estimated sets always contain the true states under unknown-but-bounded noise.

The bounded-noise condition is essential to the stated containment guarantee: uncertainty is unknown in detail but constrained in magnitude. Benchmark experiments support the method’s effectiveness and report better performance than the compared state-of-the-art approaches. The contribution connects a set-based representation of uncertainty with control, giving the controller belief regions supported by a containment result in the studied noise setting.
summary.tldr: SBRL controls partially observed systems using learned belief sets that provably contain the true state under unknown-but-bounded noise.

title: Set-membership Belief State-based Reinforcement Learning for POMDPs

abstract: The ability to accurately locate and navigate to a specific object is a crucial capability for embodied agents that operate in the real world and interact with objects to complete tasks. Such object navigation tasks usually require large-scale training in visual environments with labeled objects, which generalizes poorly to novel objects in unknown environments. In this work, we present a novel zero-shot object navigation method, Exploration with Soft Commonsense constraints (ESC), that transfers commonsense knowledge in pre-trained models to open-world object navigation without any navigation experience nor any other training on the visual environments. First, ESC leverages a pre-trained vision and language model for open-world prompt-based grounding and a pre-trained commonsense language model for room and object reasoning. Then ESC converts commonsense knowledge into navigation actions by modeling it as soft logic predicates for efficient exploration. Extensive experiments on MP3D, HM3D, and RoboTHOR benchmarks show that our ESC method improves significantly over baselines, and achieves new state-of-the-art results for zero-shot object navigation (e.g., 288% relative Success Rate improvement than CoW on MP3D).

paragraphs: An embodied agent searching for an object must connect what it sees with decisions about where to explore. Conventional object-navigation approaches often require extensive training in labeled visual environments and generalize poorly to unfamiliar objects and spaces. ESC instead transfers knowledge from pretrained models without navigation experience or additional training in those visual environments.

The method combines two sources of information. A vision-and-language model supplies prompt-based grounding for an open set of objects, while a commonsense language model reasons about rooms and objects. ESC expresses that commonsense information as soft logical predicates and uses them to guide exploration. This turns knowledge available in pretrained models into a basis for navigation actions.

Experiments on MP3D, HM3D, and RoboTHOR report substantial improvements over baselines and new state-of-the-art results for zero-shot object navigation. One example is a 288% relative success-rate improvement over CoW on MP3D. That figure describes a relative improvement in the reported comparison, supporting the usefulness of commonsense-guided exploration in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: ESC turns pretrained visual and commonsense knowledge into exploration guidance for object navigation without navigation-specific training.

title: ESC: Exploration with Soft Commonsense Constraints for Zero-shot Object Navigation

abstract: Recently, deep reinforcement learning has shown promising results for learning fast heuristics to solve routing problems. Meanwhile, most of the solvers suffer from generalizing to an unseen distribution or distributions with different scales. To address this issue, we propose a novel architecture, called Invariant Nested View Transformer (INViT), which is designed to enforce a nested design together with invariant views inside the encoders to promote the generalizability of the learned solver. It applies a modified policy gradient algorithm enhanced with data augmentations. We demonstrate that the proposed INViT achieves a dominant generalization performance on both TSP and CVRP problems with various distributions and different problem scales. Our source code and datasets are available in supplementary materials.

paragraphs: Learned routing heuristics can solve problems quickly, yet their performance often struggles when test instances differ from the training distribution or contain a different number of locations. This paper focuses on that transfer problem. It proposes an architecture intended to make a learned solver more reliable across distributions and problem sizes.

The Invariant Nested View Transformer, or INViT, combines a nested design with invariant views inside its encoders. These architectural choices are designed to promote generalization in how the solver represents routing instances. Training uses a modified policy-gradient algorithm enhanced with data augmentation, pairing the representation design with a reinforcement-learning procedure.

The authors evaluate the method on the traveling salesperson problem and the capacitated vehicle routing problem, covering varied distributions and scales. They report strong comparative generalization performance across those settings. The significance lies in treating transfer as an architectural and training objective: the solver is developed specifically for situations in which future routing instances need not resemble the examples used during learning.
summary.tldr: INViT combines invariant nested representations with augmented reinforcement learning to improve routing generalization across distributions and problem sizes.

title: INViT: A Generalizable Routing Problem Solver with Invariant Nested View Transformer

abstract: Understanding the generalization properties of large-scale models necessitates incorporating realistic data assumptions into the analysis. Therefore, we consider Principal Component Regression (PCR)—combining principal component analysis and linear regression—on data from a low-dimensional manifold. We present an analysis of PCR when the data is sampled from a spiked covariance model, obtaining fundamental asymptotic guarantees for the generalization risk of this model. Our analysis is based on random matrix theory and allows us to provide guarantees for high-dimensional data. We additionally present an analysis of the distribution shift between training and test data. The results allow us to disentangle the effects of (1) the number of parameters, (2) the data-generating model and, (3) model misspecification on the generalization risk. The use of PCR effectively regularizes the model and prevents the interpolation peak of the double descent. Our theoretical findings are empirically validated in simulation, demonstrating their practical relevance.

We present an analysis of PCR when the data is sampled from a spiked covariance model, obtaining fundamental asymptotic guarantees for the generalization risk of this model. Our analysis is based on random matrix theory and allows us to provide guarantees for high-dimensional data. We additionally present an analysis of the distribution shift between training and test data. The results allow us to disentangle the effects of (1) the number of parameters, (2) the data-generating model and, (3) model misspecification on the generalization risk. The use of PCR effectively regularizes the model and prevents the interpolation peak of the double descent. Our theoretical findings are empirically validated in simulation, demonstrating their practical relevance.

paragraphs: Principal component regression combines principal component analysis with linear regression. This paper studies its generalization when high-dimensional observations have an underlying low-dimensional structure. The analysis assumes data sampled from a spiked covariance model, providing a specific setting in which to examine how representation choice affects prediction risk.

Using random matrix theory, the authors derive asymptotic guarantees for generalization risk in high dimensions. They also analyze distribution shift between training and test data. These results separate the effects of parameter count, the data-generating model, and model misspecification, helping clarify why changes in model size alone do not fully explain prediction performance.

In the analyzed setting, principal component regression acts as a regularizer and prevents the interpolation peak associated with double descent. This connects the absence of that peak to the use of principal components under the stated data model. Simulations validate the theoretical findings, supporting their relevance to the modeled conditions and showing how the predicted behavior appears in empirical experiments.
summary.tldr: Under a spiked covariance data model, principal component regression regularizes learning and prevents the interpolation peak of double descent.

title: No Double Descent in Principal Component Regression: A High-Dimensional Analysis

abstract: Adapting to a priori unknown noise level is a very important but challenging problem in sequential decision-making as efficient exploration typically requires knowledge of the noise level, which is often loosely specified. We report significant progress in addressing this issue in linear bandits in two respects. First, we propose a novel confidence set that is ’semi-adaptive’ to the unknown sub-Gaussian parameter $\sigma_*^2$ in the sense that the (normalized) confidence width scales with $\sqrt{d\sigma_*^2 + \sigma_0^2}$ where $d$ is the dimension and $\sigma_0^2$ is the specified sub-Gaussian parameter (known) that can be much larger than $\sigma_*^2$. This is a significant improvement over $\sqrt{d\sigma_0^2}$ of the standard confidence set of Abbasi-Yadkori et al. (2011), especially when $d$ is large. We show that this leads to an improved regret bound in linear bandits. Second, for bounded rewards, we propose a novel variance-adaptive confidence set that has a much improved numerical performance upon prior art. We then apply this confidence set to develop, as we claim, the first practical variance-adaptive linear bandit algorithm via an optimistic approach, which is enabled by our novel regret analysis technique. Both of our confidence sets rely critically on ‘regret equality’ from online learning. Our empirical evaluation in Bayesian optimization tasks shows that our algorithms demonstrate better or comparable performance compared to existing methods.

paragraphs: Sequential decision-making requires balancing promising actions with exploration, and that balance depends on how noisy observations are. A conservatively specified noise level can make uncertainty estimates unnecessarily broad. This paper develops confidence sets for linear bandits that adapt more closely to the noise actually present.

The first construction is semi-adaptive: its normalized width scales with the square root of the dimension times the true sub-Gaussian noise parameter, plus the specified parameter. The standard comparison instead multiplies the specified parameter by the dimension. The improvement is especially relevant in high dimensions when the specified noise level is much larger than the true one, and it yields an improved regret bound.

For bounded rewards, the authors also develop a variance-adaptive confidence set and an optimistic bandit algorithm with a new regret analysis. Both constructions rely on an online-learning regret equality. The bounded-reward construction shows substantially improved numerical performance over prior approaches. Evaluations on Bayesian optimization tasks find better or comparable performance to existing methods, connecting the confidence-set analysis to practical sequential optimization.
summary.tldr: Noise-adaptive confidence sets improve linear-bandit guarantees and deliver better or comparable Bayesian optimization performance.

title: Noise-Adaptive Confidence Sets for Linear Bandits and Application to Bayesian Optimization

abstract: Unified multi-model representation spaces are the foundation of multimodal understanding and generation. However, the billions of model parameters and catastrophic forgetting problems make it challenging to further enhance pre-trained unified spaces. In this work, we propose FreeBind, an idea that treats multimodal representation spaces as basic units, and freely augments pre-trained unified space by integrating knowledge from extra expert spaces via “space bonds". Specifically, we introduce two kinds of basic space bonds: 1) Space Displacement Bond and 2) Space Combination Bond. Based on these basic bonds, we design Complex Sequential & Parallel Bonds to effectively integrate multiple spaces simultaneously. Benefiting from the modularization concept, we further propose a coarse-to-fine customized inference strategy to flexibly adjust the enhanced unified space for different purposes. Experimentally, we bind ImageBind with extra image-text and audio-text expert spaces, resulting in three main variants: ImageBind++, InternVL_IB, and InternVL_IB++. These resulting spaces outperform ImageBind on 5 audio-image-text downstream tasks across 9 datasets. Moreover, via customized inference, it even surpasses the advanced audio-text and image-text expert spaces. Our code and checkpoints are released at https://github.com/zehanwang01/FreeBind

paragraphs: FreeBind aims to improve an existing shared representation space for multiple kinds of data by incorporating knowledge from specialist spaces. The motivation is that enhancing large pretrained unified spaces is difficult: their models contain billions of parameters, and further learning can cause catastrophic forgetting, where previously learned capabilities are lost.

The approach treats representation spaces themselves as the units to combine. It introduces two basic connections, called Space Displacement Bonds and Space Combination Bonds, and builds sequential and parallel arrangements from them. These arrangements allow knowledge from several expert spaces to be integrated into a unified space.

This modular design also supports a coarse-to-fine customized inference strategy. Users can adjust the enhanced space for different purposes when applying it. The contribution therefore includes both a way to bring multiple spaces together and a way to tailor the resulting representation to its intended use.

The experiments combine ImageBind with image–text and audio–text expert spaces, producing ImageBind++, InternVL_IB, and InternVL_IB++. These variants outperform ImageBind on five downstream tasks involving audio, images, and text across nine datasets. With customized inference, the authors also report performance exceeding the specialist spaces. These results support the usefulness of combining unified and specialist representations in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: FreeBind combines a unified multimodal representation space with specialist spaces, improving ImageBind across evaluated tasks and enabling customization for different uses.

title: FreeBind: Free Lunch in Unified Multimodal Space via Knowledge Fusion

abstract: Generative modeling via stochastic processes has led to remarkable empirical results as well as to recent advances in their theoretical understanding. In principle, both space and time of the processes can be discrete or continuous. In this work, we study time-continuous Markov jump processes on discrete state spaces and investigate their correspondence to state-continuous diffusion processes given by SDEs. In particular, we revisit the $\textit{Ehrenfest process}$, which converges to an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process in the infinite state space limit. Likewise, we can show that the time-reversal of the Ehrenfest process converges to the time-reversed Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process. This observation bridges discrete and continuous state spaces and allows to carry over methods from one to the respective other setting, such as for instance loss functions that lead to improved convergence. Additionally, we suggest an algorithm for training the time-reversal of Markov jump processes which relies on conditional expectations and can thus be directly related to denoising score matching. We demonstrate our methods in multiple convincing numerical experiments.

paragraphs: This paper connects two kinds of stochastic processes used in generative modeling: processes that jump between discrete states and diffusion processes that move through continuous states. Time is continuous in both settings studied here. The central example is the Ehrenfest process, whose behavior approaches that of an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck diffusion as the state space becomes infinite.

The authors establish a corresponding connection for the time-reversed processes. The reversal of the Ehrenfest process converges to the reversal of the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process. This matters because it extends the bridge beyond the forward stochastic dynamics, supporting the transfer of methods between discrete-state and continuous-state formulations, including loss functions that improve convergence.

They also propose a training algorithm for reversed Markov jump processes based on conditional expectations. This construction creates a direct relationship to denoising score matching, linking the training method to the broader discrete–continuous correspondence. Numerical experiments demonstrate the proposed methods. The theoretical bridge rests on the stated infinite-state-space limit, while the experiments illustrate how the associated ideas can be used computationally.
summary.tldr: The paper connects discrete jump processes and continuous diffusions through their forward and reversed limits, enabling related training methods.

title: Bridging discrete and continuous state spaces: Exploring the Ehrenfest process in time-continuous diffusion models

abstract: Instruction tuning has unlocked powerful capabilities in large language models (LLMs), using combined datasets to develop general-purpose chatbots. However, real-world applications often require a specialized suite of skills (e.g., reasoning). The challenge lies in identifying the most relevant data from these extensive datasets to effectively develop specific capabilities, a setting we frame as targeted instruction tuning. We propose LESS, an optimizer-aware and practically efficient algorithm to estimate data influences and perform Low-rank gradiEnt Similarity Search for instruction data selection. Crucially, LESS adapts existing influence formulations to work with the Adam optimizer and variable-length instruction data. LESS first constructs a highly reusable and transferable gradient datastore with low-dimensional gradient features and then selects examples based on their similarity to few-shot examples embodying a specific capability. Experiments show that training on a LESS-selected 5% of the data can often outperform training on the full dataset across diverse downstream tasks. Furthermore, the selected data is highly transferable: smaller models can be leveraged to select useful data for larger models and models from different families. Our qualitative analysis shows that our method goes beyond surface form cues to identify data that exemplifies the necessary reasoning skills for the intended downstream application. To facilitate future work, we release code and data at princeton-nlp/LESS.

paragraphs: Instruction-tuning collections contain examples for many abilities, while an application may need a particular skill. LESS addresses targeted instruction tuning: choosing the examples most useful for developing that capability. A few examples of the desired behavior provide the target against which candidate training data are assessed.

The method builds a reusable datastore of low-dimensional gradient features and searches for training examples with similar features to the target examples. These gradients describe training-related behavior rather than just textual resemblance. LESS adapts influence estimation to the Adam optimizer and to variable-length instruction examples, making the selection procedure better suited to the actual tuning process.

Experiments show that a selected five percent of the data can often outperform full-dataset training across downstream tasks. Selections also transfer from smaller to larger models and across model families. Qualitative analysis indicates that the method can identify relevant reasoning skills beyond surface wording. Together, these findings support influence-based selection as a practical way to concentrate tuning on a desired capability.
summary.tldr: LESS selects instruction-tuning data through optimizer-aware gradient similarity, often letting a five-percent subset outperform full-data training on targeted tasks.

title: LESS: Selecting Influential Data for Targeted Instruction Tuning

abstract: We leverage multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC) to improve the performance of multi-step look- ahead Bayesian optimization (BO) methods that involve nested expectations and maximizations. Often these expectations must be computed by Monte Carlo (MC). The complexity rate of naive MC degrades for nested operations, whereas MLMC is capable of achieving the canonical MC convergence rate for this type of problem, independently of dimension and without any smoothness assumptions. Our theoretical study focuses on the approximation improvements for two- and three-step look-ahead acquisition functions, but, as we discuss, the approach is generalizable in various ways, including beyond the context of BO. Our findings are verified numerically and the benefits of MLMC for BO are illustrated on several benchmark examples. Code is available at https://github.com/Shangda-Yang/MLMCBO.

Often these expectations must be computed by Monte Carlo (MC). The complexity rate of naive MC degrades for nested operations, whereas MLMC is capable of achieving the canonical MC convergence rate for this type of problem, independently of dimension and without any smoothness assumptions. Our theoretical study focuses on the approximation improvements for two- and three-step look-ahead acquisition functions, but, as we discuss, the approach is generalizable in various ways, including beyond the context of BO. paragraphs: Bayesian optimization can choose an evaluation by considering how it might improve several later decisions. This look-ahead approach involves expectations nested inside other expectations and maximizations. Computing these quantities with ordinary Monte Carlo sampling becomes increasingly expensive as operations are nested, making the calculation of promising next steps a bottleneck.

The paper applies multilevel Monte Carlo to these calculations. The central contribution is an improvement in the computational convergence rate: for the problem considered, the method can recover the standard Monte Carlo rate despite the nesting. The stated rate does not depend on dimension and does not require smoothness assumptions. This addresses the cost of estimating look-ahead acquisition functions, which score candidate evaluations.

The theoretical analysis concentrates on two-step and three-step look-ahead functions. Numerical studies verify the findings, and benchmark examples illustrate benefits for Bayesian optimization. The authors also discuss possible extensions, including uses outside Bayesian optimization. Those broader possibilities extend the motivation, while the specific theoretical results concern the analyzed look-ahead calculations.
summary.tldr: Multilevel Monte Carlo makes nested look-ahead calculations in Bayesian optimization more efficient, with theoretical results for two-step and three-step acquisition functions.

title: Accelerating Look-ahead in Bayesian Optimization: Multilevel Monte Carlo is All you Need

abstract: The conformational landscape of proteins is crucial to understanding their functionality in complex biological processes. Traditional physics-based computational methods, such as molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, suffer from rare event sampling and long equilibration time problems, hindering their applications in general protein systems. Recently, deep generative modeling techniques, especially diffusion models, have been employed to generate novel protein conformations. However, existing score-based diffusion methods cannot properly incorporate important physical prior knowledge to guide the generation process, causing large deviations in the sampled protein conformations from the equilibrium distribution. In this paper, to overcome these limitations, we propose a force-guided $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ diffusion model, ConfDiff, for protein conformation generation. By incorporating a force-guided network with a mixture of data-based score models, ConfDiff can generate protein conformations with rich diversity while preserving high fidelity. Experiments on a variety of protein conformation prediction tasks, including 12 fast-folding proteins and the Bovine Pancreatic Trypsin Inhibitor (BPTI), demonstrate that our method surpasses the state-of-the-art method.

paragraphs: Proteins adopt multiple conformations, and understanding that range of shapes is important for understanding their functions. Physics-based methods such as molecular dynamics face difficulties sampling rare events and reaching equilibrium. Diffusion models offer a generative alternative, but existing score-based methods can produce conformations that deviate substantially from the equilibrium distribution.

The paper attributes this problem to inadequate incorporation of physical prior knowledge. Its proposed method, ConfDiff, is a force-guided SE(3) diffusion model that combines a force-guided network with a mixture of data-based score models. This brings physical guidance into a generation process that also draws on learned structural information.

ConfDiff is designed to produce diverse conformations while retaining high fidelity. Experiments include conformation prediction tasks for 12 fast-folding proteins and Bovine Pancreatic Trypsin Inhibitor, or BPTI, where it outperforms the state-of-the-art method used for comparison. The results support combining force guidance with learned scores to improve conformation generation across the evaluated protein tasks.
summary.tldr: ConfDiff combines physical force guidance with learned diffusion scores to generate diverse, high-fidelity protein conformations.

title: Protein Conformation Generation via Force-Guided SE(3) Diffusion Models

abstract: Incomplete multi-view clustering (IMVC) methods typically encounter three drawbacks: (1) intense time and/or space overheads; (2) intractable hyper-parameters; (3) non-zero variance results. With these concerns in mind, we give a simple yet effective IMVC scheme, termed as ToRES. Concretely, instead of self-expression affinity, we manage to construct prototype-sample affinity for incomplete data so as to decrease the memory requirements. To eliminate hyper-parameters, besides mining complementary features among views by view-wise prototypes, we also attempt to devise cross-view prototypes to capture consensus features for jointly forming high-quality clustering representation. To avoid the variance, we successfully unify representation learning and clustering operation, and directly optimize the discrete cluster indicators from incomplete data. Then, for the resulting objective function, we provide two equivalent solutions from perspectives of feasible region partitioning and objective transformation. Many results suggest that ToRES exhibits advantages against 20 SOTA algorithms, even in scenarios with a higher ratio of incomplete data.

paragraphs: Incomplete multi-view clustering groups samples described by several views when some view information is missing. ToRES addresses three difficulties identified in existing methods: high computational or memory demands, hard-to-manage hyperparameters, and variability in clustering results. Its design changes both the representation of incomplete data and the way cluster assignments are produced.

To reduce memory requirements, ToRES constructs relationships between prototypes and samples instead of using self-expression affinity. View-specific prototypes capture complementary information, while cross-view prototypes capture information shared among views. The authors combine these representations in a scheme designed to eliminate hyperparameters, bringing distinct and common information into the clustering representation.

To avoid variability, the method unifies representation learning with clustering and directly optimizes discrete cluster indicators. The paper provides two equivalent solutions to its objective, based on feasible-region partitioning and objective transformation. Reported comparisons against twenty state-of-the-art algorithms suggest advantages for ToRES, including when more data is incomplete. The results support jointly addressing representation quality, resource use, and assignment stability.
summary.tldr: ToRES combines prototype-based representations with direct cluster assignment to make incomplete multi-view clustering more resource-efficient and stable.

title: Towards Resource-friendly, Extensible and Stable Incomplete Multi-view Clustering

abstract: Rainbow Deep Q-Network (DQN) demonstrated combining multiple independent enhancements could significantly boost a reinforcement learning (RL) agent’s performance. In this paper, we present “Beyond The Rainbow” (BTR), a novel algorithm that integrates six improvements from across the RL literature to Rainbow DQN, establishing a new state-of-the-art for RL using a desktop PC, with a human-normalized interquartile mean (IQM) of 7.6 on Atari-60. Beyond Atari, we demonstrate BTR’s capability to handle complex 3D games, successfully training agents to play Super Mario Galaxy, Mario Kart, and Mortal Kombat with minimal algorithmic changes. Designing BTR with computational efficiency in mind, agents can be trained using a high-end desktop PC on 200 million Atari frames within 12 hours. Additionally, we conduct detailed ablation studies of each component, analyzing the performance and impact using numerous measures.

paragraphs: Beyond The Rainbow builds on the idea that several complementary improvements can jointly make a reinforcement-learning agent much stronger. Starting from Rainbow DQN, the authors integrate six additional improvements drawn from the reinforcement-learning literature. Their aim includes both strong game-playing performance and computational efficiency on a high-end desktop computer.

On Atari-60, the resulting BTR algorithm achieves a human-normalized interquartile mean score of 7.6, which the authors report as a new state of the art for reinforcement learning using a desktop PC. They also report training on 200 million Atari frames within 12 hours. These results place performance and training cost together, making the available computing setup part of the contribution.

The evaluation extends to Super Mario Galaxy, Mario Kart, and Mortal Kombat, where agents are successfully trained with minimal algorithmic changes. This provides evidence that BTR’s usefulness extends beyond Atari. Detailed component ablations examine the contributions of individual improvements using multiple measures, helping assess how the combined system achieves its results.
summary.tldr: BTR combines six improvements to Rainbow DQN to achieve strong game-playing results with training feasible on a high-end desktop PC.

title: Beyond The Rainbow: High Performance Deep Reinforcement Learning on a Desktop PC

abstract: We present a new Correlation Clustering algorithm for a dynamic setting where nodes are added one at a time. In this model, proposed by Cohen-Addad, Lattanzi, Maggiori, and Parotsidis (ICML 2024), the algorithm uses database queries to access the input graph and updates the clustering as each new node is added. Our algorithm has the amortized update time of $\log^{O(1)}(n)$. Its approximation factor is $20+\varepsilon$, which is a substantial improvement over the approximation factor of the algorithm by Cohen-Addad et al. We complement our theoretical findings by empirically evaluating the approximation guarantee of our algorithm. The results show that it outperforms the algorithm by Cohen-Addad et al. in practice.

In this model, proposed by Cohen-Addad, Lattanzi, Maggiori, and Parotsidis (ICML 2024), the algorithm uses database queries to access the input graph and updates the clustering as each new node is added. Our algorithm has the amortized update time of $\log^{O(1)}(n)$. paragraphs: This paper studies correlation clustering in a graph that grows one node at a time. The algorithm accesses graph information through database queries and updates its clustering after each insertion. The central challenge is to maintain a useful clustering while keeping the computational cost of repeated updates small as the graph becomes larger.

The proposed Sparse-pivot algorithm achieves an amortized update time of log raised to a constant power of n. Amortized time describes the cost averaged over a sequence of updates, rather than a guarantee that every individual insertion takes the same amount of work. Its approximation factor is 20 plus epsilon, substantially improving the guarantee of the prior algorithm in this insertion model.

The authors also evaluate the algorithm empirically and report better performance than that earlier method. The contribution combines a stronger theoretical clustering guarantee with inexpensive updates and supporting practical results. It directly addresses a setting where the graph and its clustering must be maintained together as new nodes arrive through an ongoing sequence of insertions.
summary.tldr: Sparse-pivot improves the approximation guarantee for node-insertion correlation clustering while retaining polylogarithmic amortized update time.

title: Sparse-pivot: Dynamic correlation clustering for node insertions

abstract: We present a nonparametric interpretation for deep learning compatible modern Hopfield models and utilize this new perspective to debut efficient variants. Our key contribution stems from interpreting the memory storage and retrieval processes in modern Hopfield models as a nonparametric regression problem subject to a set of query-memory pairs. Interestingly, our framework not only recovers the known results from the original dense modern Hopfield model but also fills the void in the literature regarding efficient modern Hopfield models, by introducing sparse-structured modern Hopfield models with sub-quadratic complexity. We establish that this sparse model inherits the appealing theoretical properties of its dense analogue — connection with transformer attention, fixed point convergence and exponential memory capacity. Additionally, we showcase the versatility of our framework by constructing a family of modern Hopfield models as extensions, including linear, random masked, top-$K$ and positive random feature modern Hopfield models. Empirically, we validate our framework in both synthetic and realistic settings for memory retrieval and learning tasks.

paragraphs: Modern Hopfield models store memories and retrieve them in response to queries, in a form compatible with deep learning. This paper reinterprets those operations as nonparametric regression over query-memory pairs. The perspective provides a common mathematical framework for understanding the original dense model and developing alternatives that require less computation.

The main efficient variant uses sparse structure and has subquadratic complexity. The authors establish that it retains several attractive theoretical properties of the dense model: a connection to transformer attention, convergence to fixed points, and exponential memory capacity. The efficiency change therefore comes with analysis showing that these specific properties survive.

The framework also yields linear, randomly masked, top-K, and positive random feature variants of modern Hopfield models. Experiments evaluate memory retrieval and learning tasks in synthetic and realistic settings, supporting the framework empirically. The broader contribution is a systematic route from a regression interpretation to multiple memory architectures, making computational design choices part of a unified treatment rather than a collection of unrelated modifications.
summary.tldr: A nonparametric regression view yields efficient Hopfield variants, including a sparse model that retains key theoretical properties.

title: Nonparametric Modern Hopfield Models

abstract: Compositional generalization is a crucial step towards developing data-efficient intelligent machines that generalize in human-like ways. In this work, we tackle a challenging form of distribution shift, termed compositional shift, where some attribute combinations are completely absent at training but present in the test distribution. This shift tests the model’s ability to generalize compositionally to novel attribute combinations in discriminative tasks. We model the data with flexible additive energy distributions, where each energy term represents an attribute, and derive a simple alternative to empirical risk minimization termed compositional risk minimization (CRM). We first train an additive energy classifier to predict the multiple attributes and then adjust this classifier to tackle compositional shifts. We provide an extensive theoretical analysis of CRM, where we show that our proposal extrapolates to special affine hulls of seen attribute combinations. Empirical evaluations on benchmark datasets confirms the improved robustness of CRM compared to other methods from the literature designed to tackle various forms of subpopulation shifts.

paragraphs: A classifier may encounter familiar attributes combined in ways that never appeared during training. The paper calls this compositional shift: some attribute combinations are entirely absent from the training distribution but present at test time. Handling this shift requires extending knowledge of the observed combinations to new ones.

The authors model the data using additive energy distributions, with each energy term representing an attribute. From this formulation they derive compositional risk minimization, or CRM. The procedure first trains an additive energy classifier to predict multiple attributes, then adjusts that classifier to address changes in which combinations occur.

The theoretical analysis establishes extrapolation to particular affine hulls of the observed attribute combinations, giving the result a specific geometric scope rather than a guarantee for every unseen combination. Benchmark experiments show improved robustness relative to methods developed for other subpopulation shifts. The work therefore links an explicit model of attribute composition to a training-and-adjustment procedure aimed at a demanding form of distribution shift.
summary.tldr: CRM uses additive attribute models and classifier adjustment to improve robustness to attribute combinations missing from training.

title: Compositional Risk Minimization

abstract: Preference-based reinforcement learning (PbRL) bypasses explicit reward engineering by inferring reward functions from human preference comparisons, enabling better alignment with human intentions. However, humans often struggle to label a clear preference between similar segments, reducing label efficiency and limiting PbRL’s real-world applicability. To address this, we propose an offline PbRL method: Contrastive LeArning for ResolvIng Ambiguous Feedback (CLARIFY), which learns a trajectory embedding space that incorporates preference information, ensuring clearly distinguished segments are spaced apart, thus facilitating the selection of more unambiguous queries. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CLARIFY outperforms baselines in both non-ideal teachers and real human feedback settings. Our approach not only selects more distinguished queries but also learns meaningful trajectory embeddings.

paragraphs: Preference-based reinforcement learning learns a reward function from human comparisons instead of requiring someone to specify rewards directly. This can help align behavior with human intentions, but comparisons become difficult when two behavior segments look similar. Unclear preferences make the labels less useful, creating a practical obstacle for learning from human feedback.

CLARIFY addresses this problem with an offline method that learns a representation of trajectories, or sequences of behavior. Its contrastive learning approach incorporates preference information into an embedding space: a representation in which clearly distinguishable segments are placed apart. This gives the method a basis for selecting comparisons that are less ambiguous for the person providing feedback.

The reported experiments show CLARIFY outperforming baselines in settings involving both non-ideal teachers and real human feedback. The findings also indicate that it selects more distinguishable queries and learns meaningful trajectory representations. These results connect the representation-learning step to the feedback problem: organizing behavior using preference information can help identify comparisons that people can judge more clearly.
summary.tldr: CLARIFY learns preference-informed representations of behavior to select less ambiguous comparisons, outperforming baselines in experiments with non-ideal teachers and real human feedback.

title: CLARIFY: Contrastive Preference Reinforcement Learning for Untangling Ambiguous Queries

abstract: Are world models a necessary ingredient for flexible, goal-directed behaviour, or is model-free learning sufficient? We provide a formal answer to this question, showing that any agent capable of generalizing to multi-step goal-directed tasks must have learned a predictive model of its environment. We show that this model can be extracted from the agent’s policy, and that increasing the agents performance or the complexity of the goals it can achieve requires learning increasingly accurate world models. This has a number of consequences: from developing safe and general agents, to bounding agent capabilities in complex environments, and providing new algorithms for eliciting world models from agents.

paragraphs: This paper examines whether flexible, goal-directed behavior requires an agent to learn how its environment works. It addresses the question formally by connecting generalization across multistep goals with predictive knowledge of the environment. The relevant capability is achieving goals through sequences of actions, where consequences extend beyond the next immediate step.

The authors show that an agent capable of this form of generalization must have learned a predictive world model. They also show that the model can be extracted from the agent’s policy, the mechanism that determines its actions. This connects an agent’s ability to act successfully with environmental knowledge recoverable from that ability.

The result further links stronger performance and more complex achievable goals to increasingly accurate world models. Its implications include studying safe general agents, placing bounds on capabilities in complex environments, and developing methods to elicit predictive models from policies. The contribution is a formal relationship between specified goal-directed capabilities and learned environmental prediction, rather than an empirical comparison of particular agent architectures.
summary.tldr: The paper formally shows that generalizing to multistep goal-directed tasks requires predictive environmental knowledge recoverable from an agent’s policy.

title: General agents need world models

abstract: Ensembles of Deep Neural Networks, Deep Ensembles, are widely used as a simple way to boost predictive performance. However, their impact on algorithmic fairness is not well understood yet. Algorithmic fairness examines how a model’s performance varies across socially relevant groups defined by protected attributes such as age, gender, or race. In this work, we explore the interplay between the performance gains from Deep Ensembles and fairness. Our analysis reveals that they unevenly favor different groups, a phenomenon that we term the disparate benefits effect. We empirically investigate this effect using popular facial analysis and medical imaging datasets with protected group attributes and find that it affects multiple established group fairness metrics, including statistical parity and equal opportunity. Furthermore, we identify that the per-group differences in predictive diversity of ensemble members can explain this effect. Finally, we demonstrate that the classical Hardt post-processing method is particularly effective at mitigating the disparate benefits effect of Deep Ensembles by leveraging their better-calibrated predictive distributions.

paragraphs: Combining several neural networks into an ensemble often improves predictive performance, but the gains may differ across socially relevant groups. This paper studies that uneven distribution of benefits, calling it the disparate benefits effect. Its focus is how an otherwise useful performance improvement interacts with fairness across protected groups.

Experiments on facial analysis and medical imaging datasets show effects on several established group fairness measures, including statistical parity and equal opportunity. The authors identify differences in the predictive diversity of ensemble members across groups as an explanation. In other words, how differently the component models predict for each group helps account for why combining them provides unequal benefits.

The study also finds that the established Hardt post-processing method is particularly effective at mitigating this effect, using the ensembles' better-calibrated predictive distributions. The contribution connects an explanation of unequal performance gains with a demonstrated mitigation strategy. It shows why evaluating an ensemble's overall improvement alone can overlook meaningful differences in how its benefits are distributed.
summary.tldr: Deep ensembles can benefit protected groups unequally, with group-specific predictive diversity helping explain the effect and post-processing helping mitigate it.

title: The Disparate Benefits of Deep Ensembles

abstract: In this work, we study offline reinforcement learning (RL) with zero-shot generalization property (ZSG), where the agent has access to an offline dataset including experiences from different environments, and the goal of the agent is to train a policy over the training environments which performs well on test environments without further interaction. Existing work showed that classical offline RL fails to generalize to new, unseen environments. We propose pessimistic empirical risk minimization (PERM) and pessimistic proximal policy optimization (PPPO), which leverage pessimistic policy evaluation to guide policy learning and enhance generalization. We show that both PERM and PPPO are capable of finding a near-optimal policy with ZSG. Our result serves as a first step in understanding the foundation of the generalization phenomenon in offline reinforcement learning.

Existing work showed that classical offline RL fails to generalize to new, unseen environments. We propose pessimistic empirical risk minimization (PERM) and pessimistic proximal policy optimization (PPPO), which leverage pessimistic policy evaluation to guide policy learning and enhance generalization. We show that both PERM and PPPO are capable of finding a near-optimal policy with ZSG. Our result serves as a first step in understanding the foundation of the generalization phenomenon in offline reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning trains a policy from previously collected experiences. This paper considers a further challenge: the data comes from multiple training environments, and the resulting policy should perform well in new environments without additional interaction. This is the zero-shot generalization property the authors seek to establish.

The proposed methods are pessimistic empirical risk minimization and pessimistic proximal policy optimization, abbreviated PERM and PPPO. Both use pessimistic policy evaluation to guide policy learning. Their shared design places conservative assessment of policy value inside the learning procedure, with the aim of improving generalization beyond the environments represented during training.

The authors show that both methods can find a near-optimal policy with zero-shot generalization in the studied setting. This responds to prior findings that classical offline reinforcement learning can fail to generalize to unseen environments. The contribution is theoretical: it establishes a route to near-optimal transfer through pessimistic learning and is presented as an initial step toward understanding the foundations of generalization in offline reinforcement learning.
summary.tldr: PERM and PPPO use pessimistic policy evaluation to establish near-optimal zero-shot generalization in the studied offline reinforcement-learning setting.

title: Provable Zero-Shot Generalization in Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Open-Set Domain Adaptation (OSDA) aims to transfer knowledge from the labeled source domain to the unlabeled target domain that contains unknown categories, thus facing the challenges of domain shift and unknown category recognition. While recent works have demonstrated the potential of causality for domain alignment, little exploration has been conducted on causal-inspired theoretical frameworks for OSDA. To fill this gap, we introduce the concept of Susceptibility and propose a novel Counterfactual-based susceptibility risk framework for OSDA, termed COSDA. Specifically, COSDA consists of three novel components: (i) a Susceptibility Risk Estimator (SRE) for capturing causal information, along with comprehensive derivations of the computable theoretical upper bound, forming a risk minimization framework under the OSDA paradigm; (ii) a Contrastive Feature Alignment (CFA) module, which is theoretically proven based on mutual information to satisfy the Exogeneity assumption and facilitate cross-domain feature alignment; (iii) a Virtual Multi-unknown-categories Prototype (VMP) pseudo-labeling strategy, providing label information by measuring how similar samples are to known and multiple virtual unknown category prototypes, thereby assisting in open-set recognition and intra-class discriminative feature learning. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance.

paragraphs: Open-set domain adaptation transfers knowledge from labeled source data to unlabeled target data that also contains unfamiliar categories. A successful method must handle differences between domains while recognizing examples that do not belong to any known category. COSDA approaches these linked problems through a counterfactual framework built around a concept called susceptibility.

Its susceptibility risk estimator captures causal information and supplies a computable theoretical upper bound for risk minimization. A contrastive feature-alignment component then helps align representations across domains. The authors use mutual-information analysis to establish that this component satisfies the exogeneity assumption required by their framework, connecting the practical alignment mechanism to its theoretical basis.

For category recognition, COSDA compares examples with known-category prototypes and multiple virtual unknown-category prototypes. These comparisons provide provisional labels that support both unknown recognition and more discriminative learning within classes. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance. The approach matters because it combines a risk framework, domain alignment, and explicit treatment of multiple unknown categories within one method, rather than addressing only the shift between familiar categories.
summary.tldr: COSDA combines causal risk modeling, contrastive alignment, and virtual unknown-category prototypes for open-set domain adaptation.

title: COSDA: Counterfactual-based Susceptibility Risk Framework for Open-Set Domain Adaptation

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit impressive in-context learning (ICL) capability, enabling them to generate relevant responses from a handful of task demonstrations in the prompt. Prior studies have suggested two different explanations for the mechanisms behind ICL: induction heads that find and copy relevant tokens, and function vector (FV) heads whose activations compute a latent encoding of the ICL task. To better understand which of the two distinct mechanisms drives ICL, we study and compare induction heads and FV heads in 12 language models. Through detailed ablations, we find that few-shot ICL is driven primarily by FV heads, especially in larger models. We also find that FV and induction heads are connected: many FV heads start as induction heads during training before transitioning to the FV mechanism. This leads us to speculate that induction facilitates learning the more complex FV mechanism for ICL.

Prior studies have suggested two different explanations for the mechanisms behind ICL: induction heads that find and copy relevant tokens, and function vector (FV) heads whose activations compute a latent encoding of the ICL task. To better understand which of the two distinct mechanisms drives ICL, we study and compare induction heads and FV heads in 12 language models. Through detailed ablations, we find that few-shot ICL is driven primarily by FV heads, especially in larger models. paragraphs: In-context learning lets a language model infer a task from a few demonstrations in its prompt. Two proposed mechanisms explain this ability differently. Induction heads locate and copy relevant tokens, while function-vector heads represent the task through an internal encoding. This paper compares their roles across 12 language models.

Detailed ablation experiments indicate that function-vector heads are the primary drivers of few-shot in-context learning, particularly in larger models. Ablations test the contribution of model components by disrupting them and observing the behavioral effect. The findings therefore help distinguish components associated with in-context learning from those that contribute more strongly to its measured performance.

The authors also examine how these mechanisms develop during training. Many function-vector heads initially behave as induction heads before transitioning to the function-vector mechanism. Based on that connection, they speculate that induction helps the model learn the more complex mechanism. The developmental observation supports this possibility, while the proposed facilitating role remains an interpretation rather than an established causal conclusion.
summary.tldr: Ablations across 12 language models identify function-vector heads as the main drivers of few-shot in-context learning, especially in larger models.

title: Which Attention Heads Matter for In-Context Learning?

abstract: In this work, we study reinforcement learning (RL) with trajectory feedback. Compared to the standard RL setting, in RL with trajectory feedback, the agent only observes the accumulative reward along the trajectory, and therefore, this model is particularly suitable for scenarios where querying the reward in each single step incurs prohibitive cost. For a finite-horizon Markov Decision Process (MDP) with $S$ states, $A$ actions and a horizon length of $H$, we develop an algorithm that enjoys an asymptotically nearly optimal regret of $\tilde{O}\left(\sqrt{SAH^3K}\right)$ in $K$ episodes. To achieve this result, our new technical ingredients include (i) constructing a tighter confidence region for the reward function by incorporating the RL with trajectory feedback setting with techniques in linear bandits and (ii) constructing a reference transition model to better guide the exploration process.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning when the agent receives only the accumulated reward for an entire trajectory. Such feedback is useful when obtaining a separate reward at every step is prohibitively expensive. The challenge is to learn effective behavior from an overall outcome without directly observing each step’s reward contribution.

For a finite-horizon Markov decision process with S states, A actions, horizon H, and K episodes, the authors develop an algorithm with asymptotically nearly optimal regret of order sqrt(SAH³K), up to logarithmic factors. Regret measures cumulative performance lost relative to optimal behavior. The result describes how this learning cost scales with the problem size and the number of episodes.

Two technical ingredients support the bound. The algorithm uses ideas from linear bandits to construct a tighter confidence region for the reward function, and it builds a reference transition model to guide exploration. Together, these address uncertainty about rewards and decisions about where to explore, yielding a near-optimal theoretical guarantee despite receiving only trajectory-level reward feedback.
summary.tldr: A new algorithm achieves asymptotically nearly optimal regret when reinforcement learning receives only total rewards for complete trajectories.

title: Minimax Optimal Regret Bound for Reinforcement Learning with Trajectory Feedback

abstract: Event cameras are innovative sensors that capture brightness changes as asynchronous events rather than traditional intensity frames. These cameras offer substantial advantages over conventional cameras, including high temporal resolution, high dynamic range, and the elimination of motion blur. However, defocus blur, a common image quality degradation resulting from out-of-focus lenses, complicates the challenge of event-based imaging. Due to the unique imaging mechanism of event cameras, existing focusing algorithms struggle to operate efficiently on sparse event data. In this work, we propose EvFocus, a novel architecture designed to reconstruct sharp images from defocus event streams for the first time. Our work includes the development of an event-based out-of-focus camera model and a simulator to generate realistic defocus event streams for robust training and testing. EvDefous integrates a temporal information encoder, a blur-aware two-branch decoder, and a reconstruction and re-defocus module to effectively learn and correct defocus blur. Extensive experiments on both simulated and real-world datasets demonstrate that EvFocus outperforms existing methods across varying lighting conditions and blur sizes, proving its robustness and practical applicability in event-based defocus imaging.
