paragraphs: Event cameras record individual brightness changes asynchronously instead of capturing conventional image frames. Their imaging mechanism offers advantages for fast motion and challenging lighting, but an out-of-focus lens can still produce defocus blur. Sparse event data also make existing focusing algorithms difficult to apply efficiently. EvFocus tackles the reconstruction of sharp images from these blurred event streams.

The work combines a reconstruction architecture with an event-based model of an out-of-focus camera. A simulator uses that model to create realistic defocused event streams for training and testing. The architecture includes a temporal information encoder, a blur-aware decoder with two branches, and a reconstruction and re-defocus module for learning to correct the blur.

Experiments use both simulated and real-world data, spanning different lighting conditions and blur sizes. The authors report that EvFocus outperforms existing methods across these conditions. The results support handling lens defocus explicitly in event-based imaging, with the camera model and simulator supplying data tailored to the reconstruction problem.
summary.tldr: EvFocus combines event-camera modeling and a blur-aware network to reconstruct sharp images from out-of-focus event streams.

title: EvFocus: Learning to Reconstruct Sharp Images from Out-of-Focus Event Streams

abstract: Retrieval-augmented generative agents rely on retrieval for grounding, yet are typically evaluated on a query-by-query basis. This isolates interactions that are geometrically coupled in a shared embedding space. For example, we show that the high document density required to serve majority interests (e.g., generic "Crime" movies) can geometrically overcrowd the retrieval neighborhood of a semantically similar minority (e.g., "Film Noir"), effectively expelling minority content from top-$k$ results. We introduce a formal framework to analyze how such goal collisions in dense retrieval induce fundamental performance limits and emergent fairness issues inherent to spatial crowding. In our static analysis, we demonstrate that for a fixed embedding space, a phase transition occurs where minority user goals suffer a catastrophic collapse in performance as the density of majority goals increases. We then extend this to a dynamic model and derive a non-linear Fokker-Planck equation that governs the evolution of document embeddings as the agent updates them to maximize retrieval accuracy. Our analysis reveals that this local relevance objective triggers an emergent global mechanism that systematically marginalizes minority interests. We prove that such objectives drive the system to self-organize into a state that exclusively serves majority interests. These results provide a theoretical foundation for understanding a critical grounding failure mode in retrieval-augmented agents.

paragraphs: Retrieval queries share an embedding space, so their outcomes can be coupled even when evaluation treats them separately. This paper studies how dense collections serving majority interests can crowd out nearby minority content. For example, documents about generic crime movies can occupy retrieval neighborhoods needed to find film noir material.

The authors formalize these interactions as goal collisions. In their static analysis of a fixed embedding space, increasing majority-goal density causes a phase transition in which minority-goal performance collapses. The mechanism concerns which documents occupy the limited top-k results: spatial competition can undermine retrieval for one group as coverage for another becomes denser.

The paper then models document embeddings changing as an agent maximizes retrieval accuracy. A nonlinear Fokker–Planck equation describes this evolution. Within that dynamic framework, the authors prove that the local relevance objective drives self-organization toward a state serving only majority interests. The analysis provides a theoretical account of how a retrieval system’s shared geometry and update objective can jointly produce marginalization.
summary.tldr: A theoretical retrieval model shows how embedding-space crowding and relevance-driven updates can marginalize minority interests.

title: The Crowded Embedding Space: A Mean-Field Mechanism for Emergent Marginalization in Retrieval-Augmented Agents

abstract: Recent research has made growing efforts to leverage large language models (LLMs) for computer-aided design (CAD), a domain that demands advanced geometric and spatial reasoning across long operation sequence. However, existing studies remain limited in addressing complex modeling tasks that necessitate step-by-step reasoning, primarily due to the scarcity of high-quality CAD datasets and the absence of fine-grained evaluation frameworks. In response to these challenges, we introduce Op-CAD, the first large-scale, multi-modal dataset for operation-oriented CAD generation, encompassing four operation types and five modalities. Furthermore, we introduce a novel CAD parsing module together with a geometry-guided hierarchical annotation pipeline, which decomposes modeling sequences into discrete operations and substantially improves the annotation accuracy of Vision-Language Models (VLMs). Based on our dataset, we redefine the CAD modeling task by decoupling geometric and spatial perspectives and introduce a novel metric, Chamfer/Fillet Intersection over Union (CF-IoU), to fill the void in assessing chamfer and fillet operations. By comprehensively evaluating eight LLMs on Op-CAD, we establish a benchmark for current models on operation-oriented tasks. Finally, we investigate performance enhancement strategies through fine-tuning on Op-CAD and propose Chain-of-Operation (COOP), a novel prompting strategy that emulates human-engineer reasoning.

paragraphs: Computer-aided design requires geometric and spatial reasoning across sequences of modeling operations. Existing language-model research in this area has been constrained by limited datasets and evaluation tools for complex, step-by-step tasks. Op-CAD addresses these needs with a large multimodal dataset covering four operation types and five modalities.

The authors introduce a CAD parsing module and a geometry-guided hierarchical annotation pipeline that break modeling sequences into individual operations. This improves the annotation accuracy of vision-language models. They also separate geometric and spatial perspectives in the task definition and introduce CF-IoU, a metric designed to evaluate chamfer and fillet operations.

The paper further investigates fine-tuning on Op-CAD and introduces Chain-of-Operation prompting, which emulates human-engineer reasoning. Together, the dataset, annotations, and metric make it possible to study the sequence of modeling decisions more directly. The enhancement strategies extend that evaluation effort toward improving how models reason through CAD operations.
summary.tldr: Op-CAD provides data, operation-level evaluation, and reasoning strategies for language-model CAD generation.

title: Op-CAD: Benchmarking and Investigating Operation-oriented CAD Generation

abstract: Cross-validation (CV) is known to provide asymptotically exact tests and confidence intervals for model improvement but only when the model comparison is relatively stable. Surprisingly, we prove that even simple, individually stable models can generate relatively unstable comparisons, calling into question the validity of CV inference. Specifically, we show that the Lasso and its close cousin, soft-thresholding, generate relatively unstable comparisons and invalid CV inferences, even in the most favorable of learning settings and when both models are individually stable. These findings highlight the importance of verifying relative stability before deploying CV for model comparison.
originalAbstract: Cross-validation (CV) is known to provide asymptotically exact tests and confidence intervals for model improvement but only when the model comparison is relatively stable. Surprisingly, we prove that even simple, individually stable models can generate relatively unstable comparisons, calling into question the validity of CV inference. Specifically, we show that the Lasso and its close cousin, soft-thresholding, generate relatively unstable comparisons and invalid CV inferences, even in the most favorable of learning settings and when both models are individually stable. These findings highlight the importance of verifying relative stability before deploying CV for model comparison.

paragraphs: Cross-validation can be used to make statistical claims about whether one model improves on another. Its asymptotically exact tests and confidence intervals depend on relative stability of the comparison. This paper examines whether stability of the individual models is enough to support that requirement.

The authors prove that even simple models that are individually stable can produce relatively unstable comparisons. Their examples involve the Lasso and the closely related soft-thresholding method. In the settings they analyze, relative instability leads to invalid cross-validation inference, even under favorable learning conditions and despite both models being stable on their own.

The result separates two questions that can easily be conflated: whether each model behaves stably and whether their comparison supports valid statistical inference. Confidence in the first does not establish the second. The practical implication is to verify relative stability before using cross-validation tests or confidence intervals to claim improvement. The paper's warning concerns the validity of those comparisons, showing that individual-model stability cannot substitute for the comparison-specific condition.
summary.tldr: Individually stable models can yield unstable comparisons and invalid cross-validation inference, so relative stability must be checked separately.

title: The Relative Instability of Model Comparison with Cross-validation

abstract: Softmax attention is a central component of transformer architectures, yet its nonlinear structure poses significant challenges for theoretical analysis. We develop a unified, measure-based framework for studying single-layer softmax attention under both finite and infinite prompts. For i.i.d. centered Gaussian inputs, we lean on the fact that the softmax operator converges in the infinite-prompt limit to a linear operator acting on the underlying input-token measure. Building on this insight, we establish non-asymptotic concentration bounds for the output and gradient of softmax attention, quantifying how rapidly the finite-prompt model approaches its infinite-prompt counterpart, and prove that this concentration remains stable along the entire training trajectory in general in-context learning settings with sub-Gaussian tokens. In the case of in-context linear regression, we use the tractable infinite-prompt dynamics to analyze training at finite prompt length. Our results allow optimization analyses developed for linear attention to transfer directly to softmax attention when prompts are sufficiently long, showing that large-prompt softmax attention inherits the analytical structure of its linear counterpart. This, in turn, provides a principled and broadly applicable toolkit for studying the training dynamics and statistical behavior of softmax attention layers in large prompt regimes.

paragraphs: Softmax attention is difficult to analyze because of its nonlinear structure. This paper studies a single attention layer by representing input tokens through a probability measure, allowing finite prompts and an infinite-prompt limit to be treated within one framework. For independent, identically distributed centered Gaussian inputs, the limiting softmax operator acts linearly on the input-token measure.

The authors quantify the connection to finite prompts through non-asymptotic concentration bounds on both outputs and gradients. These bounds describe how quickly a finite-prompt model approaches the limiting one. They also prove that concentration remains stable throughout training in general in-context learning settings with sub-Gaussian tokens, making the connection relevant to learning dynamics rather than only a fixed model.

For in-context linear regression, the tractable infinite-prompt dynamics support analysis of training at finite prompt lengths. When prompts are sufficiently long, optimization analyses for linear attention can transfer to softmax attention under the paper's framework. The result provides a route to understanding softmax training through a simpler limiting structure, while retaining explicit input assumptions and prompt-length conditions.
summary.tldr: Under stated input assumptions, long-prompt softmax attention approaches a linear limit that makes its outputs, gradients, and training dynamics tractable.

title: Softmax as Linear Attention in the Large-Prompt Regime: a Measure-based Perspective

abstract: This paper introduces Probabilistic Multi-Variable Branching (PMVB), a simple and effective technique for accelerating mixed-integer optimization using data-driven machine learning models. At its core, PMVB employs a multi-variable branching procedure that partitions the feasible region via data-driven hyperplanes and requires only two lines of code to implement. Moreover, PMVB is model-agnostic and compatible with a wide range of machine learning models. Leveraging tools from statistical learning theory, we develop interpretable hyperparameter selection strategies and propose several extensions to further enhance performance. We evaluate PMVB by integrating it into state-of-the-art MIP solvers and conducting experiments on both classical benchmark datasets and real-world instances. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of PMVB in improving MIP-solving efficiency.

paragraphs: Probabilistic Multi-Variable Branching, or PMVB, uses machine learning to accelerate mixed-integer optimization. Its intervention is in branching: the process of dividing the feasible region into smaller regions for the solver to investigate. The method uses data-driven hyperplanes involving multiple variables to determine these divisions.

The central design is deliberately compact, with the core branching procedure described as requiring only two lines of code. PMVB is also model-agnostic, allowing different machine learning models to supply the information used for branching. This separates the solver integration from the choice of predictive model and makes the procedure applicable across a range of learning approaches.

The authors use statistical learning theory to derive interpretable strategies for choosing hyperparameters, and propose extensions intended to improve performance further. They evaluate PMVB inside state-of-the-art mixed-integer programming solvers on both classical benchmarks and real-world instances. The reported results show improved solving efficiency. The paper therefore connects a small change in how the search space is divided with a theory-guided way to configure that change.
summary.tldr: PMVB accelerates mixed-integer solvers by using machine-learning-informed hyperplanes to branch on multiple variables.

title: Data-driven Mixed Integer Optimization through Probabilistic Multi-variable Branching

abstract: In this paper, we study cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) where the joint reward exhibits submodularity, which is a natural property capturing diminishing marginal returns when adding agents to a team. Unlike standard MARL with additive rewards, submodular rewards model realistic scenarios where agent contributions overlap (e.g., multi-drone surveillance, collaborative exploration). We provide the first formal framework for this setting and develop algorithms with provable guarantees on sample efficiency and regret bound. For known dynamics, our greedy policy optimization achieves a $1/2$-approximation with polynomial complexity in the number of agents $K$, overcoming the exponential curse of dimensionality inherent in joint policy optimization. For unknown dynamics, we propose a UCB-based learning algorithm achieving a $1/2$-regret of $O(H^2KS\sqrt{AT})$ over $T$ episodes.

paragraphs: This paper studies cooperative reinforcement learning when adding another agent produces diminishing returns. That reward structure, called submodularity, captures overlapping contributions: several surveillance drones or exploring agents may provide some of the same benefit. Treating team reward as a simple sum misses this overlap.

The authors formalize this setting and develop algorithms for both known and unknown dynamics. When dynamics are known, greedy policy optimization achieves a one-half approximation with computational complexity polynomial in the number of agents. This gives a guaranteed fraction of optimal performance while avoiding the exponential dependence associated with joint policy optimization.

When dynamics are unknown, the proposed learning algorithm uses upper confidence bounds and achieves a stated one-half-regret bound over repeated episodes. This measures learning performance against an approximation benchmark rather than promising convergence to the unrestricted optimum. The contribution is theoretical: it connects the diminishing-returns structure of team rewards to tractable optimization and guarantees on learning efficiency.
summary.tldr: Submodular team rewards enable cooperative reinforcement-learning algorithms with polynomial optimization and provable approximation and regret guarantees.

title: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Submodular Reward

abstract: Multi-task learning (MTL) has emerged as a pivotal paradigm in machine learning by leveraging shared structures across multiple related tasks. Despite its empirical success, the development of likelihood-based efficiently solvable algorithms—even for shared linear representations—remains largely underdeveloped, primarily due to the non-convex structure intrinsic to matrix factorization. This paper introduces a first-order algorithm that jointly learns a shared representation and task-specific parameters, with guaranteed efficiency. Notably, it converges in $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(1)$ iterations and attains a near-optimal estimation error of $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(dk/(TN))$, improving over existing likelihood-based methods by a factor of $k$, where $d$, $k$, $T$, $N$ denote input dimension, representation dimension, task count, and samples per task, respectively. Our results justify that likelihood-based first-order methods can efficiently solve the MTL problem.

paragraphs: Multi-task learning can improve estimation by letting related tasks share a representation while retaining their own parameters. Even with a linear shared representation, jointly learning these pieces produces a non-convex matrix-factorization problem. The paper addresses whether likelihood-based methods can solve this problem efficiently with strong statistical guarantees.

The authors introduce a first-order algorithm that learns the shared representation and task-specific parameters together. They establish a convergence bound of approximately constant iterations with logarithmic factors suppressed. Its estimation error scales as dk divided by TN, again up to logarithmic factors, where d is input dimension, k is representation dimension, T is the number of tasks, and N is the number of samples per task.

The reported error is near-optimal and improves on existing likelihood-based methods by a factor of k. The bound makes the value of shared data explicit: more tasks and more samples per task improve estimation relative to the dimensions being learned. The result establishes computational and statistical efficiency for the studied shared-linear-representation problem.
summary.tldr: A first-order likelihood-based algorithm jointly learns shared linear representations and task parameters with near-optimal estimation error.

title: Near-Optimal and Efficient First-Order Algorithm for Multi-Task Learning with Shared Linear Representation

abstract: Fake Image Detection (FID), aiming at unified detection across four image forensic subdomains, is critical in real-world forensic scenarios. Compared with ensemble approaches, monolithic FID models are theoretically more promising, but to date, consistently yield inferior performance in practice. In this work, we identify the intrinsic distinctness of artifacts across subdomains—a critical barrier we term the "Ji-Zhe phenomenon". Driven by this phenomenon, we diagnose the cause of this underperformance for the first time: the collapse of the artifact feature space. The core challenge for developing a practical monolithic FID model thus boils down to the "unified-yet-discriminative" reconstruction of the artifact feature space. To address this paradoxical challenge, we hypothesize that high-level semantics can serve as a structural prior for the reconstruction, and further propose Semantic-Induced Constrained Adaptation (SICA), the first monolithic FID paradigm. Extensive experiments on our $ \textit{OpenMMSec} $ dataset demonstrate that SICA outperforms 15 state-of-the-art methods and reconstructs the target unified-yet-discriminative artifact feature space in a near-orthogonal manner, thus firmly validating our hypothesis. The code and dataset will be made publicly available.

paragraphs: The paper asks how one fake-image detector can work across four forensic subdomains. Although a single model is presented as theoretically promising, such models have performed worse in practice than ensemble approaches. The authors attribute this problem to the distinct kinds of artifacts found in different subdomains, a difference they name the Ji-Zhe phenomenon.

Their diagnosis is that combining these tasks can collapse the artifact feature space: the representation loses distinctions needed for detection. The desired representation must therefore support shared detection while retaining differences among artifact types. The authors hypothesize that high-level semantic information can supply structure for rebuilding this space, and introduce Semantic-Induced Constrained Adaptation, or SICA, around that idea.

On the authors’ OpenMMSec dataset, SICA outperforms 15 state-of-the-art methods. Their experiments also show a reconstructed artifact space with a near-orthogonal organization, supporting the proposed role of semantic structure. The significance is that unified detection need not depend on merging all artifact information into an indistinct representation; the reported approach preserves discriminative structure within one model.
summary.tldr: SICA uses semantic structure to help one fake-image detector preserve distinct artifact features across four forensic subdomains.

title: Can We Build a Monolithic Model for Fake Image Detection? SICA: Semantic-Induced Constrained Adaptation for Unified-Yet-Discriminative Artifact Feature Space Reconstruction

abstract: Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) has been widely applied to automated aircraft conflict resolution due to its strong capability for cooperative control and distributed decision-making. However, existing approaches typically assume a fixed number of aircraft and neglect the unique characteristics of air traffic control instructions. This structural misalignment between model architectures and domain requirements leads to severe deficiencies in perception scalability and action stability across scenarios of varying scales. To address these challenges, we propose Structural-Aligned Reinforcement Learning (SARL), which aims to bridge the gap between perception and action. First, the Physics-Encoded Relational Graph (PERG) effectively resolves the fixed input dimensionality issue by incorporating physical inductive biases into a graph attention mechanism. Second, we design the Sparse Cognitive Mixture-of-Experts (SC-MoE) to enhance decision stability. In addition, we introduce a Kinematic Kafety Shield (KSS) based on aviation rules, which not only improves inference-time safety but also effectively guides the model to generate semantically meaningful actions that comply with aviation standards. Simulation experiment results demonstrate that SARL significantly outperforms existing reinforcement learning baselines across diverse scenarios in terms of both success rate and operational efficiency.

paragraphs: Automated aircraft conflict resolution requires decisions that remain useful as the number of aircraft changes and that fit the structure of air traffic control instructions. The paper argues that reinforcement-learning approaches often assume a fixed aircraft count and overlook instruction characteristics. These mismatches undermine both the scalability of perception and the stability of actions.

SARL addresses these requirements with three coordinated components. A Physics-Encoded Relational Graph incorporates physical inductive biases into graph attention to overcome fixed input dimensionality. A Sparse Cognitive Mixture-of-Experts improves decision stability. An aviation-rule-based kinematic shield improves inference-time safety and guides the model toward meaningful actions that comply with aviation standards.

Simulation experiments show significant improvements over existing reinforcement-learning baselines in success rate and operational efficiency across diverse scenarios. The contribution links variable-size perception, stable decision-making, and domain-constrained action generation within one framework. The reported evidence is specifically from simulation, where aligning these parts with airspace requirements improves the system's ability to handle scenarios at different scales.
summary.tldr: SARL combines physics-informed graph perception, expert-based decisions, and an aviation-rule shield to improve aircraft conflict resolution in simulation.

title: SARL: Structure-Aligned Reinforcement Learning for Bridging the Perception-Action Gap in Airspace

abstract: We consider the problem of universal transductive online classification with a possibly unbounded label space. This setting considers online learning, with the sequence of instances (without labels) known to the learner in advance. We say a concept class $\mathcal{H}$ is learnable if there is a learning algorithm $\mathcal{A}$, such that for every realizable sequence, the number of mistakes made by $\mathcal{A}$ grows at most sublinearly with the number of predictions. We characterize the learnability of this setting and show that there are only two possible optimal rates for the learnable classes: either bounded or increasing logarithmically. We introduce a new combinatorial structure, called "Level-Constrained-Littlestone-Littlestone (LCLL) tree", which, along with the indifference property, characterizes the learnability. We also extend the learnability result to the agnostic case and the case where only the stochastic process that generates the instance sequence is known.

paragraphs: This paper studies online classification when the learner knows the entire sequence of inputs beforehand but does not know their labels. The label space may be unbounded. Advance access to the inputs makes the setting transductive, while predictions still occur online. The central question is which concept classes permit the learner's mistakes to grow sublinearly.

For the main realizable setting, the required guarantee must hold for every sequence consistent with the concept class. Sublinear mistake growth means that the fraction of incorrect predictions tends toward zero. The authors characterize learnability using a new combinatorial structure called a Level-Constrained-Littlestone-Littlestone tree, together with an indifference property.

The characterization yields a sharp conclusion about optimal mistake rates for learnable classes: they are either bounded or grow logarithmically. Thus, under this formulation, learnable classes do not exhibit an unrestricted range of optimal sublinear rates. The paper also extends its learnability result to the agnostic case and to a setting where the learner knows only the stochastic process generating the input sequence, rather than the sequence itself.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes transductive online multiclass learnability and shows that learnable classes have bounded or logarithmic optimal mistake rates.

title: Universal Multiclass Transductive Online Learning

abstract: Modern Hopfield Networks (MHNs) have achieved widespread success across various domains but are confined to Euclidean/Hilbert spaces, failing to preserve the hierarchical structure of data due to geometric constraints—arbitrary tree structures cannot be embedded with low distortion, while hyperbolic spaces can naturally accommodate hierarchical structures through exponential volume growth. To address this issue, we propose Hyperbolic Associative Memory Networks (HAMNs), the first framework to embed modern associative memory into hyperbolic space: we map query and memory vectors from Euclidean space to a constant negative curvature manifold via exponential maps, define a regularized energy function based on the Minkowski inner product, and adopt curvature-aware Riemannian optimization combined with exponential map updates to achieve stable on-manifold retrieval. We put forward a hierarchy-sensitivity hypothesis—HAMNs outperform Euclidean MHNs on data with deep hierarchies but exhibit comparable performance on data with weak or shallow hierarchies, which is validated by depth-controlled experiments and cross-level metrics. As a plug-and-play, model-agnostic module, HAMNs are suitable for the storage and retrieval of representations in task architectures requiring hierarchical understanding, instantiated with the Poincaré ball in experiments, and also applicable to any hyperbolic model with constant negative curvature. The code is available at https://github.com/hbl66/HAMNs.

Modern Hopfield Networks perform this operation in Euclidean or Hilbert spaces, whose geometry can distort deep hierarchical relationships. This paper develops Hyperbolic Associative Memory Networks to use a space whose exponential volume growth can accommodate branching structures more naturally.

The framework maps query and memory vectors into a manifold with constant negative curvature through exponential maps. It defines a regularized retrieval energy using the Minkowski inner product and applies curvature-aware Riemannian optimization. Exponential-map updates keep retrieval on the manifold, making the geometry part of the memory operation itself rather than merely a representation chosen beforehand.

The authors test a hierarchy-sensitivity hypothesis: hyperbolic memory should outperform Euclidean memory on deeply hierarchical data while performing comparably on weak or shallow hierarchies. Experiments controlling hierarchy depth and using cross-level metrics support that pattern. The module is presented as model-agnostic and suitable for integration into architectures requiring hierarchical understanding. Experiments use the Poincaré ball, while the framework also applies to other constant-negative-curvature hyperbolic models.
summary.tldr: Hyperbolic Associative Memory Networks adapt memory retrieval to hierarchical geometry, with benefits demonstrated especially for deep hierarchies.

title: Hyperbolic Associative Memory Networks

abstract: In real-world scenarios, multi-view data often exhibits significant imbalance in missing patterns across views, where observation rates vary substantially among different views. Such observation bias makes it difficult for cross-view associations learned from limited complete samples to generalize to incomplete samples, leading to challenging cross-view recovery. Meanwhile, observation bias acts as a confounder, causing clustering predictions to spuriously depend on low-missing-rate views. To address these challenges, we propose CIMLN, a novel Causal-Invariant Meta-Learning Network that alleviates observation bias for unbalanced incomplete multi-view clustering. The context-aware meta-generation module formulates view recovery as a meta-learning task, enabling rapid adaptation to incomplete samples by encoding global statistical relationships through context information. The causal-invariant structure learning module constructs counterfactual scenarios by artificially masking low-missing-rate views, enforcing clustering consistency across different observation patterns. Extensive experiments on eight benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of CIMLN. The code is available at https://github.com/jinjiaqi1998/CIMLN.

paragraphs: When the same samples have several views, some views may be missing much more often than others. This imbalance creates two problems: relationships learned from fully observed samples may transfer poorly to incomplete ones, and clustering may depend too heavily on whichever views are usually available. CIMLN addresses both consequences of this observation bias.

Its recovery component treats reconstructing missing views as a meta-learning problem. Context information encodes statistical relationships across the data, helping the model adapt to incomplete samples. The aim is to make recovery responsive to the observed context instead of relying only on associations learned from the limited complete samples.

A second component deliberately masks views that ordinarily have few missing observations. These artificial counterfactual scenarios change what is visible while encouraging consistent clustering predictions. Together, the components target recovery quality and dependence on observation patterns. Experiments on eight benchmarks support the effectiveness of the combined approach for unbalanced incomplete multi-view clustering.
summary.tldr: CIMLN combines context-based missing-view recovery with clustering consistency across masking patterns to reduce observation bias.

title: Alleviating Observation Bias via Causal-Invariant Meta-Learning for Unbalanced Incomplete Multi-view Clustering

abstract: Fine-tuning lets practitioners repurpose aligned large language models (LLMs) for new domains, yet recent work reveals emergent misalignment (EM): Even a small, domain-specific fine-tune can induce harmful behaviors far outside the target domain. Even in the case where model weights are hidden behind a fine-tuning API, this gives attackers inadvertent access to a broadly misaligned model in a way that can be hard to detect from the fine-tuning data alone. We present the first systematic study of in-training safeguards against EM that are practical for providers who expose fine-tuning via an API: We evaluate whether they a) prevent broad misalignment, b) allow narrow misalignment, c) learn well on benign tasks, and d) remain coherent. We investigate five training regularization interventions: (i) KL-divergence regularization toward a safe reference model, (ii) $\ell_2$ distance in feature space, (iii) preventive steering with an evil persona vector, (iv) interleaving training examples from a general instruct-tuning dataset and (v) inoculation prompting. We demonstrate that selecting interleaving data by the perplexity gap between aligned and misaligned models yields the best results overall.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning an aligned language model on a narrow domain can sometimes produce harmful behavior well beyond that domain. This emergent misalignment can arise even through an API that hides model weights, and the fine-tuning examples alone may make the broader risk difficult to detect. The paper studies safeguards applied during training.

The evaluation considers four properties: preventing broad misalignment, allowing narrow misalignment, learning benign tasks, and maintaining coherent outputs. Five interventions are compared: regularization toward a safe reference model using KL divergence, feature-space distance penalties, preventive steering with an evil-persona vector, interleaving general instruction examples, and inoculation prompting. This makes the comparison sensitive to adaptation quality as well as broad behavioral changes.

The strongest overall results come from interleaving data selected using the perplexity gap between aligned and misaligned models. That gap guides which general instruction examples enter training. The finding highlights the importance of selecting the interleaved data, rather than treating all such examples as interchangeable. The abstract reports this as the best overall intervention among those studied, not as a guarantee that fine-tuning cannot produce misalignment.
summary.tldr: Among five training safeguards, interleaving instruction data selected by aligned–misaligned perplexity gaps gives the best overall results against emergent misalignment.

title: In-Training Defenses Against Emergent Misalignment in Language Models

abstract: Pre-trained models with parameter-efficient fine-tuning have shown strong effectiveness in Class-Incremental Learning (CIL), which seeks to balance model plasticity and stability. In this context, orthogonality constraints can significantly enhance model stability, yet their reliance on subspace inevitably compromises model plasticity over long tasks. To address this, we propose Gradient-Recycling Low-Rank Adaptation (GR-LoRA), which reconciles stability and plasticity by recycling the gradients discarded in orthogonal projection. Specifically, GR-LoRA recycles post-decomposition non-orthogonal gradient components into task-specific lightweight modules and selects optimal module via entropy to improve plasticity, while incorporating local and global mismatch suppression to preserve stability by synthesizing out-of-distribution representations across all tasks. Theoretical analysis confirms that this recycling strategy preserves stability and improves plasticity. Experimental results from multiple CIL benchmarks verify the effectiveness and general applicability of GR-LoRA.

paragraphs: Class-incremental learning must acquire new categories without damaging previously learned ones. Orthogonal gradient constraints help preserve old knowledge but can leave less room for learning as tasks accumulate. GR-LoRA aims to recover some of that lost adaptability by reusing gradient components that orthogonal projection would discard.

The method directs those nonorthogonal components into lightweight task-specific modules and uses entropy to select a suitable module. Local and global mismatch suppression, supported by synthesized out-of-distribution representations across tasks, helps preserve stability. This separates where potentially conflicting updates are stored while still letting them contribute to new-task learning.

Theoretical analysis supports improved plasticity with retained stability, and multiple class-incremental benchmarks validate the approach. The contribution is a parameter-efficient mechanism for managing the stability–plasticity tension. The abstract does not claim that all forgetting disappears indefinitely or specify how module storage grows across arbitrarily long task sequences.
summary.tldr: GR-LoRA recycles otherwise discarded gradient components into lightweight modules to balance new-class learning with retention.

title: GR-LoRA: Gradient-Recycling Low-Rank Adaptation for Class-Incremental Learning

abstract: World models require robust relational understanding to support prediction, reasoning, and control. While object-centric representations provide a useful abstraction, they are not sufficient to capture interaction-dependent dynamics. We therefore propose C-JEPA, a simple and flexible object-centric world model that extends masked joint embedding prediction from image patches to object-centric representations. By masking object-level latents and requiring each masked object state to be inferred from the surrounding context, C-JEPA imposes structured partial observability during training, creating counterfactual-like prediction queries that discourage shortcut solutions and make interaction-dependent prediction necessary under the learning objective. Empirically, C-JEPA leads to consistent gains in visual question answering, with an absolute improvement of about 20% in counterfactual reasoning over the same architecture without object-level masking. On agent control tasks, C-JEPA enables substantially more efficient planning by using only 1% of the total latent input features required by patch-based world models, while achieving comparable performance. Finally, we provide a formal analysis demonstrating that object-level masking induces useful inductive bias by controlling observability. Our code is available at https://github.com/galilai-group/cjepa.

paragraphs: A world model needs to understand how objects interact to support prediction, reasoning, and control. Simply representing objects separately does not ensure that it learns those interactions. C-JEPA addresses this by hiding selected object representations during training and asking the model to infer the missing object states from the surrounding context.

This extends masked joint embedding prediction from image patches to object-level representations. The masking creates structured partial observability: the model cannot directly access every object state needed for its prediction. According to the authors, the resulting counterfactual-like queries discourage shortcuts and make interaction-dependent prediction necessary under the training objective. A formal analysis explains the inductive bias produced by controlling observability.

Experiments show consistent visual-question-answering gains, including about 20% absolute improvement in counterfactual reasoning over the same architecture without object masking. In control tasks, C-JEPA achieves comparable performance while using only 1% of the latent input features required by patch-based world models. These results connect the training intervention to both stronger relational reasoning and more efficient planning.
summary.tldr: C-JEPA masks object representations to encourage interaction-aware prediction, improving counterfactual reasoning and reducing planning input requirements.

title: Causal-JEPA: Learning World Models through Object-Level Latent Masking

abstract: We present Mesh Field Theory (MeshFT) and its neural realization, MeshFT-Net: a structure-preserving framework for mesh-based continuum physics that cleanly separates the physics’ topological structure from its metric structure. Imposing minimal physical principles (locality, permutation equivariance, orientation covariance, and energy balance/dissipation inequality), we prove a reduction theorem for mesh-based physics. Under these conditions, the physical dynamics admit a local factorization into a port–Hamiltonian form: the conservative interconnection is fixed uniquely by mesh topology, whereas metric effects enter only through constitutive relations and dissipation. This reduction clarifies what must be fixed and what should be learned, directly informing MeshFT-Net’s design. Across evaluations on analytic and realistic datasets, physics-consistency tests, and out-of-distribution validation, MeshFT-Net achieves near-zero energy drift and strong physical fidelity (correct dispersion and momentum conservation) along with robust extrapolation and high data efficiency. By eliminating non-physical degrees of freedom and learning only metric-dependent structure, MeshFT provides a principled inductive bias for stable, faithful, and data-efficient learning-based physical simulation.

paragraphs: Mesh-based physical simulation combines how elements connect with geometric and material information. Mesh Field Theory separates these roles so a learned simulator can preserve physical structure. The paper starts from locality, permutation equivariance, orientation covariance, and an energy balance or dissipation requirement, then asks what form the dynamics must take under those conditions.

Its reduction theorem gives a local port–Hamiltonian factorization. The mesh topology uniquely fixes the conservative interconnection, while metric effects enter through constitutive relations and dissipation. This distinction tells the neural realization, MeshFT-Net, which structure to keep fixed and which parts to learn, reducing nonphysical freedom in the model.

Evaluations include analytic and realistic datasets, physical consistency checks, and tests outside the training distribution. MeshFT-Net exhibits near-zero energy drift, correct dispersion and momentum conservation, robust extrapolation, and high data efficiency. The findings support using the theorem's conditional structural decomposition as an inductive bias for learning stable physical dynamics while concentrating learning on metric-dependent behavior.
summary.tldr: MeshFT separates topology-fixed physical structure from learnable metric effects, enabling simulations with strong physical fidelity and near-zero energy drift.

title: Mesh Field Theory: Port–Hamiltonian Formulation of Mesh-Based Physics

abstract: While continuous diffusion has shown remarkable success in continuous domains such as image generation, its direct application to discrete data has underperformed pure discrete formulations. To understand this gap, we introduce token identifiability, an analytical framework characterizing how Gaussian noise corrupts discrete data through two mechanisms: discrete identity corruption and continuous rank degradation. We reveal that these mechanisms scale differently with vocabulary size, creating a temporal dissonance that forces a tradeoff between learning continuous geometry and discrete structure. To address this, we propose CANDI (Continuous ANd DIscrete diffusion), a hybrid framework that decouples discrete and continuous corruption, enabling simultaneous learning of both. This unlocks the benefits of continuous diffusion for discrete spaces: on controlled generation, CANDI enables classifier-based guidance with off-the-shelf classifiers through simple gradient addition; on text generation, CANDI outperforms masked diffusion at low NFE, demonstrating the value of learning continuous gradients for discrete spaces.

paragraphs: Continuous diffusion works well for images, but applying it directly to discrete tokens has lagged behind purely discrete approaches. This paper examines the mismatch through token identifiability: how adding Gaussian noise affects the ability to distinguish tokens. Its analysis separates damage to discrete token identity from degradation of continuous rank structure.

These two forms of corruption respond differently to vocabulary size. As a result, their progression through the noise process becomes misaligned, creating a tradeoff between learning continuous geometry and learning discrete structure. CANDI addresses this by separating the discrete and continuous corruption processes so the model can learn both kinds of information together.

The reported benefits appear in controlled generation and text generation. CANDI can incorporate guidance from existing classifiers by adding their gradients, making continuous control available within a discrete generation setting. It also outperforms masked diffusion when the number of model evaluations is low. That finding supports the value of continuous gradients for efficient discrete generation in the evaluated regime.
summary.tldr: CANDI separates discrete and continuous corruption to improve token generation and enable straightforward classifier guidance.

title: CANDI: Hybrid Discrete-Continuous Diffusion Models

abstract: Vision Transformers increasingly incorporate extra tokens beyond patch tokens—from class tokens for aggregation to register tokens for artifact mitigation. While effective for their intended purposes, these tokens typically lack semantic structure. We ask a more ambitious question: Can we design regularization constraints that transform extra tokens into disentangled representations, enabling them to decompose images into semantic parts (e.g., heads, bodies, legs) without explicit supervision? We propose XTRA, an intuitive yet powerful framework that augments Vision Transformers with dedicated “factor tokens” and enforces disentanglement via a novel Minimum Volume Constraint (MVC). A multi-stage aggregation process further enforces these factor tokens into semantically pure components, preventing token collapse that often occurs when training with MVC alone. On ImageNet-1K, XTRA achieves superior disentanglement (8.4$\times$ improvement in SEPIN@1 over DINOv2) while simultaneously improving representation quality: KNN accuracy improves by 5.8% and linear-probe accuracy by 2.3%.

paragraphs: Vision Transformers often include extra tokens for aggregation or artifact reduction, but those tokens usually lack a clear semantic organization. XTRA asks whether dedicated extra tokens can instead learn separate meaningful parts of an image, such as heads, bodies, and legs, without explicit supervision for those parts.

The framework adds factor tokens and trains them with a Minimum Volume Constraint intended to encourage disentanglement. That constraint alone can cause token collapse, so XTRA also uses multi-stage aggregation to promote semantically pure components. The combination addresses both separation between factors and the need for those factors to retain useful, distinct content.

On ImageNet-1K, XTRA reports an 8.4-fold improvement over DINOv2 in the SEPIN@1 disentanglement measure. It also improves KNN accuracy by 5.8% and linear-probe accuracy by 2.3%, as reported in the abstract. These results suggest that organizing extra tokens into semantic factors can improve representation quality alongside disentanglement, making the added structure useful for more than interpreting image components.
summary.tldr: XTRA trains extra Vision Transformer tokens to represent distinct semantic parts, improving disentanglement and representation quality on ImageNet-1K.

title: The Extra Tokens Matter: Disentangled Representation Learning with Vision Transformers

abstract: While text-to-image diffusion models achieve remarkable generation quality, they inadvertently memorize sensitive content, necessitating machine unlearning to prevent undesired outputs. However, existing unlearning methods rely on suboptimal surrogate objectives rather than directly optimizing the unlearning goal, leading to fundamental objective mismatch. Moreover, these methods preserve model utility via surface-level constraints on model parameters or outputs, yet fail to capture the intrinsic generative dynamics of diffusion models, consequently triggering catastrophic forgetting. To address these challenges, we propose Preference-calibrated Optimization with Score-level Distribution Alignment (POSDA), a unified unlearning framework that harmonizes effective erasure with fine-grained structural preservation. Specifically, we reframe unlearning as a preference optimization problem by constructing a reward that explicitly quantifies the unlearning objective. Additionally, we introduce score-level distribution alignment to ensure the invariance of the underlying manifold topology of the unlearned model, thereby preventing distributional drift. Extensive experiments across object, style, and NSFW unlearning tasks demonstrate that POSDA achieves state-of-the-art erasure efficacy while maintaining superior model utility compared to existing methods.

paragraphs: Removing unwanted content from a text-to-image diffusion model must also preserve its useful generation abilities. This paper identifies two obstacles: training objectives that only indirectly represent the desired removal, and preservation constraints that overlook the model's underlying generative dynamics. The latter can allow broad forgetting while the model is being edited.

POSDA addresses both within one framework. It expresses unlearning as preference optimization, using a reward designed to directly quantify the removal objective. It also aligns distributions at the score level to preserve the topology of the model's underlying generative structure and prevent distributional drift. This makes preservation part of how the generative process is constrained, beyond restrictions on parameters or final outputs.

Experiments cover removing objects, styles, and NSFW content. The authors report state-of-the-art erasure effectiveness together with stronger retained utility than existing methods. These results support combining a more directly targeted unlearning objective with preservation of diffusion structure, allowing the evaluated models to remove unwanted concepts while maintaining more of their useful behavior.
summary.tldr: POSDA combines preference-based content removal with score-level distribution alignment to improve diffusion-model unlearning while preserving utility.

title: Preference-Calibrated Optimization with Score-Level Distribution Alignment for Text-to-Image Diffusion Model Unlearning

abstract: Traditional 3D visual grounding typically assumes that natural language expressions unambiguously refer to target objects in a 3D scene. However, in practical applications, human instructions are often ambiguous or insufficient, which may lead existing models to associate the query with multiple possible objects, resulting in incorrect results. In this paper, we propose a new task, 3D visual grounding with referential ambiguity, which allows for referential ambiguity in language descriptions, making it more broadly applicable to real-world scenarios. To tackle this task, we propose an interactive grounding framework that performs multi-round question-answer interactions, in which the model actively generates clarifying questions and receives human-provided answers to acquire additional object attributes, spatial relationships, and other contextual information, thereby resolving referential ambiguity and achieving accurate grounding. To support the learning of interactive grounding, we construct a large-scale dataset named AmbiRefer3D, which contains 47,085 samples with 141,255 annotations of question-answer dialogues that capture interactive disambiguation processes, covering 7,316 indoor 3D scenes. Furthermore, we establish multi-round evaluation metrics to measure both disambiguation efficiency and grounding accuracy. The code is available at https://github.com/yearnallover/AmbiRefer3D.

In this paper, we propose a new task, 3D visual grounding with referential ambiguity, which allows for referential ambiguity in language descriptions, making it more broadly applicable to real-world scenarios. To tackle this task, we propose an interactive grounding framework that performs multi-round question-answer interactions, in which the model actively generates clarifying questions and receives human-provided answers to acquire additional object attributes, spatial relationships, and other contextual information, thereby resolving referential ambiguity and achieving accurate grounding. To support the learning of interactive grounding, we construct a large-scale dataset named AmbiRefer3D, which contains 47,085 samples with 141,255 annotations of question-answer dialogues that capture interactive disambiguation processes, covering 7,316 indoor 3D scenes. Furthermore, we establish multi-round evaluation metrics to measure both disambiguation efficiency and grounding accuracy. The code is available at https://github.com/yearnallover/AmbiRefer3D.

paragraphs: Finding an object in a 3D scene from a spoken or written instruction becomes difficult when several objects fit the description. Traditional 3D visual grounding generally assumes that the instruction identifies a single target. This paper instead defines a task that explicitly permits ambiguous references, bringing incomplete human instructions into the problem formulation.

The proposed framework resolves ambiguity through several rounds of interaction. The model asks clarifying questions, and a person supplies answers about object attributes, spatial relationships, or other relevant context. These exchanges provide additional evidence for selecting the intended object. Asking for clarification becomes part of the grounding process rather than something excluded by the task assumptions.

The authors introduce AmbiRefer3D to support learning this behavior. It contains 47,085 samples and 141,255 question-answer dialogue annotations spanning 7,316 indoor 3D scenes. They also define evaluation measures covering both grounding accuracy and the efficiency of disambiguation across rounds. These contributions establish a way to study not just which object a system selects, but how effectively interaction helps it resolve uncertainty.
summary.tldr: AmbiRefer3D introduces a dataset and interactive framework for resolving ambiguous 3D object references through clarifying questions.

title: AmbiRefer3D: 3D Visual Grounding with Referential Ambiguity

abstract: We present tight surrogate regret bounds for the class of proper (i.e., Fisher consistent) losses. The bounds generalise the margin-based bounds due to Bartlett et al. (2006). The proof uses Taylor's theorem and leads to new representations for loss and regret and a simple proof of the integral representation of proper losses. We also present a different formulation of a duality result of Bregman divergences which leads to a demonstration of the convexity of composite losses using canonical link functions.

paragraphs: Surrogate regret bounds relate performance under a surrogate loss to the regret of the prediction task it supports. This paper establishes tight bounds for proper losses, described in the abstract as Fisher consistent. The results generalize earlier margin-based bounds, extending the theoretical treatment to this class of losses.

The proof uses Taylor's theorem and produces new representations of both loss and regret. It also gives a simple proof of an integral representation for proper losses. These representations are part of the contribution because they provide mathematical ways to express the quantities involved in the bounds and clarify the structure of the loss family.

The authors additionally reformulate a duality result for Bregman divergences. From this, they demonstrate the convexity of composite losses constructed using canonical link functions. The paper thus connects guarantees about regret with the mathematical form of loss functions and their optimization properties. Its stated findings are theoretical, combining tight bounds, representation results, and a convexity demonstration.
summary.tldr: The paper derives tight regret bounds for proper losses and connects their representations to convexity under canonical link functions.

title: Surrogate regret bounds for proper losses

abstract: We describe an algorithm for clustering using a similarity graph. Thealgorithm (a) runs in O(n log^3 n + m \log n) time on graphs withn vertices and m edges, and (b) with high probability, finds all``large enough'' clusters in a random graph generated according to theplanted partition model. We provide lower bounds that imply that our``large enough'' constraint cannot be improved much, even using acomputationally unbounded algorithm. We describe some experimentsrunning the algorithm and a few related algorithms on random graphswith partitions generated using a Chinese Restaurant Processes, andsome results of applying the algorithm to cluster DBLP titles.

paragraphs: This paper develops a clustering algorithm for data represented by a similarity graph. Its goals are computational efficiency and a provable ability to recover groups. For a graph with n vertices and m edges, the stated running time is O(n log³ n + m log n), giving nearly linear scaling up to logarithmic factors.

The recovery guarantee applies to random graphs generated by a planted partition model. Under that model, the algorithm finds all sufficiently large clusters with high probability. The size qualification is central to the result. The authors provide lower bounds showing that it cannot be improved much, even by an algorithm with unlimited computational resources.

The paper also reports experiments on random graphs whose partitions are generated using Chinese restaurant processes, alongside related algorithms, and applications to clustering DBLP titles. The theoretical contribution links efficient computation to a recovery threshold that is close to an underlying information limit. The experiments extend the investigation to generated partitions and a document-title clustering setting.
summary.tldr: A nearly linear-time graph clustering algorithm recovers sufficiently large planted clusters with high probability, near a fundamental size threshold.

title: Finding Planted Partitions in Nearly Linear Time using Arrested Spectral Clustering
